nationalKeyInfo.title: Value-based procurement is the national standard
nationalKeyInfo.detail: The DHSC / NHS England / NHS Supply Chain national standard scores medtech tenders on wider value (social value, efficiency, patient & staff, supply chain, purpose) weighted ≥60%, with whole-life cost capped at 40%. Procurement must save money AND show value.
nationalKeyInfo.use: Frame every case as value, not price. Build it in the Value Case Calculator and hand procurement a figure they can take to finance.

nationalKeyInfo.title: New NHS Supply Chain online catalogue
nationalKeyInfo.detail: A new online catalogue and search rolled out from late 2025 (search by NPC, MPC, supplier, brand, GTIN or free text).
nationalKeyInfo.use: A genuine, non-salesy opener: “how are you finding the new catalogue?”

nationalKeyInfo.title: New Hospital Programme reset
nationalKeyInfo.detail: Reset in Jan 2025 into delivery Waves 0–3; costed ~£56bn (NAO, Jan 2026). RAAC-affected trusts are prioritised in Wave 1.
nationalKeyInfo.use: If your trust has a new build, get in at design stage — equipment is specified 12–24 months before it opens.

nationalKeyInfo.title: Carbon scored at tender (Evergreen)
nationalKeyInfo.detail: NHS Supply Chain requires Evergreen Level 1 (a Carbon Reduction Plan + net-zero commitment) at tender close from 6 April 2026.
nationalKeyInfo.use: Have your carbon and sustainability position ready — it is scored, not optional.

nationalKeyInfo.title: NIHR HealthTech Research Centres — the NHS route to your own evidence
nationalKeyInfo.detail: A network of NIHR-funded centres of excellence hosted inside NHS trusts across England, set up specifically to help medical device, diagnostic, IVD and digital companies develop, evaluate and validate health technologies. They support real-world evidence generation and health economics, so a supplier can build NHS evidence with an NHS partner rather than arriving with vendor data alone. Each centre has its own clinical focus.
nationalKeyInfo.use: The answer when a trust says 'show me it works here'. If your evidence is manufacturer-run or from another health system, this is a named, credible route to NHS-generated proof — and raising it marks you out as someone who understands how the NHS actually accepts new technology.

nationalKeyInfo.title: NHS Supply Chain has a clinical assurance gate, not just a commercial one
nationalKeyInfo.detail: The Clinical and Product Assurance function (CaPA) sits inside NHS Supply Chain. Registered clinicians — nurses, midwives and allied health professionals — work across its clinical, commercial, customer engagement and strategy directorates to make sure the medical devices, products and consumables it sources meet NHS standards of safety, quality and effectiveness. Clinical judgement sits inside the sourcing process itself, not only at the trust that eventually buys.
nationalKeyInfo.use: Stop treating a framework as a purely commercial decision. Clinical evidence, usability and patient-safety arguments carry weight inside NHS Supply Chain's own sourcing process, not just with your trust. Ask how the clinical assurance for your category was done and what it looked at.

trusts.name: Ashford and St Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: Ashford and St Peter's (ASPH) is a mid-pressure elective performer against the national 92% constitutional standard. The waiting list stands at 54,116 with 62.6% treated within 18 weeks as of the RTT period June 2026, a median wait of 13.3 weeks, 735 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 83 over 65 weeks and 18 over 78 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3 and reported 2 Never Events and 64 cases of C. difficile (of which 22 were deemed trust apportioned) in 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £7,862,351 against a total backlog of £93,392,403. CQC rated the trust Good overall as of the CQC data point dated 04/08/2026 (per layer-1; see structure/news for what CQC section this covers, not independently re-verified beyond layer-1). For a rep, the combination of a mid-table elective position, a live group merger with Royal Surrey, and an incoming ICB merger (Surrey Heartlands and Sussex combining into NHS Surrey and Sussex from 1 April 2026) means the buying conversation is in flux: who signs off spend at group level is changing faster than the waiting list numbers are.
trusts.news: Turnover was £475 million in 2024/25, employing around 4,800 staff and serving a population of more than 410,000 across Runnymede, Spelthorne, Woking and parts of Elmbridge, Hounslow and Surrey Heath (source: the trust's own About the Trust page, updated 23/04/2026). The latest published Annual Report and Accounts covers 2024/25 (1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025); no 2025/26 annual report has been published yet, so no current-year (2025/26) financial position is asserted here. The 2024/25 Annual Report and Accounts PDF, the 2024/25 Auditor's Annual Report and the 2023/24 Annual Report and Accounts are all listed and linked from the trust's Annual Accounts page, but the PDF host (ashfordstpeters.net) sits behind a genuine CAPTCHA challenge (SiteGround Security 'Robot Challenge Screen') that blocked both curl with full browser headers and an automated browser session after an 8-second wait, so detailed financial facts (deficit/surplus position, cost improvement programme, capital programme) from inside the PDF are Not verified in this pass and would need a human to clear the CAPTCHA. On catering, the trust moved to a multi-supplier procurement framework brokered by Avendra International (formerly Pelican Procurement Services), launching February 2025, replacing a single-supplier model with 15-20 SMEs and specialist providers; Head of Catering Raouf Mansour is quoted describing the collaboration on Avendra's own case study page.
trusts.structure: ASPH operates a group model with Royal Surrey NHS Foundation Trust, confirmed on the trust's own live 'About the Trust' page: in 2024 the two trusts' boards agreed to establish the group, and Louise Stead was appointed Group Chief Executive of both trusts in January 2025. Both organisations state they remain legally independent, each keeping its own executive team, board and council of governors, but work under shared group leadership for strategy, transformation and pace of change. The Group Chair, Joss Bigmore, joined the NHS in March 2023 as Chair of Royal Surrey and was appointed ASPH's own Chair in February 2026, so he now chairs both trust boards. ASPH is also one of four members of the Surrey Heartlands Trust Provider Collaborative (TPC), established July 2023 alongside Royal Surrey, Surrey and Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust and Surrey and Borders Partnership Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust, working jointly on elective care, maternity, acute paediatrics, endoscopy, mental health and systemic anti-cancer therapy (source: trust's own About the Trust page). On procurement specifically: the trust's own Supplies and Procurement page states appointments for supplier representatives go through its own Procurement Department (for goods/services) or Pharmacy Department (for pharmaceuticals), led by an Associate Director of Procurement, Melvyn Lake, named on that page. There is no statement on that page, or found elsewhere, of a shared or group-level procurement function with Royal Surrey or a Surrey Heartlands/Frimley collaborative for core goods procurement, so on the evidence available ASPH buys through its own trust procurement department, not a shared collaborative buying function, though catering specifically is now run through the Avendra-brokered multi-supplier framework described above. Not verified: whether a group-level procurement function is planned as the Royal Surrey group model matures; the trust's own procurement page as it stands does not describe one.

trusts.name: Barking, Havering and Redbridge University Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: Queen's Hospital in Romford and King George Hospital in Goodmayes, serving one of the fastest-growing populations in England. Financially this is a turnaround account: a reported deficit of £30.7m in 2024/25 sitting on an underlying deficit of £46m, with an adjusted financial performance deficit of £38.9m against £6.1m the year before. The recovery plan requires savings of £61m, equal to 6% of income. Leadership is unusually thin on permanence — Chief Executive, Chief Operating Officer and Chief People Officer are all interim as at 14/08/2026 — so expect decisions to take longer and large commitments to need more cover than usual.
trusts.news: The Board has a Finance, Investment and Performance Committee scrutinising delivery of the financial recovery plan and savings programme, chaired by Sue Lees. The trust's own recovery narrative names right-sizing medical staffing and slippage in medical premium savings as the problems to fix, and commits to “further efficiency programmes to maintain and ensure high function performance across all core theatre capacity”. Board papers for 2026/27 are published four days before each meeting but the trust's document library does not expose them directly, so the current-year financial position could not be verified here — the £61m figure is the plan set out in the 2024/25 annual report.
trusts.structure: Payment performance has deteriorated sharply and it matters if you are carrying stock: 83.1% of non-NHS invoices paid within target by volume in 2024/25, down from 91.5% the year before, and 87.4% by value against 96.2%. That is the largest single-year fall in payment performance of any trust profiled in the Hub, and it is consistent with a trust managing cash through a deficit. Spend over £30,000 is published monthly. The Finance, Investment and Performance Committee is the body scrutinising the savings programme, so proposals framed as recovery-plan contributions have a named audience. Not verified: the size and structure of the procurement team, the e-tendering portal used, and whether a rep booking or accreditation system operates — none is published on the trust's site.

trusts.name: Barts Health NHS Trust
trusts.context: The largest trust in east London and one of the biggest in the country, with 121,464 on the waiting list but a comparatively controlled position behind it — 63.9% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 12.9 weeks and 1,095 people over 52 weeks. It has just turned a corner financially: 2025/26 closed at a surplus of £24k against the prior year's £11.7m deficit, and the trust achieved an NHS Oversight Framework rating of Segment 1 in Quarter 4. That surplus is razor-thin — a rounding error on turnover — so treat this as a trust that has fought its way to breakeven, not one with money to spare. Capital, by contrast, is substantial and rising: £173m invested in infrastructure and equipment in 2025/26, up from £118.7m.
trusts.news: Barts runs four hospitals each with its own chief executive and its own executive board — St Bartholomew's, The Royal London and Mile End, Newham, and Whipps Cross — so a trust-wide pitch has four internal customers and a site-level conversation has a named owner. A £16m Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme at Newham Hospital has entered active delivery, expected to generate recurrent energy savings of around £174k a year. The trust is also a partner in the roughly £800m Whitechapel life sciences cluster alongside private investors BGO, Lateral and H.I.G. The trust warns of “continued financial pressures in the year ahead as national reforms and system changes begin to take effect”, with emphasis on productivity, long-term workforce sustainability and accelerated adoption of digital innovation.
trusts.structure: Two things matter commercially. First, social value is measured and reported here as a procurement output, not an aspiration: over £17.15m of social value was generated through the trust's procurement system in 2025/26. A tender response that cannot evidence social value is competing badly at this trust. Second, Barts is part of the recently launched North East London Procurement Partnership, so establish early whether your category is bought by Barts alone or across the NEL sector — the answer changes the size of the prize and who you should be talking to. The annual plan and capital programme are structured to align explicitly with stated priorities, and the trust describes stronger integration between estates, facilities, clinical teams, procurement, digital and corporate functions, with sustainable procurement and supply-chain transformation named as workstreams. The audit and risk committee oversees cost improvement programmes alongside the revenue plan and capital programme. Not verified: no e-tendering portal or supplier representative booking system is published on the trust's public site, and not publishing one is not proof there isn't one.

trusts.name: Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: A two-site trust formed by the 2020 merger of Luton and Dunstable University Hospital and Bedford Hospital, around 9,000 staff, in NHS oversight segment 3. The access position is difficult — 82,592 on the waiting list, 59.1% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 14.6 weeks and 731 people over 52 weeks. Financially it runs at the line: an adjusted financial performance surplus of £415k in 2024/25 on operating expenses of £908m, with the statutory deficit driven by the impairment of new buildings brought into use during the year. The trust has a named turnaround function that has already gone after theatre and outpatient productivity, and it says non-pay cost is the focus area for 2025/26 — which is precisely where a supplier proposition lands.
trusts.news: Pippa Nightingale has taken over as Chief Executive, arriving from London North West University Healthcare where she led the trust out of special measures and delivered financial breakeven across three acute sites; her background is as a registered midwife and she was awarded an MBE for services to nursing and midwifery leadership. The trust's Financial Turnaround Team identified 66 schemes worth £23.6m, covering theatre productivity, outpatient productivity, reducing out-of-hours operating and demand management in pathology and imaging — and the trust makes a point of having done it “on sustainable improvements rather than using external consultants”. That work has become a Strategic Financial Planning programme with a named lead. Not verified: the 2025/26 annual report and accounts had not been published when this profile was written, so no current-year outturn is stated.
trusts.structure: Procurement is held directly by the Director of Finance. Matt Gibbons's published board responsibilities are Finance, Financial Management, Procurement and Sustainability Champion — so finance, buying and the sustainability agenda sit with one person, and a case that covers all three at once is talking to a single owner. He has been in post since October 2019 and joined the organisation in 2002, so expect deep familiarity with the existing supplier base. Clinical Directors are a joint responsibility of the Medical Director and the Deputy Chief Executive, and the Medical Director, Mr Paul Tisi, explicitly owns GIRFT — a vascular and general surgeon by background, which matters if you sell into vascular or general surgery. Cathy Jones as Deputy Chief Executive holds clinical service lines, operational management, performance and business development. One stated gap worth knowing: the trust reports “a lack of a unified Electronic Patient Record system across sites” and limited interoperability with external partners, which shapes any digital or data-dependent proposition. Board correspondence goes through Victoria Parsons, Associate Director of Corporate Governance and Company Secretary, at Nova House, Luton and Dunstable University Hospital. Not verified: no e-tendering portal or supplier representative booking system is published on the trust's public site, and not publishing one is not proof there isn't one.

trusts.name: Birmingham Community Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: A community trust, so it files no consultant-led RTT return and carries no acute oversight segment — the data panel above will be thinner than for an acute trust, and that is correct rather than missing. Its own waiting position is comparatively good: 80.2% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 8.7 weeks and nobody over 52 weeks on a 14,961 list. The single most important fact about selling here is that BCHC does not run its own procurement. It receives procurement support on a shared basis from the BSol Procurement Collaborative, hosted by University Hospitals Birmingham, which buys for five trusts across the whole Birmingham and Solihull ICS. Win the category at BSol and you have addressed five organisations; lose it and BCHC is not a separate route back in.
trusts.news: BCHC reported a £2.6m surplus on the adjusted control-total basis for 2024/25 against a statutory deficit of £1.7m, but its cost improvement programme under-delivered — 84.5% of the year-to-date plan against a 95% target — while the capital programme over-delivered at 96.87% against a 90% target. External auditor Mazars identified no significant weaknesses in the trust's arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Not verified: the 2025/26 annual report and accounts had not been published on the trust's site when this profile was written, so no current-year outturn is stated here.
trusts.structure: Procurement is delivered by the BSol Procurement Collaborative, hosted by University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust and serving UHB, Birmingham Women's and Children's, the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital, Birmingham Community Healthcare and Birmingham and Solihull Mental Health — one of the first procurement teams in the country to work across an entire ICS, and winner of the HCSA 2023 Procurement and Supply Chain Team of the Year. It is led by Simon Clarke, Managing Director, whose senior management team reports into a quarterly Partnership Board and chairs the BSol Procurement Collaborative Operational Delivery Group. It holds a 'Good' CCIAF accreditation. The team is published in five parts, each with its own generic inbox, so a supplier can address the right function directly: Strategic Procurement (BSOLCategoryTeams@uhb.nhs.uk), which agrees CIP targets with finance leads, writes strategic sourcing documents for major projects and produces contract award reports; the Clinical Procurement Specialist team (ProcurementCPSTeam@uhb.nhs.uk), clinical experts reporting to a Head of Clinical Procurement who source alternatives during stockouts and national shortages and drive standardisation across the ICS; Data Analytics, Catalogue and Systems (ProcurementData@uhb.nhs.uk), which owns the BSol Master Products Catalogue — the route to getting a product code listed; Transactional Procurement (BSOLProcurementBuyers@uhb.nhs.uk), with set buyers per trust across six different ordering systems; and Pharmacy Procurement (Pharmacy.Procurement@uhb.nhs.uk). The Collaborative is based at 1 Regent Court, George Road, Edgbaston, Birmingham B15 1NU. Contracts are awarded in compliance with procurement law, trust standing financial instructions and the scheme of delegation. Not verified: whether a rep booking or accreditation system operates — none is published by BCHC or the Collaborative, and not publishing one is not proof there isn't one.

trusts.name: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: A mid-sized teaching trust serving around 667,000 people across seven sites, in NHS oversight segment 3, with a comparatively contained access position — 69.3% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 10.9 weeks and 55 people over 52 weeks on a 31,604 list. It beat its financial plan in 2024/25, closing a £4.9m deficit against a planned £9.7m, but the year ahead is much harder: a projected £17m deficit for 2025/26 requiring £33m of productivity savings. The opening is capital rather than revenue — three named new-build schemes are in flight, and all three are directly relevant to devices and consumables.
trusts.news: The trust names three new capital developments as live opportunities to improve services: a new Community Diagnostic Centre, a dedicated day case unit at St Luke's Hospital, and a new endoscopy suite. Financial governance runs through a programme the trust calls 'Closing the Gap', alongside development of an Estates Strategy and prioritisation of backlog maintenance. Internal audit during the year covered Estates Procurement (BH48 2024) and Procurement and Business Cases (BH25 2025), so procurement process is under active internal scrutiny. Not verified: the 2025/26 annual report and accounts had not been published when this profile was written, so no current-year outturn is stated.
trusts.structure: Procurement is unambiguously a finance function here. The trust's own table of executive directors' key responsibilities puts Finance, Procurement, Contracting and Capital all under the Chief Finance Officer — so the CFO is the accountable owner of a buying decision, not a distant approver, and a business case that reads as a finance case will travel further than one that reads as a clinical wish. Estates, the Capital Programme, Clinical Engineering and Sustainability sit together under the Director of Estates and Facilities, which is the route for equipment, maintenance and backlog cases. The trust also works with West Yorkshire partners on joint projects spanning procurement, so check whether a category is bought at West Yorkshire level before assuming it is a Bradford decision. One observable quirk worth knowing: five of the seventeen Bradford buyer contacts in the Hub's own contacts data were named on notices whose title begins 'Waiver' — single-tender waivers published as award notices — and no other trust in this batch shows any. That is counted over published notice titles only, and it is a signal about how contracts here get published, not proof of how they get awarded. Not verified: no e-tendering portal, procurement team structure or supplier representative booking system is confirmed — the trust's public website is behind bot protection and could not be read directly, so none of this could be checked on the live site.

trusts.name: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: Cambridge University Hospitals (Addenbrooke's and the Rosie Hospital) carries a waiting list of 59,372 with 65.0% of patients treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 11.5 weeks, 922 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 51 over 65 weeks and 2 over 78 weeks (RTT data to June 2026). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 2. It reported 6 Never Events (April 2025 to March 2026) and 138 cases of C. difficile against a total of 222 (2024/25). High-risk backlog maintenance stands at £29,102,774 against a total backlog maintenance bill of £238,059,284, with capital cost to eradicate high and significant risk backlog of £18,186,341. For a rep this reads as a trust with a comparatively better elective performance than many peers but a live estate-risk problem and an active Never Events count that puts patient safety and infrastructure investment on the table alongside routine elective capacity conversations.
trusts.news: The Trust's 2024/25 Annual Report and Accounts (the latest published; no 2025/26 report is out yet) records a statutory deficit of £14.3m for the year, which includes a £27.4m impairment of the Trust's estate arising from a 'modern equivalent asset (alternative site)' revaluation methodology rather than deterioration in the physical estate. Excluding that and other non-recurrent adjustments, the Trust's Adjusted Financial Performance for the year, as defined by NHS England, was a small surplus of £0.05m, which the report states is the fifth consecutive year the Trust has achieved breakeven or better on that adjusted basis. Operating income rose by £188m in 2024/25 to £1,627m. Capital additions in year were £91.8m (up from £74.1m in 2023/24), and cash reserves stood at £100.7m as at 31 March 2025, down from £139.6m a year earlier. The Board Assurance Framework in the same report names an active risk that the Trust fails to work effectively with regional partners, particularly on specialised services, resulting in 'regulatory intervention and/or the recurrence of a financial deficit' (risk ref 014/C1), and a separate live risk (009b/C3) around 'Addenbrooke's 3' capital redevelopment proposals beyond the already-approved Cambridge Children's Hospital and Cambridge Cancer Research Hospital schemes. Source: Annual Report and Accounts 2024-25, https://media.cuh.nhs.uk/documents/Annual_Report_and_Accounts_2024-25_1.pdf (sections 2.6 and Board Assurance Framework table).
trusts.structure: CUH runs its own procurement function rather than buying through a group or lead trust. The Trust's own finance and procurement page (cuh.nhs.uk) lists product sourcing, supplier and contract management, materials management and eCommerce as in-house responsibilities, gives a dedicated procurement contact (cuh.procurement@nhs.net) and a separate tenders contact, and confirms the Trust runs its own Bravo e-tendering system under its own standing financial instructions. A regional body, the East of England Collaborative Procurement Hub, exists and covers Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Essex, Hertfordshire, Norfolk and Suffolk, but the Hub's own about-us page does not list its member organisations, so CUH's membership of it is Not verified from a primary source; this profile treats CUH as procuring for itself unless and until that is confirmed. No evidence was found of any group or shared-executive arrangement between CUH and Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust (RT1); the two are treated as separate, unlinked trusts in this batch and no such link should be assumed. CQC's overall rating for the Trust, shown live on its own provider page (cqc.org.uk/provider/RGT) as 'Good', is worth flagging as dated: the rating displayed is dated 26 February 2019, from an inspection carried out 30 October to 29 November 2018, so while it is the current live published rating it is not a recent reassessment. A 2023 CQC inspection separately rated the Trust's maternity services 'Requires improvement', which does not itself change the trust-wide overall rating shown.

trusts.name: Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: Chelsea and Westminster is a large, well-rated London acute trust carrying a big list rather than a broken one. The waiting list stands at 73,514 (NHS England referral to treatment, June 2026), with 68.0% treated within 18 weeks against the constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 12.6 weeks, 915 patients waiting over 52 weeks and none over 65 or 78 weeks. CQC rates the trust Good (rating current as at 04/08/2026) and NHS England places it in oversight segment 1, the lowest-scrutiny tier. Infection control shows 49 C. difficile cases counted against the trust in 2024/25 within 94 cases reported in total. The Hub's data layer carries no Never Events count for this trust for April 2025 to March 2026, so none is asserted here. On the estate (ERIC 2024/25) the trust reports total backlog maintenance of £22,691,320 with nothing classified as high risk, and capital investment in medical equipment of £5,034,157. Read together that is an unusual commercial profile. Segment 1 and a Good rating mean the trust is not being told what to buy by a regional improvement team, so it has more genuine discretion than a segment 3 or 4 trust, and the estate is not eating the capital. The pressure is volume: a very long list with almost no ultra-long waiters, which means the argument that lands is throughput per session, day-case conversion and diagnostic turnaround, not backlog rescue. The specialities with the longest median waits are Trauma and Orthopaedics (16.6 weeks), ENT (16.4), General Surgery (15.7), Ophthalmology (13.9) and Urology (13.2), all June 2026, and those five are where a capacity or productivity proposition has a number attached to it. A medical equipment capital line of over £5m in a single year is a real budget, not a token one.
trusts.news: The trust's own Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25 reports an adjusted surplus of £0.11m against a breakeven control total, an overall reported deficit of £5.2m for the year before adding back £5.0m of impairment reversals and £0.3m of other adjustments, and full delivery of a £23.5m cost improvement programme. Its external auditor, Deloitte LLP, reported nothing by exception on use of resources, saying in terms 'We have nothing to report in respect of this matter'. That is a materially healthier audit position than most acute trusts of this size. Capital spend in 2024/25 was £63.5m, made up of £19.9m on the Chelsea and Westminster Treatment Centre, £16.1m on the Ambulatory Diagnostic Centre at West Middlesex, £2.8m on the Neptune Ward refurbishment, £13.6m on estates works and maintenance across both sites, £5.0m on medical equipment and £5.8m on IT goods and services. The report states the enhanced Day Surgery Unit at Chelsea and Westminster was set to open in June 2025 and will incorporate surgical robotics, and that the five-storey Ambulatory Diagnostic Centre at West Middlesex will double capacity for cancer, renal and imaging services, with completion planned in 2026. Fresher than the accounts: the North West London Acute Provider Group Board in Common public pack of 28 April 2026 carries the three-year operating plans submitted to NHS England on 12 February 2026 and resubmitted on 18 March 2026. For this trust (CWFT in the pack's own shorthand) they show a breakeven income and expenditure plan for 2026/27 with an efficiency requirement of £33.442m (3.1%), then planned deficits of £6.6m in 2027/28 and £4.0m in 2028/29, and a 2026/27 capital delegated expenditure limit of £40.656m including £7.25m of cash-backed public dividend capital for diagnostics. The pack records that CWFT previously held a £32m capital system reserve on behalf of the integrated care board and in the final 18 March submission included only its own £5.6m share. On the clinical side, the 2024/25 report says the trust became the first hospital globally to deploy an autonomous artificial intelligence teledermatology service for skin cancer assessment, launched at the Chelsea and Westminster site in December 2024, developed by Skin Analytics and supported by CW Innovation, which it says frees up over 35% of specialist appointments.
trusts.structure:
Two things decide how you sell here, and neither of them is the trust's own procurement department. First, buying is done through a shared service the trust does not host. The trust's 2024/25 annual report refers to 'our procurement colleagues at NWL Procurement' in its sustainability section, and Central London Community Healthcare NHS Trust's own news page states that North West London Procurement Services 'will provide a single shared service for nine NHS partner organisations', is 'hosted centrally by Central London Community Healthcare NHS Trust (CLCH)' and is 'governed by a Board consisting of Chief Financial Officer representatives from each organisation'. The nine named partners include Chelsea and Westminster alongside Imperial College Healthcare, London North West University Healthcare, The Hillingdon Hospitals, the Royal Marsden, West London, CNWL, CLCH itself and the North West London ICB. A supplier winning here is therefore transacting inside a nine-organisation buying function, and the first approach is to that function, not to a Chelsea and Westminster purchasing officer.

Second, the trust sits inside a four-trust group. Its own live board page states that as part of the North West London Acute Provider Group the trust 'operates within a Board in Common (BIC) arrangement across the four partner organisations', bringing together the full boards of Chelsea and Westminster, Imperial College Healthcare, The Hillingdon Hospitals and London North West University Healthcare, and that 'A single Chair and Group Chief Executive are appointed across the four trusts', while 'each Trust remains a separate organisation with its own statutory responsibilities'. The 2024/25 annual report adds that the collaborative was approved in July 2022 and came into being on 1 September 2022. Practically, strategy, operating plans, efficiency targets and capital limits are set and published at group level, in one public pack covering all four trusts, while the individual trust board still owns its own statutory decisions.

Third, and this is the part most reps miss, there is a second route to capital here that is genuinely unusual in size. CW+ is the trust's official charity. The trust's own annual report says 'The Trust is committed to actively promoting and supporting CW+, and several directors of the Trust Board are CW+ Trustees', and the live board page lists the CW+ Chief Executive Officer as a non-voting director in attendance at the trust board. The charity's Impact Report 2024/25 reports total income of £7,722,000, total expenditure of £9,452,000 and £2,492,000 spent on its grants programme, awarding 310 grants in the year, and names equipment among what those grants bought, including rehabilitation equipment for the stroke unit at West Middlesex University Hospital. Its live grants page sets out the current tiers, the largest being Big Ideas at £10,000 to £25,000 'For projects that promote new clinical innovations, services, facilities and technologies, including pilots to develop business cases in the Trust'. That last clause is the commercial point: the charity will fund the pilot that builds the trust's own business case. The page also says 'Projects over £10,000 need to get all appropriate endorsements from the Trust (IC, IT, Medical Equipment, etc)' and that 'The project must meet all Trust regulations, including IPC, IG, procurement procedures etc', so a charity-funded purchase still lands in the normal procurement route, it is just funded from outside the capital limit. Only trust staff can apply, so a rep's job is to equip a clinician to apply, never to apply themselves.

No published rep booking or access system was found on the trust's website. The only supplier-facing procurement page found on the trust domain is a procurement exemption list, which sets out which goods and services are exempt from the trust's 'no PO, no pay' policy and names no contact.

Not verified: whether Chelsea and Westminster retains any independent clinical product sign-off where North West London Procurement Services has awarded across the nine partners, or whether a collaborative award binds it; the shared service's own governance terms of reference, or a direct enquiry to the service, would settle this.
Not verified: the current Managing Director of North West London Procurement Services. The only published name found is Lee Jackson, on a CLCH news page dated 21/04/2023, which is over three years old; the service's own current contact page, or a fresh CLCH staff listing, would settle this.
Not verified: whether the joint chief executive arrangement with The Hillingdon Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is still in force. The 2024/25 annual report records that Lesley Watts took up the role of Joint Chief Executive for both trusts from 13 January 2025 and was appointed Single Accountable Officer for both, but the live board page read on 28/08/2026 describes her only as Trust Chief Executive Officer of Chelsea and Westminster and makes no mention of Hillingdon; a current group scheme of delegation, or a Board in Common paper naming the post, would settle this.
Not verified: the maximum single grant CW+ will now award. The trust's 2024/25 annual report says staff 'can apply for grant funding up to £50,000 for any single major project', while the charity's live grants page read on 28/08/2026 shows a top standard tier of £10,000 to £25,000. Both are reported here with their dates rather than reconciled; the CW+ Trustees' Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, or the grants team, would settle it.
Not verified: any 2025/26 outturn. No 2025/26 annual report or accounts have been published by this trust, so no current-year outturn is asserted. The freshest published financial position used here is the April 2026 Board in Common plan pack, which is a plan, not an outturn.

reportFacts.fact: The trust's official charity is a second, separate route to capital, and the group's own capital plan says so in its own words. Charitable donations and grants sit outside the capital limit entirely, so a charity-funded purchase does not compete with the trust's capital programme. For a rep this is the single most useful structural fact about this account.

trusts.name: County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: As of the June 2026 RTT reporting period, the waiting list stands at 53,455 with 65.5% treated within 18 weeks, well below the 92% constitutional standard. Median wait is 11.7 weeks, with 943 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 24 over 65 weeks and no breaches over 78 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier. Specialty-level 52-week breach rates are highest in Dermatology (16.4%), General Surgery (13.1%) and Gynaecology (11.8%). C. difficile cases stood at 50 against a trajectory of 156 for 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £3,386,913 against a total estate backlog of £43,987,084, and capital-funded backlog equipment need is £2,870,015. For a rep, that combination points to elective throughput and diagnostic capacity as the live pressure, with segment 4 oversight meaning spending has to be argued on activity delivered or cost released.
trusts.news: The Boards of County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust (CDDFT) and South Tyneside and Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust (STSFT) confirmed a strategic alliance on 11/05/2026, covering a combined population of over 1 million people and around 15,000 staff across more than 1,000 square miles in the centre of the North East. CDDFT's own account of the alliance states plainly that both trusts remain separate legal entities, each keeping its own statutory Board, responsibilities and accountability structures: this is a collaboration agreement, not a merger or a shared-board group model. Stated aims are safe, high-quality care with good outcomes, supporting staff to innovate and develop, shaping services around future need, and better use of NHS resources, framed as supporting the NHS 10-Year Plan's shift towards community-based, prevention-focused and digitally enabled care. CDDFT Chief Executive Steve Russell is quoted: the alliance is 'an important and positive step for both organisations'. The same announcement records shared clinical leadership appointments spanning both trusts, including Dr Eliot Sykes as Chief Medical Officer and Gill Hunt as substantive Chief Nurse, plus Lorraine Nelson seconded as Alliance Director to oversee how the collaboration develops. Steve Russell himself took up post as CDDFT Chief Executive on 29/09/2025, succeeding Sue Jacques, who retired after more than a decade leading the trust. Source: https://www.cddft.nhs.uk/about-us/news/nhs-trusts-confirm-strategic-alliance-heart-north-east and https://www.cddft.nhs.uk/about-us/news/new-chief-executive-appointed-county-durham-and-darlington-nhs-foundation-trust
trusts.structure: CDDFT runs its estates, facilities and procurement through a wholly owned subsidiary company, Synchronicity Care Limited (SCL), which the trust's own subsidiaries page describes as providing 'high quality estates, facilities and procurement services'. SCL is legally separate from the trust (it is audited separately, per the 2024/25 annual report and CDDFT's external audit tender, which covers 'the Trust, its Charity, and its wholly owned subsidiary'), but exists to support CDDFT rather than acting as a cross-trust group procurement collaborative: no separate CDDFT procurement or tenders webpage was found, and no evidence was found of CDDFT buying through a joint procurement hub shared with other trusts. SCL also holds at least one contract with a third-party PFI landlord (soft FM services at University Hospital of North Durham, awarded July 2023, per the annual report), so it does generate some non-CDDFT income, but the trust's own clinical and non-clinical purchasing runs through this subsidiary rather than directly through the trust's board structure. The 11/05/2026 strategic alliance with South Tyneside and Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust is a collaboration agreement between two boards that each remain separate and statutorily distinct; it is not evidence, on the sources checked, of any shared procurement, shared board, or group leadership model of the kind seen at some other North East trusts. Not verified: whether CDDFT's alliance with STSFT will in time extend to joint procurement; nothing on either trust's own site currently states that.

trusts.name: Doncaster and Bassetlaw Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: As of the June 2026 RTT reporting period, Doncaster and Bassetlaw Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust held a waiting list of 54,323 patients, with 64.1% seen within 18 weeks. 1,445 patients were waiting over 52 weeks, 69 over 65 weeks and 5 over 78 weeks; the median wait was 12.2 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. C. difficile cases stood at 47 against a trajectory of 167 for 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance was valued at £15,827,781 out of a total estate backlog of £151,328,533, against capital equipment of £22,293,000. The trust's most recent published CQC inspection (fieldwork August-September 2023, published 28 March 2024) rated it Requires Improvement overall, with Caring rated Good and Safe, Effective, Responsive and Well-led all rated Requires Improvement; this is the current live rating with no more recent CQC report published as at this check (28/08/2026).
trusts.news: The trust's leadership changed twice within 2026: Mark Bailey, previously a Non-Executive Director since February 2020 and Chair of the Trust's People Committee, became Chair of the Board in January 2026, and Richard Jenkins is Interim Chief Executive as at August 2026, following Richard Parker OBE's retirement. These are confirmed from the trust's own live Board of Directors page; earlier reporting naming Suzy Brain England as Chair and Zara Jones as Acting Chief Executive is now superseded. Not verified: the exact date Richard Parker's tenure ended or the date Richard Jenkins started, as the live page does not state transition dates beyond 'August 2026' next to Richard Jenkins's title.
trusts.structure: DBTH runs three main hospital sites: Doncaster Royal Infirmary (500+ beds, 24-hour Emergency Department, trauma unit), Bassetlaw Hospital (170+ beds, 24-hour Emergency Department) and Montagu Hospital (50+ inpatient beds, non-acute/rehabilitation), plus outpatient services at Retford Hospital, Sandringham Road Clinic and Devonshire House. The trust states it serves more than 440,000 people across South Yorkshire, North Nottinghamshire and surrounding areas, and trains 25% of the region's medical students and 30% of other healthcare professional students as a teaching trust. On procurement: the trust runs its own Procurement Department (Head of Procurement: Richard Somerset, r.somerset@nhs.net), using an e-tendering portal ('Atamis', under the 'Working Together NHS' banner) for frameworks, formal tendering and quotes over £5,000, so DBTH buys for itself rather than through a fully centralised group. Alongside this, DBTH participates in the South Yorkshire Acute Federation's collaborative procurement and mutual aid programme: its 2024/25 Annual Report states this delivered over £1.16 million in collaborative procurement savings and supported 560+ patients into faster elective care via mutual aid across partner trusts in South Yorkshire. The South Yorkshire ICS procurement page confirms this is a collaborative-alongside model, not a replacement: 'the bulk of these purchases are made through the procurement teams that sit within each Acute, Mental Health and Clinical Commissioning group', with the collaborative adding negotiated system-wide contracts and standardisation on top.

trusts.name: East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: East Kent is one of the most pressured trusts in the South East on every measure the national publishers record. NHS England's Referral to Treatment return for June 2026 shows a waiting list of 82,363 with only 56.1% treated within 18 weeks, against the constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 15.5 weeks, 2,462 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 166 over 65 weeks and 12 over 78 weeks. Median waits by speciality in the same return are worst in Trauma and Orthopaedics at 20.0 weeks and ENT at 19.1 weeks, then Cardiology at 17.2, Gynaecology at 14.8, General Surgery at 14.3, Ophthalmology at 12.4, Urology at 10.1 and Dermatology at 9.5. The Care Quality Commission rating held on 04/08/2026 was Requires Improvement, and the trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier. It reported 8 Never Events in the year April 2025 to March 2026, which is a high count for a single trust, and 73 C. difficile cases in 2024/25 against a total of 229 for its category in the same return. The 2024/25 Estates Returns Information Collection records high-risk backlog maintenance of £86,727,747 within a total backlog of £239,886,177, and capital investment in medical equipment of £1,199,210 in that year. Commercially that combination is unusually legible. Long orthopaedic, ENT and cardiology waits with a median wait above 15 weeks put throughput, day-case conversion and theatre productivity on the agenda; 8 Never Events puts surgical safety, counting, labelling and never-event-prevention systems on it; and a high-risk backlog of £86.7m against £1.2m of medical equipment capital in the same year tells you the estate is consuming the money that equipment renewal would otherwise take. Segment 4 is the constraint on all of it. Every spend is visible to NHS England, so a case argued on activity delivered, length of stay released or recurrent cash saved will be heard, and a case argued on preference will not.
trusts.news: The Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25 carries an external auditor exception report naming two significant weaknesses that were first identified on 23 June 2023 and were still live at the 2024/25 assessment. The first is financial sustainability: the auditors record that the trust achieved its agreed 2024/25 deficit of £7.4m but only with £78.5m of deficit funding behind it, that the Cost Improvement Plan for 2025/26 still had a large volume of unidentified schemes, and that the medium-term financial plan required finalising, with a recommendation to reach breakeven by the end of 2027/28. The second is governance, specifically how the trust makes informed decisions and manages risk in the light of significant cultural and leadership challenges; the auditors note the highest ever staff survey response rate but no significant improvement in scores. The Group consolidated deficit for 2024/25 was £16.3m against £153m the year before, adjusted to £7.4m after impairments and donated income. Since then the board's own papers have moved considerably further. The Interim Chair's Report to the Board of Directors on 28 July 2026 states that the trust remains subject to additional licence conditions under Section 111 of the Health and Social Care Act 2012 and to Enforcement Undertakings accepted under Section 106 of the same Act, remains in oversight segment 4 following the publication of the NHS Oversight Framework 2026/27 on 11 June 2026, and is one of five organisations receiving support through NHS England's Intensive Recovery Programme. An Integrated Improvement Plan is due to NHS England by 30 September 2026. Leadership is in transition: recruitment of a substantive Chair and further substantive Non-Executive Directors is under way through the Council of Governors with interviews planned for September 2026, and the route to recruiting a substantive Chief Executive has been confirmed. On services, the Finance and Performance Committee assurance report in the same pack records that the trust achieved its revised 2025/26 year-end position with £60m of savings and a deficit of approximately £49m, and that the 2026/27 Cost Improvement Programme target is around £76m alongside a need for around 730 whole time equivalent reductions. The Care Quality Commission rated urgent and emergency care at William Harvey Hospital as Requires Improvement following an unannounced inspection in February 2026, rated Good for Caring, Effective and Well-Led and Requires Improvement for Safe and Responsive. On maternity, the 2024/25 annual report records that the CQC inspected maternity at William Harvey and Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother in December 2024 and rated both Good overall, up from Inadequate, and the trust's own commitment to embedding the lessons of the Reading the Signals report published by Dr Bill Kirkup in 2022. The Acting Chief Executive Officer's Report of 28 July 2026 records that East Kent was one of twelve NHS trusts selected for Baroness Amos's independent national maternity and neonatal services investigation, whose final report and individual trust reports have now been published, and that the report identifies improvements made since Reading the Signals while also highlighting concerns raised by families and staff. The same report announces that East Kent has become the first NHS trust to pilot MEMORI, an artificial intelligence infection-risk tool developed with UK health technology company Sanome, on Harvey Ward at Kent and Canterbury Hospital, co-designed with clinical teams and integrated into the Sunrise electronic patient record.
trusts.structure: East Kent does not buy the way a standalone acute trust buys, and getting this wrong will send a rep to the wrong door. The trust is the parent of a Group. Its 2024/25 accounts consolidate two wholly owned subsidiaries: Healthex Limited, parent of Spencer Private Hospitals Limited, which runs a private hospital; and 2gether Support Solutions Limited, established as a Property Facilities Management Company providing an Operated Healthcare Facility to the trust. 2gether commenced trading on 1 August 2018 with the full Operated Healthcare Facility effective 1 October 2018, and under the supporting agreements the trust sold assets including land, buildings and equipment to 2gether in 2018 and now leases them back. That structure shows up directly in the accounts: Note 7 Operating Expenses reports Supplies and services - general of £25,998,000 at Group level but £151,400,000 at trust level, because the trust's payments into the subsidiary sit in the trust column and are eliminated on consolidation. The practical consequence is that estates, facilities and capital works are procured by the subsidiary, not by the trust. The Find a Tender award notice for Major capital works at East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust, published 3 October 2025, names the buyer as 2Gether Support Solutions Limited, with lots for general projects, higher-value projects, mechanical works and electrical works up to £10,000,000. Anything touching the estate, plant, theatres as buildings, or installed equipment routes through 2gether. Clinical consumables and drugs stay with the trust and are large: Group clinical supplies of £112,282,000 and drug costs of £101,184,000 in 2024/25. Above the trust sits the Kent and Medway system. The Kent and Medway Pathology Network assurance report to the board records a phased pathology Joint Venture across the system, with Phase 2 single management and governance now largely complete and a fully integrated single service Joint Venture targeted for April 2027, hosted by Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust for the next two years with a longer-term hosting decision still to be taken. Any pathology or laboratory proposition is therefore a system conversation hosted elsewhere, not an East Kent one. The Acute Provider Collaborative's agreed 2026/27 priorities, set out in the Provider Alliance update to the 28 July 2026 board, include referral management across at least ten specialities naming gastroenterology, Trauma and Orthopaedics and MSK, ophthalmology, ENT and neurology, moving to single patient tracking lists, radiology with an immediate focus on consolidation or single management, reducing independent sector use and repatriating activity from outside Kent, and cancer centre, oncology and chemotherapy. Diagnostic imaging is explicitly being taken to an acute provider collaborative approach across Kent and Medway. Medicines optimisation is recorded as being led by the Chief Pharmacists group and digital by the CDIO group, both outside the collaborative's own programme. For access, the trust publishes monthly transparency-in-spending reports listing every invoice over £25,000, the latest being July 2026, which is the most reliable public route to seeing who it already pays and at what scale. Not verified: the name, structure and size of the trust's own procurement team. The trust has no live procurement or supplier page (both /about-us/procurement/ and /health-professionals/procurement/ return 404 as at 28/08/2026), and its Freedom of Information page states in its own words that it will not publish details of contracts currently tendered or the list and value of contracts awarded, citing commercial confidentiality, and directs enquirers to contact the trust; the trust's Standing Financial Instructions, which it says contain the tendering procedures, or a direct FOI request would settle the team structure and thresholds. Not verified: whether the trust operates any published rep booking, credentialing or access system. Nothing on the live site describes one as at 28/08/2026 and no board paper found says so; the procurement team or the medical devices group would settle this. Not verified: any procurement contact by name. Layer 1 holds no named contact for RVV and no notice examined gave a named individual, only the generic mailbox published on the trust's own pages. Not verified: any 2025/26 published annual report or accounts. The 2024/25 Annual Report and Accounts is the latest published as at 28/08/2026, so no audited 2025/26 outturn is asserted here; the £60m savings and approximately £49m deficit figures quoted above are the Finance and Performance Committee's own reported position in a board assurance report, not audited accounts. Not verified: the substantive occupancy of the Chief Executive post. The live board page names an Acting Chief Executive and the board's own papers say substantive recruitment is in progress.

reportFacts.fact: This is the single most actionable capital fact about East Kent. NHS England handed the trust money specifically to buy two more surgical robots, taking it from three systems to five across all three main sites, and the business case names consumables as the principal ongoing revenue cost. For any surgical device, instrument or consumables rep, robotic-assisted surgery here is funded, board-approved and expanding across multiple specialities, and the recurring consumable spend is the contested line, not the capital.
reportFacts.figure: Total capital cost £4.7m for two additional robotic assisted surgery systems, funded entirely by NHS England from the Constitutional Standards 2025/26 capital allocation, which must be fully spent by 31 March 2026. Worst-case revenue impact calculated at circa negative £600k per annum from capital charges, depreciation and consumable costs. The trust already had three robots: one active at Kent and Canterbury Hospital and one each in implementation at William Harvey and Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother.
reportFacts.where: Report to Board of Directors 25/103.2, Robotic Assisted Surgery Strategy Business Case, 4 December 2025, Purpose of the Report and Summary of key issues (Capital and Revenue)

reportFacts.fact: The trust is spending more capital in 2026/27 than it ever has, and the board minutes say in terms that the programme is spread across many smaller schemes including equipment replacement rather than a few large builds. That is the shape of programme a device or diagnostics rep can actually get into. The same minute records the board's own concern about back-end loading, which means proposals landing early in the financial year have a materially better chance than proposals landing in quarter four.
reportFacts.figure: Capital programme rising from £75.5m in 2025/26 to £85.2m in 2026/27, with a further £8m secured through the Estates Safety Fund, bringing the total programme to approximately £93m. Described as the largest capital programme undertaken to date, with successful bids across maternity, Same Day Emergency Care, diagnostics, urgent and emergency care and critical estate infrastructure, and equipment replacement including CT and MRI scanners.
reportFacts.where: Minutes of the Board of Directors meeting held 4 June 2026, minute 26/030.3, 2026/27 Capital Plan Update, reported by the Chief Strategy and Partnerships Officer

reportFacts.fact: Read this before pitching anything at East Kent. Segment 4 is not the whole story here: the trust is also under formal licence enforcement and inside a named national recovery programme with only a handful of peers. Every decision is being evidenced to NHS England against agreed milestones. A proposal that cannot be tied to a recovery domain, a constitutional standard or recurrent cash will not survive that scrutiny, however good the clinical argument.
reportFacts.figure: The trust remains subject to additional licence conditions under Section 111 of the Health and Social Care Act 2012 and to Enforcement Undertakings accepted under Section 106 of the same Act, remains in Segment 4 under the NHS Oversight Framework 2026/27 published 11 June 2026, and is one of five organisations receiving support through NHS England's Intensive Recovery Programme. An Integrated Improvement Plan is to be submitted to NHS England by 30 September 2026.
reportFacts.where: Interim Chair's Report to the Board of Directors, 28 July 2026, Introduction, Governance leadership and regulatory oversight, NHS Oversight Framework 2026/27 and Immediate Priorities sections

reportFacts.fact: The savings target is the commercial weather here. A £76m cost improvement requirement, against a year in which £60m was actually delivered, plus a workforce reduction of around 730 whole time equivalents, means every conversation is a cost conversation. It also means the two propositions with the clearest path are the ones that reduce staffed time per procedure and the ones that reduce length of stay, because those are the only levers that release recurrent cash alongside a workforce reduction rather than fighting it.
reportFacts.figure: 2025/26 revised year-end position achieved, delivering £60m of savings against a forecast deficit of approximately £49m. 2026/27 Cost Improvement Programme target of circa £76m, described as a key risk with a substantial gap between identified opportunities and risk-adjusted deliverable savings, alongside the need for a detailed plan to deliver circa 730 whole time equivalent reductions. A business case was approved to appoint a strategic delivery partner to support the CIP. Estates backlog cited at circa £240m.
reportFacts.where: Minutes of the Board of Directors meeting held 4 June 2026, minute 26/039.3, Finance and Performance Committee Chair Assurance Report

reportFacts.fact: This is the size of the prize and where it sits. Clinical consumables and drugs are close to equal in scale here, together making up the bulk of non-pay, and the accounts state that clinical supplies and medicines together account for 53.8% of the Group's non-pay costs. Note the split between the Group and trust columns: the trust's own Supplies and services - general figure is nearly six times the Group figure because payments into the wholly owned facilities subsidiary sit there. That single line is why estates and facilities propositions go to 2gether Support Solutions and clinical consumables propositions go to the trust.
reportFacts.figure: Group 2024/25: Supplies and services - clinical (excluding drugs costs) £112,282,000 (2023/24: £107,296,000); Drug costs £101,184,000 (2023/24: £95,371,000); Supplies and services - general £25,998,000. Trust only 2024/25: clinical supplies £54,745,000 and Supplies and services - general £151,400,000. Total Group costs £1,114.7m (2023/24: £1,084.7m).
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Notes to the Accounts, Note 7 Operating expenses (Group), read with the Performance Report, Operating expenses section

reportFacts.fact: The 2024/25 capital programme is published in full by scheme, which is rare and useful. It tells a rep exactly which named lines equipment money came out of and how small they were in that year, which is the baseline against which the much larger 2026/27 programme should be argued. Medical Devices Replacement and the Diagnostics Clinical Equipment Replacement Programme are the two lines a device or imaging rep should be able to name in a first meeting.
reportFacts.figure: Group capital expenditure 2024/25 total £26.2m, comprising Critical Priorities (PEIC) £4.53m, Medical Devices Replacement £3.23m, Diagnostics Clinical Equipment Replacement Programme £0.82m, IT Systems Replacement £1.36m, Electronic Medical Records £0.88m, Mechanical Thrombectomy £1.8m, Stroke HASU £0.81m, Maternity Estates Review £0.54m, Diagnostics Imaging (QEQM MRI) £0.21m, Pathology GP and Community Order Comms (LIMS) £0.14m, and subsidiaries 2gether £0.65m and Spencer Private Hospitals £0.27m.

trusts.name: East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: Ipswich and Colchester hospitals plus community services across east Suffolk and north Essex. The 2024/25 accounts show a £38.6m deficit, but £43.8m of that is a non-cash asset impairment — on the control total NHS England actually judges them on, they delivered a £3.5m surplus against a £0.25m target. So this is not a trust in crisis; it is one that hit its number. The softer spot is the quality of its savings: £22.7m delivered but only £12.7m of it recurrent, and the auditors identified weaknesses in how cost improvement delivery is tracked. Both executive leadership posts a supplier cares about — Chief Executive and Chief Finance Officer — are held on an interim basis as at 14/08/2026, so major commitments may move slowly.
trusts.news: Two surgical hubs are the story for anyone selling into theatres: a dedicated elective orthopaedic centre with its own theatres, three wards and 72 inpatient beds, and a surgical hub at Ipswich opened July 2024 with three specialist theatres and a same-day admissions ward covering general surgery, ENT, oral surgery and urology. The Clacton Site Transformation and Redevelopment (STAR) will significantly increase diagnostics activity. Board papers for 2026/27 are published but the trust's document library does not expose the finance report directly — the current-year position is therefore not verified here.
trusts.structure: A trust that has put social value and local supply at the centre of how it buys, and says so in its own annual report: it is a member of the Suffolk and North East Essex ICB Procurement Anchor Group, states that it buys locally wherever possible from small and medium sized businesses, and in its soft facilities management tender required bidders to state how and to what extent they would achieve social value and sustainability objectives. If you have a Carbon Reduction Plan and a local supply or employment story, lead with it here — it is scored, not decorative. Contracts are published on the trust's own contract register and all spend over £25,000 is published monthly. Payment is reasonable: 77.8% of non-NHS invoices paid within target by volume and 89.8% by value in 2024/25. Not verified: the e-tendering portal used, and whether a rep booking or accreditation system operates.

trusts.name: East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust
trusts.context: East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust reported a waiting list of 55,850 in June 2026, the RTT month layer-1 is drawn from, with 68.6% of patients treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard. 368 patients had waited over 52 weeks, 4 over 65 weeks and 2 over 78 weeks, with a median wait of 10.7 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. It reported 4 Never Events (April 2025 to March 2026) and 59 cases of C. difficile against a target of 136 for 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance stands at £6,558,218 out of a total backlog maintenance cost of £170,737,063. For a rep, the elective picture (waiting list size, sub-target 18-week performance, a live 52-week tail) sits alongside an infection-prevention and estates-risk story that has its own named cost attached, and segment 3 means spending decisions are under enhanced but not the most intensive tier of national oversight.
trusts.news: The Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25 (published October 2025, signed by Jayne Black as Chief Executive) records a statutory deficit for the year of £33,345,000 (2023/24: £7,380,000 deficit), driven mainly by £24,376,000 of net impairments, including the impairment of £11.9 million of spend on the case for a new hospital following its delay to 2037. On the adjusted, control-total basis used for the Trust's breakeven duty, the deficit was £8,941,000 (2023/24: £5,004,000), described in the accounts as caused by excess costs of industrial action, higher drug and device costs, and increased emergency care activity that fell outside the Trust's baseline plan. The Trust set itself an efficiency (cost improvement) target of £36.7 million for 2024/25 and reported delivery of £37.7 million, £1.0 million ahead of plan, of which £25.9 million was recurrent and £11.8 million non-recurrent; the largest single workstream was Grip and Control arrangements at £11.0 million, followed by Operational productivity (£6.1 million) and Clinical Improvement and Elective Capacity (£6.7 million). Procurement and Non-Pay efficiency contributed £4.2 million. For 2025/26 the Trust has set an efficiency aspiration of £49.6 million. Gross capital expenditure in 2024/25 was £72,563,000 (2023/24: £72,402,000), against a Capital Resource Limit of £71,249,000, an underspend of £663,000. Capital spend included £23.1 million on the Sussex Surgical Centre and £7.0 million on digital development including a new electronic patient record business case. The CQC's own provider page shows the Trust's overall rating as Good, but that rating was published 27 February 2020, over six years old, so it should not be read as reflecting current performance; layer-1 carries the same 'G' rating with no more recent CQC field, so it is stated here only with that caveat attached.
trusts.structure: The Trust's own procurement pages show no evidence of a Sussex-wide shared or group procurement arrangement. The Purchase Plans page at www.esht.nhs.uk/procurement/purchase-plans/ is hosted on the Trust's own domain under its own procurement section, gives the general Trust switchboard as its only contact, and lists no PIN notices tying it into a shared function. The Trust runs its own procurement mailbox, esht.procurement@nhs.net, referenced in Freedom of Information disclosure logs published on the Trust's own site. The annual report's related-party transactions note lists Sussex Community NHS Foundation Trust, University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust, Sussex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust and Sussex ICB among bodies with over £500,000 of income or expenditure transactions with East Sussex Healthcare in 2024/25, alongside NHS England and Kent and Medway ICB, but this is a standard related-party income/expenditure disclosure, not evidence of a shared executive team, shared board or shared procurement function of the kind confirmed for other trusts in this worklist (for example Hull and Northern Lincolnshire and Goole). No page on esht.nhs.uk or sussexcommunity.nhs.uk states that the two trusts share procurement, and no group chair, group chief executive or joint board was found for East Sussex Healthcare. On the evidence gathered, East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust buys for itself. Not verified: which national frameworks (NHS Supply Chain, Crown Commercial Service, NHS Commercial Alliance) the Trust routes specific categories of non-pay spend through; the annual report confirms use of the Crown Commercial Service Pre-Qualification Questionnaire above the prescribed threshold but does not itemise framework usage by category. The Trust's own current procurement notices would settle this.

reportFacts.fact: The headline figure the Trust itself reports is the £8.9m adjusted deficit, but the statutory accounts show a much larger loss once impairments are included. A rep should frame any business case around recurrent savings, since the accounts describe the underlying deficit as driven by costs excluded from the original plan, including drugs, devices and industrial action.
reportFacts.figure: Statutory deficit for 2024/25 of £33,345,000 (2023/24: £7,380,000 deficit); adjusted financial performance deficit on the control-total basis used for the breakeven duty of £8,941,000 (2023/24: £5,004,000)
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Accounts Introduction and Note 35 Breakeven duty financial performance

reportFacts.fact: The Trust beat its own efficiency target in 2024/25 and has set a materially larger target for 2025/26, which signals continuing pressure to release cash from non-pay and clinical spend, procurement's own contribution being a relatively small share of the total delivered.
reportFacts.figure: £36.7 million efficiency target for 2024/25 against £37.7 million delivered (£1.0 million ahead of plan); £25.9 million recurrent and £11.8 million non-recurrent; Procurement and Non-Pay contributed £4.2 million; 2025/26 target set at £49.6 million
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Accounts Introduction, Efficiency Delivery section

reportFacts.fact: Capital spend ran close to plan overall but includes a specific write-off on the new hospital case following its delay, which shows where major estate investment is currently paused rather than available.
reportFacts.figure: Gross capital expenditure of £72,563,000 in 2024/25 (2023/24: £72,402,000) against a Capital Resource Limit of £71,249,000, an underspend of £663,000; capital spend included £23.1 million on the Sussex Surgical Centre and £7.0 million on digital development/EPR; £1.7 million of 2024/25 spend (plus £10.2 million from earlier years) on the case for a new hospital was impaired after the scheme was delayed to 2037

trusts.name: East and North Hertfordshire Teaching NHS Trust
trusts.context: East and North Hertfordshire Teaching NHS Trust reported an RTT waiting list of 53,689 in June 2026, with 65.2% of patients treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard. 540 patients were waiting over 52 weeks, 16 over 65 weeks and 1 over 78 weeks, with a median wait of 11.5 weeks. The trust sits in NHS Oversight Framework segment 2, and its 2024/25 annual report records that it moved into segment 2 from segment 3 in April 2025, citing exit from the National Maternity Safety Support Programme, top-quartile RTT 18-week performance and a reduction in 65-week waits as the drivers. It carries a Care Quality Commission rating of Requires Improvement, dated 04/08/2026. C. difficile cases stood at 65 against a trajectory of 151 for 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is valued at £952,160 against a total estate backlog of £56,013,813, with capital-funded equipment risk of £6,328,769.
trusts.news: The trust was awarded teaching status with effect from 14/04/2025 and formally renamed East and North Hertfordshire Teaching NHS Trust, reflecting its role providing placements for over 1,300 student nurses and 227 student doctors in 2023/24 and its partnerships with the University of Hertfordshire, University of Cambridge and UCL Medical School ahead of the new Hertfordshire Medical School opening in 2026 (source: Healthcare Management UK, https://www.healthcare-management.uk/hertfordshire-trust-awarded-teaching-status, and the trust's own 2024/25 annual report). Separately, chief executive Adam Sewell-Jones, in post since 2022, left the trust in 2024 to become chief executive of Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust, with no successor named at the time of departure (The Comet, https://www.thecomet.net/news/26015419.boss-east-north-herts-nhs-trust-leave-role/). The trust's live board page now names Martin Armstrong as chief executive, not flagged as interim on the page itself; this is a change from the name in the 2024/25 annual report and should be treated as the current, verified position.
trusts.structure: The trust runs its own procurement operationally and is the named contracting authority on its own Find a Tender notices (for example waste management, fire safety and estates contracts), confirming it buys directly for itself for many requirements. It also draws on a shared regional service, publicly referred to as Hertfordshire NHS Procurement / Hertfordshire and West Essex ICS NHS Procurement (http://www.hertsprocurement.nhs.uk/joomla/), which describes providing strategic procurement, transactional procurement and site-based materials management to "Provider member Trusts" across the former Hertfordshire and West Essex ICS footprint (now part of the Central East ICB area). That service's own page does not name East and North Hertfordshire NHS Trust specifically as a member, so the trust-to-shared-service link is Not verified from a primary source naming this trust; treat it as the reported regional arrangement rather than a confirmed fact. The trust's annual report also separately references support from an "ICS Procurement Team" on a sustainability project, consistent with this shared regional structure existing alongside the trust's own direct tendering.

reportFacts.fact: The trust reported an adjusted surplus against its planned control total, but only after a significant cost improvement programme addressing a much larger underlying deficit. A rep should frame any business case in terms of recurrent savings released, not headline pounds spent, given the scale of the underlying run-rate gap.
reportFacts.figure: Adjusted financial performance surplus of £1.5m against a planned £1m surplus for 2024/25, achieved via delivery of a £33.7m cost improvement programme (plan: £33.6m, 5%) set to address an underlying run-rate deficit of £22.9m
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Performance Report, Financial Performance section, page 41-42
