trusts.name: Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: Epsom and St Helier is a two-site south west London trust with a moderate elective list and one of the better 18-week performances in this batch. The waiting list stands at 56,990 with 66.9% treated within 18 weeks against the constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 11.4 weeks, 512 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 26 over 65 weeks and 1 over 78 weeks, all for June 2026. Speciality medians for June 2026 show Dermatology at 16.4 weeks, General Surgery 14.7, Cardiology 14.6, Trauma and Orthopaedics 12.8, Gynaecology 13.3, Urology 11.1, ENT 10.0 and Ophthalmology 6.3. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. It reported 5 Never Events for April 2025 to March 2026 and 52 trust-apportioned C. difficile cases out of 133 total for 2024/25. ERIC 2024/25 records high-risk backlog maintenance of £64,629,926 within a total backlog of £142,100,648, against capital equipment spend of £4,393,005 in the same year. For a rep, that combination points toward estate and infrastructure risk as the standing story here: a high-risk backlog more than 14 times last year's capital equipment spend means estate-dependent risk is being carried, not bought out, so anything that reduces estate dependency, defers a capital job, or displaces need for further building work argues well. Segment 3 means NHS England is watching every spending decision, so any proposal has to be argued on activity delivered or recurrent cash released, never on preference. Layer-1 records the CQC field as G (Good) with a snapshot date of 04/08/2026; that overall trust rating is unchanged since the CQC's last full comprehensive inspection in May 2019 (published 19/09/2019), but it now sits alongside a more recent, more granular picture at individual hospital level, set out in news below.
trusts.news: The CQC's own provider and location pages, both read on 28/08/2026, show a split picture beneath the unchanged trust-level Good rating. Epsom General Hospital is rated Good overall (www.cqc.org.uk/location/RVR50). St Helier Hospital and Queen Mary's Hospital for Children was downgraded to Requires improvement overall in a report published 11/06/2026, following inspection in December 2025 (www.cqc.org.uk/location/RVR05): Safe and Well-led are rated Requires improvement, Effective, Caring and Responsive are Good, and the focused Surgery and Urgent and Emergency Services ratings (also published 11/06/2026) are both Requires improvement, while Maternity and Medical Care are Good. The trust's own external-assessment page (www.epsom-sthelier.nhs.uk/external-assessment/) still quotes the 2018 Requires improvement result and has not been updated with the 2026 location-level findings, so it should not be relied on. The 2024/25 annual report and accounts, published on the trust's own site and read 28/08/2026, records a reported deficit of £5.1m against a planned deficit of £5.1m for the year, which the trust states in its own words understates the underlying pressure: the reported position includes £46.7m of deficit support funding received from NHS England via South West London ICB, and without it the trust would have reported a deficit of £51.7m, which was in fact the planned position before that funding. £6.7m of non-recurrent benefits were included in the 24/25 position and will not repeat, and the report states plainly that 'the challenge in 25/26 will be greater than that indicated in the 24/25 accounts'. Capital expenditure was £40.0m against a plan of £40.4m, of which £15.3m went into backlog maintenance and estate work across both sites, including £2.0m on B4 works to meet Human Tissue Authority requirements at St Helier, £1.3m on fire remedial works across both sites, and £4.6m on enabling works for the New Hospital Programme. The going concern note in the accounts flags material uncertainty and records an agreed 2025/26 financial plan deficit of £26.2m. No 2025/26 annual report or audited outturn has yet been published, so all figures above are 2024/25 and are labelled as such; the trust has been in technical breach of the statutory breakeven duty since 2021/22 per its own accounts (Note on breakeven performance).
trusts.structure: Epsom and St Helier became part of the St George's, Epsom and St Helier Hospital Group (gesh) in January 2022, and its own 2024/25 annual report states this in its own words: the two organisations 'continue to operate as separate, sovereign trusts' and 'there are no Group financial accounts, therefore for the purpose of this annual report there is no consolidation of accounts'. Since 2023/24 the two boards have delegated extensive authority to a shared Group Board, and the annual report confirms all Board meetings held in 2024-25 were held as Group Board meetings, with the same executive team (Sir Mark Lowcock as Chair since April 2025 and Matthew Shaw as Group Chief Executive Officer, both confirmed live on www.epsom-sthelier.nhs.uk/meet-our-board/, read 28/08/2026) sitting across both trusts. However, this hint's premise that a St George's procurement win therefore carries automatically to Epsom and St Helier does not hold up against Epsom and St Helier's own site. Two things separate the sites. First, Epsom and St Helier's own accounts carry no disclosure of the South West London Procurement Partnership that St George's annual report names as hosted by St George's: Note 1.3 in the Epsom and St Helier accounts covers only the trust's charitable fund, and its separate Note 17 on interests in other entities states plainly 'The Trust has no disclosure of interests in other entities'. Second, and decisively, Epsom and St Helier publishes and runs its own buying process (www.epsom-sthelier.nhs.uk/our-buying-process, read 28/08/2026), with its own procurement helpdesk (0208 296 4692 and 0208 296 4690) and its own eTendering portal at nhssourcing.co.uk/epsom-sthelier, and states its own value-banded quotation and tender thresholds up to the OJEU/Find a Tender threshold of £113,057. A live Find a Tender notice confirms the trust buys under its own name directly: notice 2025/S 000-010564 ('NOUS at ESTH', a medical imaging services procurement) names the contracting authority as Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust at its own Dorking Road address, though the named enquiry contact, Chris Pathmadeva, holds a stgeorges.nhs.uk email address, which shows some procurement staff resourcing is already shared across the group even while the trust remains the named buyer and runs its own supplier-facing portal. So the accurate read is: shared executive leadership and a shared Group Board, but Epsom and St Helier is not shown by its own published sources to buy through the South West London Procurement Partnership that St George's hosts, and it still operates its own buying process, helpdesk and eTendering portal as the supplier-facing front door. Not verified: whether Epsom and St Helier is, in practice, a member of or served by the South West London Procurement Partnership for higher-value contracts; its own annual report and buying-process page are silent on this, and only St George's own annual report names the partnership. An FOI to Epsom and St Helier, or sight of the partnership's own membership list, would settle this. Not verified: any published policy for medical representative access or ward visiting at Epsom and St Helier; a search of the trust's own domain on 28/08/2026 found no such policy, so no rep access route is asserted here.

reportFacts.fact: The reported deficit is far smaller than the underlying financial gap once one-off NHS England funding is stripped out. Without £46.7m of deficit support funding, the 2024/25 deficit would have been £51.7m, which was in fact the trust's original plan. Any proposal here needs to show recurrent cash released or activity delivered, not one-off savings, because the trust itself says the position eases only through exceptional funding.
reportFacts.figure: Reported deficit £5.1m against a planned deficit of £5.1m; excluding £46.7m of deficit support funding from NHS England via South West London ICB, the underlying deficit was £51.7m, which was the trust's original planned position
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Financial performance section, page 21

reportFacts.fact: High-risk backlog maintenance is more than fourteen times last year's capital equipment spend, and the trust's own report shows the money going into estate risk (fire safety, roofs, lifts, HTA compliance) rather than new capacity. This is the clearest opening for anything that reduces estate dependency or displaces the need for further building work.
reportFacts.figure: ERIC 2024/25 high-risk backlog maintenance £64,629,926 within a total backlog of £142,100,648, against capital equipment spend of £4,393,005 in the same year; the annual report separately records £15.3m spent in year on backlog maintenance and estate work, including £2.0m on HTA-related works at St Helier and £1.3m on fire remedial works across both sites
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Capital investment section, pages 21-22; ERIC 2024/25 return figures per layer-1

This is a site-specific, not trust-wide, safety and flow story, and it is fresher than the trust's own external-assessment page, which still quotes the superseded 2018 result.

trusts.name: Gloucestershire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: The best access performance in this batch by a wide margin — 73.6% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 10.3 weeks and just 14 people waiting over 52 weeks on a 69,241 list — and NHS oversight segment 2, so this is a comparatively stable trust rather than one in mandated support. The commercially important fact is structural, not financial: Gloucestershire Hospitals hosts the Gloucestershire Finance, Procurement and Estates Shared Services, so its procurement function buys beyond its own boundary. Financially it is running very close to the line. 2024/25 closed at a £67k adjusted surplus — effectively breakeven, and only reached through non-recurrent measures including one-off savings, slippage on investments and one-off income.
trusts.news: The trust submitted a breakeven plan for 2025/26 carrying a savings requirement of about £41.8m, of which 65% must be recurrent. That sits inside a much harder system picture: the Gloucestershire ICS carried a material underlying deficit of about £129m from 2024/25 and submitted a 2025/26 break-even plan requiring roughly £89m of sustainability solutions — about 5.9% of the ICS funding allocation, and a significant increase on anything delivered in previous years. Chief Digital Information Officer Lee Pester joined in February 2025 from University Hospitals Plymouth and has a background in NHS procurement, which is worth knowing before a digital pitch. Not verified: the 2025/26 annual report and accounts had not been published when this profile was written, so no current-year outturn is stated here rather than letting last year's figures read as current.
trusts.structure: This trust is the host of the Gloucestershire Finance, Procurement and Estates Shared Services, confirmed in its own accounts as a role it carries out alongside being a provider. Treat a Gloucestershire Hospitals procurement conversation as potentially a county-wide one and establish early which organisations a given category covers. Cost improvement is run through a Programme Management Office with divisional colleagues building plans from both locally identified opportunities and national benchmarking, explicitly naming Model Hospital and Getting It Right First Time — bring GIRFT and Model Hospital evidence, because that is the language the savings plans are already written in. An Efficiency Board is in place, and the trust is developing a five-year estates capital programme and responding to NHS England national capital programmes. Procurement is developing social value questions for its tenders. Not verified: no procurement team structure, e-tendering portal or supplier representative booking system is published on the trust's public site; the trust's procurement pages returned no accessible content when checked, and not publishing is not proof there is no system.

trusts.name: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: The largest clinical supplies buyer in this batch by a wide margin — £418m a year, more than Leeds, Nottingham and Birmingham put together — and the largest waiting list of any trust in the Hub directory. Financially it performs: a £12.7m surplus against a breakeven plan in 2024/25 on the measure NHS England judges it by. But it missed its savings target, delivering £72.1m of a £93.8m programme, and 2026/27 raises the bar to a £115m efficiency requirement under a trust-wide campaign called Future Ready. The single most important structural fact: procurement here is a shared service that also buys for four other trusts, so one relationship reaches well beyond Guy's and St Thomas'.
trusts.news: Reported to the Board on 22/07/2026: the breakeven plan for 2026/27 is underpinned by a £115m efficiency requirement, described as requiring “a sustained and disciplined response across all clinical groups and corporate directorates”, with the Future Ready campaign launched in April to drive it. The Board was told service pressures experienced in 2025/26 were likely to intensify. CQC service inspections began in mid-March. The procurement team's new operating model went live on 1 April 2025 and the next phase is a new operating model for the supply chain team, covering materials management, logistics and warehousing.
trusts.structure: Procurement at Guy's and St Thomas' is a shared service that also supports Lewisham and Greenwich NHS Trust, Great Ormond Street Hospital, South London and Maudsley, and Oxleas NHS Foundation Trusts — five trusts buying through one function. That changes the value of the account entirely: a product accepted here has a route into four other organisations without a fresh procurement relationship each time. The team completed an operating model review in the year to 2024/25 and the new structure and shared-service relationships went live on 1 April 2025, so the people and remits you dealt with before that date may have changed — confirm who owns your category now. The supply chain team (materials management, logistics, warehousing) is the next part to be restructured, so expect disruption and opportunity there. Clinically the trust is organised into clinical groups each with its own chief executive — Women's and Children's, Cancer Surgery, Integrated and Specialist Medicine, and Heart, Lung and Critical Care — which means the clinical buying conversation has a named group leader, not just a directorate manager. Not verified: the e-tendering portal used and whether a rep booking or accreditation system operates.

trusts.name: Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: Hull is the most pressured elective performer in this batch. The waiting list stands at 84,186 with only 56.8% treated within 18 weeks, the worst figure of the batch against a constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 15.1 weeks and 3,188 patients waiting over 52 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier, and reported 6 Never Events and 63 cases of C. difficile. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £16,847,256. For a rep, that combination is the classic elective-recovery and estate-risk opening: capacity, throughput, theatre and diagnostic productivity, and infection prevention all have a named problem attached to them here. But segment 4 also means every spending decision is visible to NHS England, so anything pitched has to be argued on activity delivered or cost released, not on preference.
trusts.news: The 2024/25 annual report, signed on 20/06/2025, carries an external auditor's exception report naming a significant weakness in the trust's arrangements for financial sustainability. The auditors found the trust set a deficit plan, reported a year-end surplus only because it received deficit support funding, and did not fully deliver a cost improvement programme that leaned heavily on non-recurrent savings, all of which increased the cumulative deficit. They also record that as at April 2025 the trust had not identified all the savings needed for its 2025/26 CIP target and that a significant level of that CIP was rated high risk. Separately, the report confirms the trust opened Community Diagnostic Centres in Grimsby and Scunthorpe, expected to deliver up to 300,000 additional diagnostic tests a year, with a further centre in Hull opening in summer 2025 and the final phase of the Day Surgery Unit and the Allam Centre for digestive diseases and endoscopy coming online at Castle Hill Hospital. The Capital and Major Projects Committees-in-Common agenda for 2024/25 included an EPR business case review, the Community Diagnostic Centre developments and the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme.
trusts.structure: The group arrangement is CONFIRMED by the trust's own site, not inferred. www.hey.nhs.uk/about-us/our-senior-team/ now returns a 301 permanent redirect to the Northern Lincolnshire and Goole board page, and www.hey.nhs.uk/about-us/corporate-documents/ points its annual reports link to the same NLaG domain, where the reports for both trusts are published jointly under the name NHS Humber Health Partnership. That shared board page states in its own words that NLaG and Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust 'operate under a Group model of leadership' with 'one, shared, executive team but two separate boards, overseen by a Group Chairman'. The 2024/25 HUTH annual report says the same from the trust's side: it joined with NLaG in August 2023 in a new group structure with a Group Chief Executive and group executive team, the group name NHS Humber Health Partnership was formally launched in spring 2024, and joint clinical services across both trusts, called care groups, were formed at the same time and split into north and south site management. Commercially this is the single most important fact about Hull. You are not selling to one trust with its own executive; you are selling to a shared executive team that buys for two trusts, meets as Boards-in-Common and Committees-in-Common, and holds procurement, capital and cost improvement at group level via the Performance, Estates and Finance Committees-in-Common. Procurement goes further still. Hull is the HOST organisation for the Humber and North Yorkshire Procurement Collaborative, described on its own page as 'a single procurement function covering three local NHS Trusts' - Hull, NLaG and York and Scarborough Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust - employing 119 staff and managing an annual influenceable non-pay spend of £538m, governed by a Procurement Board accountable to all three trust boards. A supplier winning at Hull is therefore potentially transacting across three trusts, and the buying contacts sit in a shared team rather than in Hull alone. Not verified: whether York and Scarborough's clinical decision-making is bound by collaborative awards or whether it retains its own clinical sign-off - the collaborative page describes a single procurement function and a shared governance board but does not state how far individual trusts can deviate on clinical product choice; the collaborative's Procurement Board terms of reference would settle this. Not verified: the current post-holder for the Group Chief Digital Officer beyond the interim listed, and the identity of the 'Director of Procurement (EJ)' recorded in the annual report's committee attendance table, which gives initials only and does not match any name on the live procurement contact page; a direct approach to the procurement team, or the group's declarations-of-interest register, would settle both. Not verified: any 2025/26 in-year financial position - the 2024/25 report is the latest published, so no current-year figure is asserted here.

trusts.name: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust
trusts.context: One of the largest acute and specialist trusts in England, running St Mary's, Charing Cross, Hammersmith, Queen Charlotte's & Chelsea and the Western Eye hospitals, with total income of £2,029.7m in 2025-26. Waiting list 83,936 with 70.6% treated within 18 weeks, a median wait of 10.7 weeks and only 28 patients waiting over 52 weeks — a large but comparatively well-controlled list. NHS oversight segment 1, the best band, so this is not a trust under special measures and its leadership has headroom to make its own decisions rather than having them made by a regional turnaround team. Against that, 5 Never Events and 70 cases of C. difficile. The single dominant commercial fact is a high-risk backlog maintenance liability of £446,418,142, by far the largest in this batch. The trust's own 2025-26 accounts put that in the going-concern note, stating the estate's condition is a significant risk and that failures would be 'unaffordable for the Trust to rectify within its own resources'. Three main sites were pushed into Wave 3 of the New Hospital Programme in January 2025, with construction not expected between 2035 and 2038, so the ageing estate has to be kept running for another decade on revenue and small capital allocations.
trusts.news: Big governance change in 2026. The North West London Acute Provider Group was formally established on 01/04/2026, bringing Imperial together with Chelsea and Westminster, London North West University Healthcare and The Hillingdon Hospitals under a single accountable officer, a chair in common and a board in common — 12 hospitals, 33,000 staff, a population of around 2.2 million. Professor Tim Orchard, previously Imperial's chief executive, became the first Group chief executive and single accountable officer on 01/04/2026, and Professor Julian Redhead stepped up as Imperial's trust chief executive from the same date, announced on an interim basis for at least 12 months. Bob Alexander OBE has been interim chair in common since 01/04/2026; on 28/07/2026 the trust announced Dame Alwen Williams, formerly group chief executive of Barts Health, as the permanent chair, taking up the role on 01/11/2026. Commissioning also changed: NHS West and North London ICB was created on 01/04/2026 from the merger of North West London and North Central London ICBs, covering over 4.5 million people across 13 boroughs, and around 58 per cent of Imperial's income comes from it. In May 2025 there was a fire at St Mary's Hospital requiring remedial works, and reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC) was found in the outpatients building at St Mary's, with feasibility assessments funded in the 2025-26 capital programme.
trusts.structure: Imperial does NOT run its own standalone procurement function. Its Standing Financial Instructions define the term explicitly: 'Procurement or the Procurement service refers to North West London Procurement, who now provide procurement support to the Trust as part of a shared service to the NWL sector.' That is the single most important thing for a supplier to know — a rep who pitches a clinician at Charing Cross and assumes a local Imperial buying decision will follow is working the wrong route. The chief financial officer, Jazz Thind, owns the relationship with that shared service and is responsible for holding it to account; competitive tender and quotation thresholds sit in the Trust's Scheme of Delegated Financial Authority, and single tender waivers must be approved by the Procurement Service, the CFO or the chief executive, with all waivers reported to the Audit, Risk and Governance Committee. So the trust buys through a sector shared service, not for itself and not as a host buying for others. On top of that, the 2025-26 annual report states the trust is 'seeing the benefits from sector-wide procurement and management of digital services, both of which create efficiencies that are shared across north west London', and non-pay procurement improvements were one of the named contributors to the £80.1m efficiency target. The trust also co-chairs a north west London-wide social and sustainable procurement working group, and states that social value and net zero principles are embedded in its procurement processes — expect those weightings in tender scoring. Clinical leadership is unusually concentrated: there are TWO medical directors (Professor Raymond Anakwe, and Dr David O'Callaghan who holds quality, safety and clinical governance), three clinical divisions each with its own director reporting to the chief operating officer, and Professor Bob Klaber OBE holds strategy, research and innovation — the natural door for anything positioned as innovation or a research partnership. Not verified: the exact competitive tender and quotation monetary thresholds. The Standing Financial Instructions repeatedly point to the Scheme of Delegated Financial Authority for the actual figures, and that schedule is not published alongside the SFIs on the trust website. An FOI request to the trust, or a request to North West London Procurement, would settle it. Not verified: whether the formation of the North West London Acute Provider Group on 01/04/2026 has changed the procurement operating model beyond the shared-service arrangement described in the SFIs. The published Standing Financial Instructions carry an adoption date of March 2022 (version 7.0) with a stated review deadline of March 2025 for the Executive and March 2026 for the Audit, Risk and Governance Committee, so the document may pre-date the Group. It does cite a January 2024 policy, indicating some in-life updating, but a rep should confirm the current arrangement directly rather than assume. Not verified: whether North West London Procurement holds a published supplier portal or contracts register — no such page was found on the trust's own site during this session; the trust publishes only monthly expenditure-over-£25,000 CSV returns.

reportFacts.fact: The savings target rises again in 2026-27, and the trust says only around half of last year's savings were recurrent. That is the sales objection you will meet in every meeting: a proposal that adds cost has almost no route through. Lead with a costed, recurrent saving — reduced length of stay, fewer returns to theatre, consumable standardisation — and quantify it, because the trust's own report admits it needs more recurrent schemes and less one-off benefit.

reportFacts.fact: The £446m high-risk backlog maintenance liability is real and the trust says so in its own going-concern note — it cannot afford to fix it from its own resources, and New Hospital Programme construction will not start until 2035-2038. Practically, only £35.3m of capital went at backlog and fire safety in 2025-26. For a rep this means anything requiring new estate, a new room, significant ventilation, water or power is very hard to land; anything that works within existing infrastructure, or lets an ageing space keep functioning, is much easier. It also makes Eric Munro's estates directorate a live buyer in its own right.

trusts.name: King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: One of the largest acute trusts in England, running Denmark Hill, Princess Royal University Hospital, Orpington and Beckenham Beacon, with national specialist services in liver, neurosciences, haemato-oncology and cardiac care. The elective account is very big and under strain: a waiting list of 89,923, with 67.5% treated within 18 weeks against the 92% standard, 1,708 patients waiting over 52 weeks and a median wait of 11.6 weeks. The Trust sits at segment 3 of the NHS Oversight Framework, having exited segment 4 in April 2026 and come off NHS England's Recovery Support Programme. Infection control is a live pressure with 93 C. difficile cases, and there is £1,216,386 of high-risk backlog maintenance on the estate. For a rep, this is a trust with enormous volume, genuine specialist prestige, and a finance function under explicit regulatory scrutiny, so nothing gets bought on clinical enthusiasm alone.
trusts.news: The 2025/26 Annual Report and Accounts were published in July 2026 and show the group returning a surplus of £10.837m, a control-total surplus of £4.951m after adjusting for impairments and donated assets. The Trust confirms it exited NHS England's National Oversight Framework segment 4 in April 2026 and was removed from the Recovery Support Programme, which the Chief Executive frames as evidence of recovery rather than completion. Against that, the July 2026 public Board pack reports the King's group (the Trust plus KFM and KCS) £1.8m in deficit year to date at May 2026, and an underlying deficit of £18.0m once non-recurrent items are stripped out. Four Care Quality Commission service inspection reports published during 2025/26 found the Trust's improvements were not universal. Matthew Trainer is Chief Executive; search engines still return a previous post-holder, and the Trust's own executive directors page confirms the current line-up.
trusts.structure: The single most important structural fact for anyone selling to King's is that the Trust does not run its own procurement. The Trust's own support services page states that "Procurement activity is managed by King's Facilities Management (KFM) on behalf of the Trust, following best commercial practice and public procurement regulations." KFM is King's Facilities Management LLP, a Trust-owned entity created to run nine diagnostic and treatment facilities (theatres, adult critical care, radiology, cardiac catheter laboratories, liver laboratories, endoscopy, renal dialysis, children's critical care and dental), maintaining the equipment and supplying the consumables, implants and devices used in those procedures. Separately from the managed-facilities contract, the 2025/26 Annual Report states KFM "provides an end-to-end procurement and supply chain function for the Trust" and is explicitly tasked with delivering cost improvement programme savings through more focused contract management. KFM has also run the outpatient pharmacy service on the Trust's behalf since 2019. So the answer to the buy-for-itself, shared-service or buy-for-others question is: all three at once. KFM buys for King's, and KFM's own procurement and supply chain page markets end-to-end procurement, supply chain and logistics to "King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and a growing healthcare client base" beyond it. A supplier relationship built at KFM is therefore potentially a route into other clients, not just this trust. Practically, suppliers must register on the Atamis eProcurement system to bid, opportunities are advertised on Contracts Finder and the Find a Tender Service as well as through Atamis, and the Trust states the commercial procurement pipeline is published on the KFM website. Cold-calling a clinician at Denmark Hill will not get a purchase order; the route is Atamis registration plus the KFM pipeline. Two other Trust-owned companies matter commercially: King's Commercial Services Limited, which returned a £0.7m surplus to the Trust in 2025/26 and owns the Trust's stake in the Synnovis LLP pathology joint venture (so pathology buying sits inside Synnovis, not the Trust), and KCH Management Limited, which runs hospital management and consultancy overseas, mainly in the Middle East, returning £0.1m. The Trust is also part of a South East London Acute Provider Collaborative with Guy's and St Thomas' and Lewisham and Greenwich, established in May 2020 and building specialty-based elective hubs across the patch, so high-volume low-complexity elective capacity decisions are being taken at collaborative level rather than by King's alone. Not verified: the size of KFM's addressable procurement spend as distinct from the Trust's total non-pay spend, and the identity of KFM's procurement director or category leads. Neither is disclosed in the Annual Report or the July 2026 Board pack. A Freedom of Information request to the Trust, or KFM's own Companies House filings, would settle the first; the second would be settled by KFM's published pipeline or a direct approach through Atamis. Not verified: which named individuals hold category ownership for medical devices or consumables. Not verified: whether the reported KFM contract extension to 2036 that appears in secondary coverage is accurate; it does not appear in the 2025/26 Annual Report or the July 2026 Board pack read for this profile, and only a Trust or KFM primary source or a published contract award notice would settle it.

trusts.name: Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: Lancashire Teaching Hospitals' waiting list stood at 60,680 in June 2026 (RTT period), with 58.7% treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 14.9 weeks, and 666 patients waiting over 52 weeks (no 65 or 78-week breaches recorded). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier, and reported 2 Never Events (April 2025 to March 2026) and 142 cases of C. difficile against a target ceiling (274 total for 2024/25). High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £4,698,144 against a total backlog maintenance figure of £66,202,910, with capital-cost-to-eradicate figures of £2,028,000 for equipment. The CQC rated the trust Requires Improvement, published 04/08/2026. For a rep, segment 4 combined with the financial position below (see reportFacts) means every purchasing decision is under external scrutiny: value-for-money and cost-release arguments will land better than preference-based pitches.
trusts.news: The 2024/25 annual report's independent auditor's report identifies a significant weakness in the trust's arrangements for financial sustainability. The trust set a £58.0m financial recovery plan (FRP) for 2024/25; by mid-October 2024 it was forecasting a £31.9m shortfall against that plan, and final delivered FRP savings were £26.1m. The auditors found that the projected full-year underperformance in cost improvement plan (CIP) delivery was not reported to the Finance and Performance Committee and Trust Board until October, and that divisional-level accountability was not sufficient to ensure effective monitoring and risk assessment of CIP delivery. Separately, NHS England moved the trust from oversight Segment 3 to Segment 4 (for finance only) in February 2025, placing it on the National Recovery Support Programme, and at the same time issued a Notice of Intent to impose an Additional Licence Condition on governance arrangements under Section 111 of the Health and Social Care Act 2012. On capital projects, the trust's own site confirms that as of 30 March 2026 it had completed purchase of the final section of land (between Stanifield Lane and Wigan Road, Farington, near the M65) for a proposed replacement Royal Preston Hospital under the national New Hospital Programme, though the trust states no final decision has been made and construction is not expected to start before 2037 to 2039 following the government's January 2025 programme review; the existing Royal Preston Hospital continues operating in the meantime.
trusts.structure: Lancashire Teaching Hospitals is a standalone foundation trust, not part of a group or shared-executive model: it has its own Chair (Prof. Mike Thomas, since January 2025) and Chief Executive (Prof. Silas Nicholls, since 8 January 2024), distinct from the separately-chaired and separately-led East Lancashire Hospitals NHS Trust and Blackpool Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. There is no evidence of a Group Chair, Group Chief Executive or shared board arrangement across the three trusts, unlike the confirmed Hull/NLaG model. Procurement, however, IS shared: the trust buys through the Lancashire Procurement Cluster (LPC), a shared procurement, commercial and supply chain service for three trust partners, Blackpool Teaching Hospitals, East Lancashire Hospitals and Lancashire Teaching Hospitals, hosted by East Lancashire Hospitals NHS Trust, per the Lancashire and South Cumbria Provider Collaborative's own procurement page. The LPC's own domain (lancashireprocurement.nhs.uk) currently returns a suspended-account page, so it could not be used as a direct source here; the arrangement is instead cited via the Provider Collaborative's own page. For a rep, this means routing a pitch through the trust's own buyers alone will miss where contracting actually happens for shared categories.

trusts.name: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: One of the largest acute teaching trusts in England, £2.12bn total operating income in 2024/25 across the LGI, St James's, Chapel Allerton, Wharfedale, Seacroft and the Leeds Children's Hospital. Eight consecutive years of surplus to 2024/25 — but 2026/27 is a breakeven plan carrying a £95m Waste Reduction Programme, and Q1 closed £14.0m in deficit, £3.1m adverse to plan, partly on under-delivery of that programme. The new hospital at the LGI sits in Wave 2 of the New Hospital Programme with no construction before 2033–2035, so the existing estate has to last: the trust describes itself as carrying one of the highest backlog maintenance levels in the NHS, much of it critical infrastructure. A trust that has been good at savings, is now being asked for more, and cannot build its way out.
trusts.news: Q1 2026/27 reported to the public Board on 30/07/2026: £14.0m year-to-date deficit against a breakeven plan, with a Fundamental Review risk range of breakeven (best), £49m deficit (mid) and £93.7m deficit (worst). Capital is running behind — £12.3m spent to 30/06/2026 against a £24.2m ask, with 40% of the programme due by September. New organisational strategy 2026–2029 published, built on People, Improvement & innovation, Partnerships and Outcomes.
trusts.structure: Procurement sits inside the Finance Directorate under the Chief Finance Officer, and is over 100 staff across five disciplines: Procurement and Contracting, Logistics and Materials Management, Supplier Relationship Management, Data and eProcurement, and Commercial Activity. Tendering runs through Atamis, the Health Family Single e-Commercial System — register once and the same account works across other health family organisations; opportunities also appear on Find a Tender and Contracts Finder, and the trust publishes a forward Commercial Pipeline worth reading before you approach. The team is accredited at 'Best' (91%) against the national Commercial Continuous Improvement Assessment Framework and holds Cabinet Office Customer Service Excellence accreditation, so expect a professional, process-led buyer rather than an informal one. Pathology is not bought trust-by-trust: the Pan Pathology Managed Service Contract is a collaborative contract spanning Leeds, Mid Yorkshire and Calderdale & Huddersfield. The trust does not publish a rep booking or accreditation system — Not verified whether one exists; ask your named contact.

trusts.name: Lewisham and Greenwich NHS Trust
trusts.context: As of June 2026 (RTT), Lewisham and Greenwich has a waiting list of 57,451 with 66.6% treated within 18 weeks, against a constitutional standard of 92%. Median wait is 12.3 weeks, with 905 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 63 over 65 weeks and 8 over 78 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3 and reported 2 Never Events (April 2025 to March 2026) and 44 cases of C. difficile against a threshold of 71 for 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance stands at £9,580,545 against a total backlog of £65,763,529, and capital-funded equity is recorded as zero. Specialty-level 18-week performance is weakest in Urology (17.3%) and ENT (16.8%), with General Surgery, Trauma & Orthopaedics, Cardiology and Gynaecology all also below the standard, indicating pressure spread across several surgical specialties rather than concentrated in one.
trusts.news: The Trust's 2024/25 annual report (covering the year to 31 March 2025) reports a Community Diagnostic Centre at Eltham now operational, with a second CDC at Sidcup due online in 2025/26. Capital investment of over £55 million in 2024/25 included infrastructure upgrades at Queen Elizabeth Hospital and the first phase of a new Urgent Treatment Centre at University Hospital Lewisham. The Chief Financial Officer's statement in that report records that its author was stepping down after six years at the Trust, with David Cooper named as interim CFO from 9 June 2025; the Trust's live board page now names Caroline Owusu-Bennoah as Chief Financial Officer with no interim label, so the substantive appointment has moved on since the report was signed. No 2025/26 annual report has yet been published, so all financial figures below are 2024/25 and are labelled as such.
trusts.structure: The Trust runs two acute sites, University Hospital Lewisham and Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Woolwich, plus over a dozen community settings in Lewisham and some services at Queen Mary's Hospital, Sidcup, serving over one million people across Lewisham, Greenwich and Bexley (trust's own About Us page). It is an active member of the South East London Integrated Care System and named partner in the South East London Acute Provider Collaborative, alongside borough-based partnership boards in Bexley, Greenwich and Lewisham (About Us page). On buying: the Trust's own procurement page states plainly that it does not run procurement independently. It is a member of SmartTogether, a shared procurement and supply chain service hosted by Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, also covering Dartford and Gravesham NHS Trust, with a sourcing team managing over £300m of expenditure across clinical and non-clinical spend categories and a supply chain function running one of the largest automated inventory management systems in Europe. The Trust's own page also lists framework routes used alongside SmartTogether: London Procurement Partnership, Crown Commercial Service, G-Cloud Digital Marketplace and NHS Supply Chain. The direct procurement contact given on that page is LG.Procurement@nhs.net. Not verified: SmartTogether's own site was not reached directly in this pass (the description above is sourced from the Trust's own procurement page, which names and describes the shared service); a supplier wanting SmartTogether's own contact structure or category leads should go to Guy's and St Thomas' as host trust. Not verified: whether clinical product standardisation decisions are taken at SmartTogether level or retained by each member trust; the Trust's page does not state this and it would need a direct approach to the shared service to settle.

trusts.name: Liverpool University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: As at June 2026 the RTT waiting list stood at 61,511 with 61.4% treated within 18 weeks, against the constitutional standard of 92%, and a median wait of 13.7 weeks. 759 patients were waiting over 52 weeks, with no patients recorded waiting over 65 or 78 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier. It reported 3 Never Events (April 2025 to March 2026) and 147 attributable cases of C. difficile against a total of 315 (2024/25). High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £500,000 against a total estates backlog of £59,304,977, plus a capital equipment backlog of £666,655. For a rep, the segment 4 status combined with a live, multi-year cost improvement drive means any pitch needs to be argued on activity delivered or cost released rather than preference, while the scale of the elective backlog and the estates figure both point to capacity, theatre productivity and infection prevention as the openings with a named problem already attached.
trusts.news: James Sumner, chief executive of NHS University Hospitals of Liverpool Group (UHLG) since the group's formation and of this trust since April 2022, announced on 27 April 2026 that he would step down once a successor was appointed. Professor David Loughton CBE, previously chief executive of the Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust for two decades, joined as Interim Group Chief Executive around 1 July 2026, with a permanent recruitment process reported to be under way; the exact handover date is not confirmed by a single primary source and should be checked before use in a live conversation. Jen Huyton, previously Director of Finance at Liverpool Women's NHS Foundation Trust, was appointed Interim Group Chief Finance Officer around August 2026, succeeding Robert Forster. On the estate, the new Royal Liverpool University Hospital itself opened in October 2022; the redevelopment now under way is of the surrounding old hospital site, with planning permission approved for a further phase (an extended podium and two-way entrance, plus a new road, footpath and cycleway) due to start around August 2026 and complete by the end of 2027. Not verified: the trust's current or recent financial position. The trust's own site (uhliverpool.nhs.uk) is behind a full Cloudflare browser challenge that blocked every access attempt this pass, so no annual report, board paper or other primary-source figure on deficit, cost improvement or capital programme could be retrieved or verified, and none is asserted here.
trusts.structure: This trust (Liverpool University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, formed 1 October 2019 by the merger of Royal Liverpool and Broadgreen University Hospitals NHS Trust with Aintree University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust) sits inside NHS University Hospitals of Liverpool Group (UHLG), formed with Liverpool Women's NHS Foundation Trust on 1 November 2024 and joined by Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust from around October 2024/April 2025, so the group now spans three separate foundation trusts under one Group Chair and, since July 2026, one interim Group Chief Executive. David Flory CBE has chaired this trust since February 2023, became joint Chair with Liverpool Women's in March 2024, and continues as UHLG's Group Chair. On procurement, the trust's own 10-year, £53m Electronic Patient Record contract with Nervecentre (announced April 2026) was let by this trust for its own three hospitals (Aintree, Broadgreen and the Royal Liverpool), while Liverpool Women's, Liverpool Heart and Chest, The Walton Centre and The Clatterbridge Cancer Centre are separately progressing business cases to adopt the same system - so this is coordinated group direction, not a single group-wide procurement decision, for that contract. A separate shared service, Health Procurement Liverpool (HPL), covers Alder Hey, Liverpool Heart and Chest, Clatterbridge and The Walton Centre; no source found confirms this trust is itself a member of HPL. Not verified: the trust's own procurement/contact page (uhliverpool.nhs.uk/contact-us/procurement) and its board/leadership pages are behind a full Cloudflare browser challenge that blocked every access attempt (via curl with full browser headers and via WebFetch), and the Wayback Machine was unavailable at the time of research, so this trust's own procurement contacts and current board listing could not be read directly; the facts above are built instead from the trust's press coverage, NHS Cheshire and Merseyside's and partner trusts' own pages, and CQC's own site.

trusts.name: London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust
trusts.context: London North West carries one of the larger elective lists in the capital and one of the most unusual regulatory combinations in this batch. The waiting list stood at 81,241 in the June 2026 RTT return, with only 65.3% treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard and a median wait of 12.4 weeks. Median waits by speciality in the same return run from 6.9 weeks in ophthalmology to 16.9 in dermatology, 15.5 in ENT, 14.6 in trauma and orthopaedics and 13.1 in general surgery. The long tail, though, is nearly gone: 542 patients waited over 52 weeks and none waited over 65 or 78 weeks. The CQC rating recorded as at 04/08/2026 is Requires improvement, and the trust reported 3 Never Events between April 2025 and March 2026 and 69 cases of C. difficile in 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £65,744,826 within a total backlog maintenance figure of £463,212,926 (ERIC 2024/25). Despite the size of the list and a Requires improvement rating, the trust sits in NHS oversight segment 1, the highest tier, which is the single most commercially significant thing on this page. Segment 1 is a judgement about capability, governance and improvement trajectory rather than about queue length, and it means this trust is trusted to make its own decisions with the least NHS England intervention of any tier. For a rep, that is the opposite of the segment 4 conversation: the buying decision genuinely sits inside the organisation rather than needing regional sign-off, so a well-argued case can move. The commercial openings the numbers point to are elective throughput and outpatient productivity (65.3% against 92%), the specialities with the longest medians (dermatology, ENT, orthopaedics, general surgery), infection prevention, and an estate carrying £65.7m of high-risk backlog. What the numbers do not support is an elective long-wait pitch: with zero patients over 65 weeks, the 52 and 65-week crisis framing that works elsewhere will land badly here.
trusts.news: The trust has published a 2025/26 annual report, so a current-year outturn is available rather than a carried-forward one. It reports a retained deficit for the year of £7.038m which, after £11.964m of technical adjustments for impairments, donated asset income and the PFI re-measurement, becomes an adjusted surplus of £4.926m against the statutory break-even duty, compared with an adjusted deficit of approximately £22.9m in 2024/25. Total income was £1.179bn and total operating expenditure £1.167bn. The trust states it achieved approximately £48.5m of financial efficiencies in the year. It also states plainly that it has not met the break-even duty on the rolling assessment: the cumulative deficit measured under that duty is £346.6m, and the report says recovery of the cumulative deficit is not covered by the trust or the system recovery plans. The annual governance statement records that KPMG's review for the year notes the trust has continued to improve its arrangements for financial management and internal governance, and that the Head of Internal Audit gave an opinion of moderate assurance on the system of internal control. On performance, the report gives a March 2026 position of 64% on 18-week referral to treatment against a local operating plan target of 60%, which the trust describes as the second largest improvement nationally, alongside 75.8% four-hour emergency performance for the year, 79.6% on the 28-day faster diagnosis standard and 82.2% on the 62-day cancer standard. Diagnostics is the weak point: 65.4% within six weeks in March 2026 against a national operating plan trajectory of 99%, with additional capacity bought in through insourcing arrangements for non-obstetric ultrasound and echocardiography. The trust also reports rolling out the Federated Data Platform and deploying LUNA ROVA AI to review clinical correspondence and identify clock stops. Capital investment was approximately £55.9m in 2025/26, £21m more than the year before, funded by £30.5m internally generated capital, £23.2m of Public Dividend Capital and £2.2m donated or grant funding, and it included two new surgical robots, the start of the Northwick Park neonatal unit refurbishment, a new energy centre at Ealing due to complete in 2026/27, and continued electronic patient record work. The planned 2026/27 capital programme is approximately £78.4m but is dependent on securing approximately £40.9m of Public Dividend Capital, so it is not yet money in hand. Cash improved to about £39.4m at year end from £11m. The trust's CQC position is unchanged at Requires improvement, with emergency and urgent care services inspected during 2025/26.
trusts.structure: This is the highest-value structural finding on this trust, and it is confirmed from the trust's own and the group's own live pages rather than inferred. On 1 April 2026 the four acute NHS trusts in north west London, Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust, London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust and The Hillingdon Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, formally became the North West London Acute Provider Group. They remain four separate statutory organisations, but there is now a single accountable officer for all four, the Group chief executive Professor Tim Orchard CBE, a single chair in common (Bob Alexander OBE, interim, with NHS England running recruitment for a permanent chair), and a board in common. The group covers 12 hospitals, 33,000 staff and a population of around 2.2 million. Corporate functions are actively being centralised: the trust's own news release of 02/06/2026 confirms that Group chief people officer (Kevin Croft) and Group chief governance director (Peter Jenkinson) are new permanent group posts that replace the separate trust-level posts at all four trusts, that Dame Janice Sigsworth is Group lead chief nursing officer and Dr Roger Chinn Group lead chief medical officer, and that recruitment was then under way for a Group chief finance officer, Group chief delivery officer, Group lead director of communications and engagement and Group lead director of strategic partnerships. LNWH's own chief executive, Mark Titcomb, reports into the Group chief executive, and that post is explicitly an interim role for up to a year following Pippa Nightingale's departure at the end of July 2026. The commercial reading is straightforward: the centre of gravity for anything corporate, workforce, governance or finance-related is moving from the trust to the group, and a supplier winning at LNWH is increasingly transacting with an executive layer that also covers Imperial, Chelsea and Westminster and Hillingdon. Procurement sits in a second, separate shared arrangement that predates the group and does not map onto it. Since 01/09/2022 North West London Procurement Services has been a single shared procurement service for nine NHS partner organisations, hosted not by LNWH but by Central London Community Healthcare NHS Trust, and governed by a board of chief financial officer representatives from each organisation. The nine named partners are CLCH, Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust, Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, The Hillingdon Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust, London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust, the North West London ICB, The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust and West London NHS Trust. So the procurement footprint is wider than the acute group, and LNWH is a partner in it rather than the host. That said, LNWH's own Detailed Scheme of Delegation (December 2024, next review December 2026) still describes a trust Procurement Department, a trust e-tendering system that paper tenders are rejected by, and an Associate Director of Procurement who must countersign single tender waivers alongside the Chief Executive Officer or Chief Financial Officer. Treat the buying route as two-layer: category and tendered work through the shared service, local specification and clinical sign-off still inside the trust. One more structural fact matters for orthopaedic and theatre suppliers: the North West London Elective Orthopaedic Centre sits on LNWH's Central Middlesex Hospital site, opened on 04/12/2023, is expected to perform around 4,000 procedures a year and provides much of the routine adult inpatient orthopaedic surgery for the whole of north west London, run in partnership across all four trusts. Selling orthopaedic implants or theatre consumables into that centre is a sector-wide decision hosted by LNWH, not a single-trust one. Not verified: whether the LNWH Procurement Department is staffed and managed by North West London Procurement Services or is a separate trust team, and who currently holds the Associate Director of Procurement post; the scheme of delegation names the role but no individual, and no named procurement contact is published on the trust website. A direct approach to the trust procurement team, or the shared service's own governance papers, would settle this. Not verified: whether the group intends to bring procurement under the Group chief finance officer once that post is filled, which would move it away from the CLCH-hosted shared service; the 02/06/2026 appointments release names the post as under recruitment but says nothing about procurement, and the Group chief finance officer's terms of reference would settle it. Not verified: whether Mark Titcomb has since been made substantive; the live trust board page read on 28/08/2026 lists him as Chief Executive Officer with no interim qualifier, while the 02/06/2026 news release describes the post as interim for up to a year, and a board-in-common paper or an updated trust announcement would settle which is current. Note also that the 2025/26 annual report's governance section lists the board as at 31 March 2026 with Matthew Swindells as chair and Pippa Nightingale MBE as chief executive, so anything quoting that report on leadership is already out of date.

trusts.name: Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust
trusts.context: Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells sits in the middle of the batch on elective pressure. NHS England's Referral to Treatment return for June 2026 shows a waiting list of 50,743 with 73.5% treated within 18 weeks, against the constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 10.2 weeks, 11 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 1 over 65 weeks and 1 over 78 weeks. The longest specialty medians in the same return are ENT at 13.8 weeks and Gynaecology at 11.4 weeks, then Cardiology at 10.1, General Surgery at 10.4, Trauma and Orthopaedics at 9.5, Ophthalmology at 9.0 and Urology at 7.4. The Care Quality Commission rating held on 04/08/2026 was Requires Improvement, and the trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3, one tier below the mandated-intensive-support segment 4. It reported 4 Never Events in the year April 2025 to March 2026, and 71 C. difficile cases in 2024/25 against a category total of 201 in the same return. The 2024/25 Estates Returns Information Collection records high-risk backlog maintenance of £4,408,998 within a total backlog of £46,592,463, and £0 of capital investment in medical equipment in that year through the ERIC return specifically, against £50.5m of gross capital investment trust-wide in the same year (see structure/news for where that capital actually went). Commercially the estate and equipment position is the sharper opening than waiting times here: a zero ERIC medical-equipment capital line against £50.5m of gross capital spend elsewhere (predominantly the Kent and Medway Orthopaedic Centre, a new Community Diagnostic Centre and digital pathology) suggests routine equipment renewal is competing hard against major-project capital. Segment 3 means the trust is not under the most intensive NHS England oversight, but every spend decision remains visible.
trusts.news: The Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25 records a surplus of £0.2m on turnover of £831.0m, the seventh consecutive year the trust has delivered a surplus, achieved against a Cost Improvement Programme (CIP) of £34.3m that was £3m adverse to plan. For 2025/26 the trust set its largest ever CIP target of £49m, plus a further £23m of savings expected from work across the wider Kent and Medway system, citing a system-wide financial challenge. The statutory accounts show a £13.60m deficit before technical adjustments (impairments and donated-asset accounting), reducing to an adjusted financial performance surplus of £0.16m after those adjustments; both figures are the trust's own, for 2024/25. The Kent and Medway Orthopaedic Centre, a new three-theatre elective hub at Maidstone Hospital, opened in September 2024 (£2.51m of 2024/25 capital) and a new Community Diagnostic Centre, the Hounsfield Unit, opened in February 2025 (£5.64m of 2024/25 capital); digital pathology equipment accounted for a further £2.9m of capital that year. In February 2026 the trust was reported as one of only three in England (alongside Calderdale and Huddersfield, and Homerton Healthcare) treating 85.7% of cancer patients within the 62-day referral-to-treatment standard, against a national average of 69.1%, published 25/02/2026. Separately, in June 2026 the Technology and Construction Court refused to enforce a £1,655,385.49 adjudication award against the trust in a construction dispute over a new theatre block (Premier Modular Limited v Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust [2026] EWHC 1404), on the grounds the adjudicator had breached natural justice; the underlying payment dispute is unresolved as reported.
trusts.structure: Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells is confirmed, from the trust's own annual report and from NHS Kent and Medway's own pages, as the HOST trust for the Kent and Medway Pathology Network (KMPN). KMPN is described on the ICS's own site as a formal partnership of seven laboratories across three pathology services in four acute trusts: East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust, Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust, Dartford and Gravesham NHS Trust, and Medway NHS Foundation Trust (which together with Dartford and Gravesham forms the North Kent Pathology Service), serving a population of nearly two million with around 800 staff. Chief Executive Miles Scott personally chairs the Kent and Medway Pathology Network committee alongside the Kent and Medway Cancer Alliance, per his own board biography in the 2024/25 annual report. The trust's accounts show this hosting role is a funded arrangement, not an informal one: non-patient care income rose by £2.9m in 2024/25 specifically from hosting KMPN, and a further £2.1m of West Kent Health and Care Partnership and KMPN staff costs were funded directly by Kent and Medway ICB. This confirms the JV from the hosting trust's own side: MTW does not merely participate in Kent-wide pathology, it employs and hosts the network's shared management function on behalf of the other three trusts, funded by the ICB. Outside pathology, the evidence points the other way: the annual report describes MTW's own in-house procurement team (a Social Value & Sustainable Sourcing Specialist was recruited into it in 2024/25) working to national frameworks and policy (PPN 02/23 on modern slavery in supply chains, NHS Supplier Code commitments), with no equivalent to East Kent's wholly owned procurement subsidiary or Hull's shared group-procurement function. Not verified: whether MTW buys any categories through a formal Kent-wide procurement collaborative beyond KMPN itself; the trust's own procurement/FOI pages returning current contact and framework details could not be resolved live (see caveats), so this is stated as "buys largely for itself outside pathology" rather than confirmed absolutely. A rep should treat pathology consumables, equipment and informatics as a KMPN-wide, MTW-hosted conversation reaching four trusts, and treat other categories (surgical, orthopaedic, diagnostic imaging, general equipment) as MTW's own procurement decision.

trusts.name: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: The largest waiting list in England — 166,009, with 63.8% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 13.1 weeks and 1,430 people over 52 weeks — on income of £3.09bn across ten hospitals. Despite that scale it sits in NHS oversight segment 1, the most stable tier, because it delivered its financial plan: year one of a three-year Financial Recovery Plan closed with an adjusted surplus of £3.6m and the full £148.3m 'Value for Patients' productivity programme delivered against a £148.0m plan. The 2025/26 ask is bigger again at £165.8m on a breakeven plan. Cash is the pressure point, having more than halved in a year. The trust is organised into Clinical Groups with their own Chief Executives, so a trust-wide pitch has several internal customers.
trusts.news: Work has begun on decarbonising Trafford Hospital, with £20m secured to develop what the trust describes as the first Carbon Net-Zero inpatient hospital. Its EPR is Hive, and a 'Choosing Wisely' project launched in 2024/25 built soft and hard stops into Hive to cut unnecessary over-ordering of lab tests, medication and imaging — directly relevant if you sell diagnostics or consumables into request-driven demand. The Chief Finance Officer post changed hands twice in 2024/25: Jenny Ehrhardt to 30/06/2024, Marcus Thorman on an interim basis, then Claire Wilson from 31/12/2024, who remains in post.
trusts.structure: There is one procurement condition here that is not optional and is stated plainly: since April 2024, **all suppliers to MFT have been required to submit a carbon reduction plan or commitment as part of new procurements and contracts**. Arrive without one and the conversation stops. The trust has also adapted its internal 'new product request' forms to include a sustainability assessment question as part of routine product switches — so even a like-for-like swap is now assessed on sustainability, not just price and clinical preference. Supply Chain and Procurement runs its own reuse programmes with published numbers, including a Walking Aid Reuse scheme sustaining a 24% average return rate and saving roughly 84 tCO2e and £34,300, and an internal reuse community that repurposed 340 items of furniture, IT and stationery plus over 10,000 individual items of PPE. A proposition framed around reuse, take-back or remanufacture is speaking the language this team already reports in. Not verified: no e-tendering portal or supplier representative booking system is published on the trust's public site, and not publishing one is not proof there isn't one.

trusts.name: Mersey and West Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: MWL is the only CQC Outstanding trust in this batch, and on the layer-1 numbers it is a middling elective performer carrying an unusually light estate risk. The waiting list stands at 81,118 with 66.8% treated within 18 weeks (RTT, June 2026) against the constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 11.8 weeks, 1,468 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 11 over 65 weeks and none over 78 weeks. Speciality median waits (June 2026) are worst in Dermatology at 16.0 weeks, ENT at 13.5 and General Surgery at 13.0, with Trauma and Orthopaedics the shortest at 9.7. The CQC rating is Outstanding (as at 04/08/2026) and the trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. It recorded 2 Never Events (April 2025 to March 2026) and 87 trust-apportioned C. difficile cases out of 207 total (2024/25). ERIC 2024/25 records high-risk backlog maintenance of just £1,165,000 against a total backlog of £31,675,117, with £2,154,000 of capital investment required to eradicate high-risk backlog. Commercially that combination reads very differently from a typical acute trust. There is no 78-week cohort and only 11 patients past 65 weeks, so a pitch built on rescuing long waiters will not land; the pressure is in the 18-to-52-week middle, in Dermatology, ENT and General Surgery, and the argument that works is throughput and clinic productivity in named specialities rather than backlog rescue. The near-absent high-risk estate backlog removes the usual estate-risk opening entirely, so anything sold as remedial estate work has no published problem to attach to here. Segment 3 means the trust is not in mandated national support but is not free of scrutiny either, and the two Never Events plus a trust-apportioned C. difficile count of 87 give genuine, specific hooks for safety and infection-prevention propositions.
trusts.news: The 2024/25 annual report, signed by Chief Executive Rob Cooper on 24 June 2025, is the latest published set of accounts and covers the first full financial year of the merged trust. Turnover grew from £817m in 2023/24 to £1,004.8m in 2024/25, a 22.3% increase, and the trust posted a year-end deficit of £14.7m on the adjusted financial performance basis against a revised plan of £10.9m, taking the assessed cumulative deficit to £4.4m. It delivered a £48.0m efficiency target, of which £35.4m was recurrent and £12.6m non-recurrent. Capital schemes totalled £45.3m, broken down in the report as £10.8m on information technology including DHSC Frontline Digitalisation funding, £8.2m on new land and buildings, £8.0m on Southport and Ormskirk refurbishments, £7.7m on the built estate including backlog maintenance, £4.3m on leased equipment, £4.2m on PFI lifecycle replacement and £2.2m on medical equipment including replacement theatre and diagnostic kit. Unusually for the sector, the audit is clean: Grant Thornton reported an unqualified opinion on the financial statements on 27 June 2025 and, in the completion report certifying the audit on 7 January 2026, confirmed it had 'nothing to report' on the trust's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. On the low backlog maintenance figure, the trust's own report gives the mechanism and the answer is mostly genuine, with a real reporting caveat. St Helens and Whiston Hospitals were 'both constructed less than 15 years ago', with all PFI construction complete in November 2012 and the contract running to August 2047, and Note 22 records that nearly 70% of the trust's building assets and 13% of plant and machinery relate to on-Statement of Financial Position PFI contracts. Hard facilities management on that estate is contracted to Vinci for the life of the scheme, so lifecycle replacement is contractually funded rather than deferred, and the trust paid a unitary payment of £79,480,000 to the service concession operator in 2024/25 plus £40,909,000 charged to operating expenditure for IFRIC 12 schemes. That is the artefact: on roughly two-thirds of the building estate the maintenance risk sits with the special purpose vehicle and shows up as a unitary payment and £4.2m of PFI lifecycle capital, not as backlog in the ERIC return. The older half is treated separately again. Southport and Ormskirk Hospitals are 'between 30 and 40 years old' and the report states 'the facilities in many cases do not meet current hospital building standards, but a three-year programme is now in place to address the high risk backlog maintenance', funded by £8m of NHS England money in 2024/25 with a further £8m approved for 2025/26. So the low figure is a real estate position for the PFI half and a live, separately funded programme on the older half, not a trust that has quietly stopped counting. The CQC position needs the same care. The overall Outstanding rating on the CQC's own provider page for RBN carries a report publication date of 20 March 2019 and was inherited: the annual report confirms 'On completion of the transaction, the CQC rating for the Trust was maintained for the new organisation', that there were no CQC inspections during 2024/25, and that the last comprehensive inspection was of the legacy St Helens and Knowsley trust. The rating therefore describes an organisation that no longer exists in that form and predates the merger by more than four years. The freshest financial picture is the Trust Board papers for the meeting of 29 July 2026, reporting Month 3 of 2026/27. The approved 2026/27 plan is a balanced position that includes £16.7m of Deficit Support Funding and assumes delivery of £49.7m of CIP, all of it to be delivered recurrently. At Month 3 the trust reported an adjusted deficit of £6.8m, or £11.0m excluding deficit support funding, in line with plan, with £9.9m of CIP transacted year to date and £55.7m of schemes identified against the £49.7m target. Cash at Month 3 was £2.9m. The capital plan for 2026/27 is £42.2m including PFI lifecycle and lease remeasurements, with £2.5m spent year to date, £5.4m below plan. The same board meeting noted that in the NHS Oversight Framework national performance rankings MWL had climbed 27 places to become the fourth most improved trust in the country.
trusts.structure: MWL was created by merger on 1 July 2023, when Southport and Ormskirk Hospital NHS Trust and St Helens and Knowsley Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust combined; the two had already been operating under a management arrangement from September 2021. The trust now runs Whiston, St Helens, Southport, Ormskirk and Newton Community hospitals plus an Urgent Treatment Centre and the Marshalls Cross Medical Centre, employed 10,612 whole time equivalent staff in 2024/25 and serves a catchment of about 650,000 people across five boroughs and, importantly for anyone planning territory, two integrated care systems: NHS Cheshire and Merseyside and NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria. The organisational structure the merger produced is four clinical divisions, Medicine and Urgent Care, Surgery, Women and Children, and Clinical Support and Community Services, with corporate services including Estates and Facilities, Informatics and Medicines Management held centrally. The practical effect of the merger for a supplier is that legacy contracts and legacy product choices from two different trusts are still being rationalised into one, which is why standardisation and single-catalogue arguments carry weight here that they would not at a long-established single trust. The trust buys in its own name. Its published contract register, dated 26 August 2025, lists 529 contracts all held by Mersey and West Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust as the contracting authority, and the route to market is overwhelmingly through existing national frameworks and below-threshold direct award rather than open competition. The published enquiry route is a single generic mailbox, purchasing@merseywestlancs.nhs.uk at Whiston Hospital, Warrington Road, Prescot, L35 5DR, which is the contact given on the trust's own Find a Tender notices; no named buyer is published against it. What makes MWL commercially distinctive is that it runs services for other organisations at real scale, and this is the key fact to understand before approaching it. The trust is the NHS Lead Employer for over 13,000 doctors, dentists and public health specialists in training across eight NHS England regions (North West, East of England, West Midlands, East Midlands, Thames Valley, London and South East, South West, and Yorkshire and Humber), providing employment services, case management, workforce information, payroll and occupational health for them. It provides the payroll function for other organisations in Cheshire and Merseyside, and it hosts the Mid-Mersey Digital Alliance, which supplies informatics services to other NHS bodies and GP surgeries. Non-patient care services to other bodies brought in £34,869,000 in 2024/25, described in the accounts as covering pathology, CIPHA scheme incomes, IT and HR/payroll services. For a rep this cuts two ways: a corporate, workforce or digital proposition sold here can reach far beyond the trust's own 10,612 staff, while a clinical device proposition is still a single-trust sale. On digital specifically, the trust agreed with Warrington and Halton Teaching Hospitals to re-procure a single shared-instance electronic patient record; the July 2026 board papers record a Joint EPR Programme Board and carry corporate risk 630, 'If the Trust cannot move to a single EPR then there is a risk of duplication of effort, barriers to integrating clinical services and suboptimal use of available facilities', opened 30 April 2025, graded 15 and owned by Director of Informatics Malcolm Gandy. Not verified: whether the trust operates a formal representative booking or access system, and what its policy is on unsolicited supplier visits. No such page or policy is published on merseywestlancs.nhs.uk; a direct enquiry to purchasing@merseywestlancs.nhs.uk would settle this. Not verified: the identity of the Head or Deputy Head of Procurement. The Chief Finance Officer, Gareth Lawrence, is the board-level owner of finance, contracting and procurement, but the trust publishes no named procurement staff, and no name has been taken from a procurement notice, so none is asserted here; the trust's own organisation chart or a direct approach would settle it. Not verified: how the ERIC 2024/25 high-risk backlog figure of £1,165,000 reconciles with the £7.7m of capital the annual report says was spent in the same year on the built estate 'including ongoing work to address backlog maintenance', and how much of the Southport and Ormskirk three-year programme is captured in the return. The trust's own ERIC submission and the estates section of its board papers would settle this. The July 2026 board papers record it as an ongoing programme with an assurance report to the Executive Committee but name no award. Not verified: any 2026/27 outturn. reportFacts.fact: The single most time-critical commercial fact about this trust. A large share of its medical equipment has sat inside a managed equipment service bundled into the PFI, and that MES expires in 2026. At expiry the trust has to buy the functioning equipment at net book value or replace it, which means an equipment re-provision decision of unusual scale is live in the current year. Any capital equipment rep should be asking about this before anything else.
reportFacts.figure: 'The PFI arrangement also incorporates a managed equipment service (MES) provided by GE which expires in 2026. The legal title of equipment remains with GE for the duration of the contract, passing to the Trust at the end of the contract term. At that point, the Trust will purchase all functioning MES equipment at a price equivalent to the current net book value.' The trust also holds two further managed service contracts inherited from Southport and Ormskirk, one for energy management and one for radiology equipment, both accounted for as service concession arrangements.
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Notes to the Accounts, Note 28 On-SoFP PFI, LIFT or other service concession arrangements

reportFacts.fact: This is the money a device, consumables or pharma rep is competing for, and 2024/25 is the first clean full-year baseline for the merged trust. Treat the year-on-year jump as merger arithmetic, not demand growth: MWL only came into being on 1 July 2023, so the 2023/24 comparatives cover nine months of the combined organisation and three months of the legacy St Helens and Knowsley trust alone. Total operating expenditure of £1,012,071,000 sets the scale of the account.
reportFacts.figure: Supplies and services - clinical (excluding drugs costs) £66,927,000 in 2024/25 (2023/24: £51,307,000). Supplies and services - general £8,240,000 (2023/24: £5,647,000). Drug costs (drugs inventory consumed and purchase of non-inventory drugs) £49,028,000 (2023/24: £38,793,000). Total operating expenses £1,012,071,000 (2023/24: £790,253,000).
