reportFacts.fact: The live in-year position, and the number that governs whether anything gets bought this year. The whole 2026/27 plan rests on delivering £49.7m of cost improvement recurrently, with no non-recurrent cushion at all, and cash at Month 3 was down to £2.9m. Capital is also running well behind plan. Any proposition here has to be argued as recurrent cash released or activity delivered, and a capital-funded product should be timed against the board's monthly capital reporting rather than pitched cold.
reportFacts.figure: 2026/27 plan is 'a balanced positon, which includes £16.7m Deficit Support Funding and assumes delivery of £49.7m recurrent CIP'. At Month 3 (June 2026) the adjusted position was a £6.8m deficit, or £11.0m excluding deficit support funding, in line with plan. CIP transacted year to date £9.9m, with £55.7m of schemes identified in year against the £49.7m target. Cash balance at Month 3 £2.9m. Capital plan £42.2m including PFI lifecycle and lease remeasurements, with £2.5m spent year to date, £5.4m below plan. £32.2m of capital PDC funding assumed for 2026/27.
reportFacts.where: Trust Board Papers, meeting of 29 July 2026, Integrated Performance Report, Board Summary - Finance, and the Finance and Performance Committee assurance report, Finance Report Month 3 2026/27

reportFacts.fact: MWL is not a distressed buyer, and that changes the pitch. Where many trusts carry an auditor's exception report naming a weakness in financial sustainability, MWL's auditors reported an unqualified opinion and expressly had nothing to report on value for money. That means proposals here are judged on merit and business case rather than filtered through external regulatory scrutiny of every spending decision, but it also means there is no crisis to lever and no burning platform argument available.
reportFacts.figure: 'In our auditor's report, issued on 27 June 2025 ... we reported an unqualified opinion on the Trust's financial statements' and 'we have nothing to report in respect of whether the Trust has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources for the year ended 31 March 2025'. Certified by Sarah Ironmonger, Key Audit Partner, for Grant Thornton UK LLP, Manchester, 7 January 2026.
reportFacts.where: Independent auditor's report to the directors of Mersey and West Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, year ended 31 March 2025, sections 'Audit completion' and 'Report on other legal and regulatory requirements'

reportFacts.fact: How this trust actually awards business. Its own published contract register shows a buyer that routes almost everything through existing national frameworks or below-threshold direct award, with open competition a rarity. A supplier that is not already on NHS Supply Chain, NHS Shared Business Services, Crown Commercial Service or HealthTrust Europe frameworks is structurally disadvantaged here, and framework position is a more useful conversation than tender-watching. Derivation rule, so it can be judged: counted as the number of the 529 contract rows in the register whose 'Procurement Route' field records each route; 235 rows record no route at all, so the counts describe only the 294 rows where a route is stated and no percentage of total spend is claimed.
reportFacts.figure: 529 contracts listed, all with Mersey and West Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust as contracting authority, register dated 2025-08-26 12:41:28 GMT. Only 9 rows record an 'Open Procedure' route. Framework direct award, framework further competition and below-threshold direct award account for the large majority of routed rows. Named frameworks appearing include NHS Supply Chain, NHS Shared Business Services, Crown Commercial Service (CCS RM references), HealthTrust Europe ComIT and Total Orthopaedic Solutions.
reportFacts.where: MWL Contract Report for Publication, as of 2025-08-26, Procurement Route and Framework Title columns

reportFacts.fact: The commercial reason to treat MWL as bigger than its bed base. It sells services to other NHS organisations at scale, so a workforce, payroll, occupational health, informatics or pathology proposition sold here can be sold once and used across many organisations. The Lead Employer service alone touches more than 13,000 doctors in training across eight NHS England regions, and the trust hosts the Mid-Mersey Digital Alliance, which supplies informatics to other NHS bodies and GP surgeries. A clinical device sale, by contrast, remains a single-trust sale.
reportFacts.figure: Non-patient care services to other bodies income £34,869,000 in 2024/25 (2023/24: £36,368,000), described as 'services provided to other NHS bodies, including pathology, CIPHA scheme incomes, IT and HR / payroll services'. Education and training income £30,024,000. The trust 'acts as a Lead Employer for over 13,000 Resident Doctors in training across the country, on behalf of NHS England'.
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Note 4 Other operating income and the note beneath it, read with section 1.2 Overview of the purpose and activities of the Trust

trusts.name: Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust
trusts.context: As of the June 2026 RTT period, Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust carries a waiting list of 55,547, with 65.5% of patients treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 11.9 weeks, and 319 patients waiting over 52 weeks (8 over 65 weeks, none over 78). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier, and reported 105 total C. difficile cases (63 trust-apportioned) in 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £3,899,000 against a total estates backlog of £70,345,000. Its highest-pressure specialities on the 18-week measure are Trauma & Orthopaedics (16.4%) and ENT (15.4%). For a rep, the segment-4 tier means spending decisions are visible to NHS England and any proposition needs to be argued on activity delivered or cost released, and the estates backlog figure signals theatre/ward equipment and infrastructure risk as a live opening.
trusts.news: The Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26 (year ended 31 March 2026), the trust's own most recently published report, records an operating deficit for the year of £14,276,000 (2024/25: £28,304,000) and an adjusted financial performance deficit of £21,100,000 on the control-total basis used to assess NHS trusts (2024/25: £15,220,000 adjusted deficit). The external auditor's exception report confirms a significant weakness in financial sustainability first identified in June 2025 for 2024/25 remains in place for 2025/26, stating the trust's three-year plan forecasts a breakeven position in 2026/27 dependent on £27m of additional funding and delivery of £57.3m of efficiencies. The trust reported 7 Never Events in 2025/26. Gross capital expenditure was £39,996,000 in 2025/26 (2024/25: £24,472,000), and the trust plans to spend approximately £37.2 million on capital in 2026/27 subject to funding approval from NHS England. Separately, a recruitment process for a new Chair was underway in 2026 via GatenbySanderson and NHS England's non-executive opportunities listings, and the trust's own recruitment microsite for the Chair role is now marked inactive, consistent with applications having closed; the identity of any incoming Chair is not yet confirmed on the trust's live board page. Not verified: the outcome or start date of that Chair recruitment.
trusts.structure: Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust runs hospital and community services from three main sites (Pinderfields, Dewsbury and Pontefract) and became a teaching trust in May 2023 under a sponsored partnership with the University of Leeds, having previously traded as Mid Yorkshire Hospitals NHS Trust; its own news page confirms the name change and the Leeds sponsorship. On procurement, the trust's own partnerships page states it is 'an active member of the West Yorkshire Integrated Care System' and works 'with WYAAT members to further develop procurement services across the acute Trusts', confirming a shared arrangement rather than describing a fully standalone procurement function. The West Yorkshire Association of Acute Trusts (WYAAT) is a collaboration of six acute trusts across West Yorkshire and Harrogate (Airedale, Bradford Teaching Hospitals, Calderdale and Huddersfield, Harrogate and District, Leeds Teaching Hospitals, and Mid Yorkshire Teaching), and WYAAT's own procurement page states it 'hosts the procurement collaboration on behalf of all providers of NHS services in West Yorkshire', bringing together procurement specialists to standardise products and reduce pricing across the region. WYAAT's page does not state that it purchases directly on every member trust's behalf, so treat this as a standardisation and price-leverage collaborative sitting alongside each trust's own buying, rather than a single central purchasing agency in the way Hull's Humber and North Yorkshire Procurement Collaborative operates. Not verified: a dedicated Mid Yorkshire-specific procurement or supplier contact page could not be found on midyorks.nhs.uk at the time of research; procurement notices for the trust are published via Find a Tender under its own name, and a direct approach to the trust's corporate/communications team (01924 543637) would be needed to identify a named procurement contact.

trusts.name: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: A large elective list under real strain, but an estate that looks almost untroubled, and the gap between those two things is the whole commercial story. The waiting list stands at 70,637 with 62.4% treated within 18 weeks against the constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 13.5 weeks, 1,888 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 202 over 65 weeks and 4 over 78 weeks (NHS England RTT, June 2026). Median waits by speciality run from 11.4 weeks in Dermatology and 12.6 in Ophthalmology up to 16.1 in Gynaecology and 18.3 in Trauma and Orthopaedics, so orthopaedics and gynaecology are where the pressure actually sits. The CQC rating is Requires Improvement (as at 04/08/2026) and the trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. It recorded 1 Never Event (April 2025 to March 2026) and 56 C. difficile cases against a return total of 186 (2024/25). The estate figures are the outlier: high-risk backlog maintenance of just £941,605 out of a total backlog of £5,050,624, and no critical infrastructure risk recorded against equipment (ERIC, 2024/25). Those are tiny numbers for an acute trust of this size, and the reason is structural rather than virtuous, which the structure section sets out. For a rep, that combination points the conversation away from estate replacement and towards throughput: orthopaedic and gynaecology capacity, theatre and diagnostic productivity, and anything that shortens a pathway. Segment 3 means the trust is not in mandated support but is under enhanced oversight, so a business case still has to be argued on activity delivered or recurrent cost released rather than on clinical preference alone.
trusts.news: The audited 2024/25 annual report reports a breakeven position against a breakeven plan on the NHS reporting basis, with closing cash of £93.4m. It also carries an external auditor's exception report. The auditors inspected a 2024/25 breakeven plan containing £50.1m of efficiencies, 'which is significantly higher than the levels previously delivered by the Trust', and raised a significant weakness in the trust's arrangements for improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness, concluding there was 'a significant risk of financial loss if the Trust is unable to deliver the savings and efficiency gains required'. Against that £50.1m plan the trust delivered £43.7m. Capital investment more than doubled year on year, to £70.6m from £35.8m, and the report names the four largest schemes: Diagnostic Assessment Centre £31.9m, Electronic Patient Record £17.8m, Clinical Equipment Replacement £7.0m and other digital investment £3.6m. The report also records that the trust has had no external Use of Resources review since December 2019, when it was rated Requires Improvement, and that a 2024 self-assessment left it at the same rating. Much fresher than the accounts: the Norfolk and Waveney University Hospitals Group Board papers for the meeting in public on 05/08/2026 give a live 2026/27 position for NNUH. Year to date the trust reported a deficit of £6.0m against a planned £6.1m, so slightly ahead of plan, with cost improvement delivery of £6.5m against a £6.07m target, but 'the current forecast outturn projects a £14.1m deficit against the Trust's break-even plan', driven by an anticipated shortfall in cost improvement delivery later in the year. The same paper names the two cost lines moving the wrong way: 'There has been an increase in supplies costs and an adverse variance in net drugs expenditure', partly offset by a £1.3m underspend on care group pay. Capital expenditure is reported as below plan because of delays to the NaNOC2 project. The 03/06/2026 Group Board minutes record the Acting Executive Managing Director reporting that NNUH had reduced the residual gap against 'its £52 million CIP requirement' for the year.
trusts.structure: NNUH does not stand alone any more, and getting this wrong will cost a rep the meeting. Since May 2025 it has been one of three trusts in the Norfolk and Waveney University Hospitals Group, alongside James Paget University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust and The Queen Elizabeth Hospital King's Lynn NHS Foundation Trust. The group's own Declarations of Interest register as at 01/04/2026 puts the arrangement beyond doubt: David Roberts is recorded as Interim Chair of JPUH, QEH and NNUH, Lesley Dwyer as Chief Executive of JPUH, QEH and NNUH, and each entry adds that the appointment is 'Appointed to all three NHS Foundation Trust Boards. Group appointment is hosted by NNUH.' The same is true of the Group Chief Finance Officer, Chief Medical Officer, Chief Nurse and the group non-executive directors. So one executive team, one Group Board sitting as a General Purpose Joint Committee, and NNUH is the host organisation for the group appointments. Each trust nonetheless remains a separate statutory body with its own Executive Managing Director on its own board, and the Group Chief Finance Officer told the Board on 03/06/2026 that the three trusts 'each needed to maintain materially correct income and expenditure positions' and that 'the External Auditors would assess each statutory organisation individually'. Practically that means strategy, oversight and clinical leadership are group-level while the profit and loss account you are affecting is still trust-level. On procurement, NNUH's own published procurement pipeline page states that the pipeline covers 'potential commercial activity above £2m in value that NNUH may progress in coming months and years' and that 'Some of the commercial activity listed may be progressed in collaboration with other organisations, for example Norfolk and Waveney Procurement Collaboration which is a partnership of all the NHS provider trusts in the Norfolk and Waveney Integrated Care System.' The published route in for a supplier is a single mailbox, Corp.Proc@nnuh.nhs.uk. The estate is the other structural fact. The main hospital is a Private Finance Initiative building: contracts were concluded with Octagon Healthcare Limited on 09/01/1998 for an 809 bed hospital plus a 144 bed extension signed 14/07/2000, payments began on 15/08/2001, and a 2003/04 refinancing extended the minimum term from 30 to 35 years. The trust carries a legal obligation to pay Octagon for maintenance of the PFI hospital over the life of the contract, which is why the ERIC backlog maintenance figures in the context paragraph are so low: most of that risk sits with the PFI special purpose vehicle, not with the trust. A rep selling anything that touches the fabric of the building, fixed installation, plant or ward infrastructure at the Norwich site is dealing with a PFI contractor's change process, not simply with an NHS estates team. On RAAC: reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete is a real and material issue in this group, but it is not at NNUH. It is at the two partner hospitals. The Group Board papers of 05/08/2026 record discharge lounge space at QEH 'now available following completion of the RAAC works', and both QEH and JPUH are in the national New Hospital Programme, with the group's own new hospital build page describing two new hospitals at King's Lynn and Gorleston. Not verified: whether Norfolk and Waveney Procurement Collaboration operates as a single buying function with binding awards, as a category-led alignment, or as a looser forum. NNUH's page names it but does not describe its governance, and there is no separate published collaboration site; the collaboration's terms of reference, or a direct question to Corp.Proc@nnuh.nhs.uk, would settle it. Not verified: whether NNUH has a clinical procurement nurse or equivalent standardisation gatekeeper, and whether the trust operates a formal rep booking or credentialing system. No such page is published on nnuh.nhs.uk; the procurement mailbox would settle both. Not verified: any 2025/26 audited outturn. No 2025/26 annual report has been published, so nothing here asserts a 2025/26 outturn; the current-year figures quoted are 2026/27 in-year board figures, which are unaudited and explicitly described as subject to further validation. Not verified: whether the £88m technology investment referenced in group communications is capital available to NNUH specifically or is a system-wide envelope, so no NNUH share is asserted.

reportFacts.fact: One chief executive and one chair now sit on all three Norfolk acute trust boards, and NNUH is the host. This is the single most important commercial fact about the trust. trusts.name: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: The elective picture is large but not catastrophic, and the safety picture is where the problem sits. The waiting list stands at 76,029 with 60.2% treated within 18 weeks in June 2026, against a constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 14.0 weeks and 330 patients waiting over 52 weeks, but nobody at all beyond 65 or 78 weeks in that month. By speciality the June 2026 median waits run Cardiology 17.0 weeks, Trauma and Orthopaedics 16.4, ENT 15.9, Gynaecology 15.7, General Surgery 13.2, Ophthalmology 12.9, Dermatology 12.1 and Urology 11.4. The trust is rated Requires improvement by the Care Quality Commission as at 04/08/2026 and sits in NHS oversight segment 3. Against that, it reported 6 Never Events across April 2025 to March 2026 and 116 cases of C. difficile in 2024/25, and it carries £7,761,092 of high-risk backlog maintenance inside a total backlog of £70,368,955 on the 2024/25 ERIC return. For a rep, the commercial reading is that this is not primarily a long-waiter recovery account, because the 65 and 78-week tails are already cleared and the median is inside 18 weeks in every one of the eight tracked specialities. It is a safety, infection prevention and theatre-process account. Six Never Events and the highest C. difficile count in this batch give a named problem to surgical safety, checklist and site-marking products, decontamination and equipment cleaning, antimicrobial stewardship and single-use versus reprocessed device arguments. The high-risk maintenance backlog says the same thing from the estate side. Segment 3 means the trust is expected to diagnose and fix its own problems rather than being told what to do, so a proposal that arrives with the trust's own numbers attached will get a hearing that a generic capacity pitch will not.
trusts.news: The 2024/25 annual report and accounts records a sixth consecutive year of financial balance on the regulator's control total basis, a £0.0m surplus, while the statutory Statement of Comprehensive Income shows a £17.05m deficit for the year against a £65.0m deficit in 2023/24. The external auditor reported nothing by exception on value for money, stating 'We have nothing to report in this respect' on significant weaknesses in arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness, which puts this trust in a materially better audit position than several of its peers. The same report declares seven Never Events in 2024/25, three of which had not previously been declared, with the incident summaries covering wrong-side block and related surgical events at Peterborough City Hospital. The public board pack for the meeting of 9 July 2026 is considerably fresher and shows the 2026/27 year going backwards: an adjusted year-to-date position of £4.9m deficit against a planned £3.3m deficit at Month 2, £1.6m adverse to plan, driven by £0.7m of industrial action costs and £0.9m of under-delivery on variable elective and unbundled diagnostic income. Financial improvement plan delivery is running at 40% of target and £4.7m behind plan, with every division except Facilities under-delivering, and agency spend has exceeded the cap year to date by almost double, 68% of it medical consultant cover. On safety the same pack is more encouraging: the Hospital Management Committee 'noted the continued trend of zero Never Events since January 2026', C. difficile rolling twelve-month performance is running 12.6% below the 2025/26 threshold, and no new MRSA cases had been reported since November. The infection prevention report for May 2026 records 10 C. difficile cases in the month, seven at Peterborough City Hospital, two at Hinchingbrooke and one community-onset healthcare-associated, taking the year to date to 25 cases, three over local trajectory, and names antibiotic prescribing and overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics as the main focus for 2026/27 after a previous focus on equipment, bed and mattress cleaning. On capital, the 2026/27 total capital programme is planned at £77,833k, of which the New Hospital Programme accounts for £50,248k, with £30.3m approved over five years for Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete remediation at Hinchingbrooke and £9,701k of that falling in 2026/27. The Peterborough Community Diagnostic Centre is in construction, the final element of the Stamford site sale completed in May 2026, and an Electronic Patient Record has an indicative funding notification of £2.55m split between capital and revenue but no national approval yet.
trusts.structure: North West Anglia buys for itself. It is a single foundation trust running three acute sites, Peterborough City Hospital, Hinchingbrooke Hospital and Stamford and Rutland Hospital, with no group model, no shared executive team and no host role for anybody else's procurement. Procurement sits under the Chief Finance Officer: the trust's own executive profile for Joel Harrison states he is responsible for 'Finance, IM&T and Procurement', and the 2024/25 annual report's own description of the same post says 'Finance, Procurement, Estates and Facilities'. That single reporting line matters commercially, because the person who signs off a purchase also owns the financial improvement programme that is currently 40% delivered and £4.7m behind plan. The trust's supplier notice sets out the actual route in: tender opportunities are published through Atamis, the NHS eCommercial platform, with no pre-requisites before registering; suppliers need an NHS Shared Business Services account and must hold a valid purchase order or at minimum a PO number before supplying; accounts payable is handled by NHS Shared Business Services on 30-day terms from receipt of an acceptable invoice. Two email routes are published, a general purchasing inbox and a separate inbox specifically for the Hinchingbrooke Hospital Redevelopment Programme, which is the single clearest signal in the trust's public material about where new money is going. The estate adds a second buying route that is easy to miss: Peterborough City Hospital is a PFI site, the accounts carry a PFI finance-lease building asset of £331.7m at 31/05/2026 alongside £66.2m in an 'M1 programme for asset replacement (PFI)', and the July 2026 board pack shows the Uninterruptible Power Supply scheme forecast cut from £2,724k to £1,124k while the trust waits on a revised cashflow and programme from the PFI contractor, with main construction now pushed to 2027/28. Anything touching that estate goes through the PFI contractor, not through the trust alone. On the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough question specifically: the trust's published Trust Strategy 2025/26 to 2031 names Cambridgeshire Community Services, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust, Cambridge University Hospitals and Royal Papworth Hospital as system partners, says 'No single organisation can deliver transformation of this scale alone and therefore as a system we have agreed to work collectively to deliver change at pace', and records that the trust hosts 'one of the system's two Health and Care Partnerships, the North Place'. The 2024/25 annual report likewise describes a Cambridgeshire and Peterborough joint capital plan setting investment priorities across all organisations in the system, and records that cost improvement and long-term financial sustainability actions are being taken by the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Integrated Care System. Not verified: whether any of that system working extends to joint or shared procurement. Nothing on the trust's own procurement or supplier pages, in the Trust Strategy, or in the 2024/25 annual report describes a shared procurement service, a lead-provider buying arrangement or a category-management collaborative with Cambridge University Hospitals, Royal Papworth or Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust, so no such arrangement is asserted here; a direct question to the purchasing inbox, or the trust's Standing Financial Instructions and scheme of delegation, would settle it. Not verified: whether the trust is a member or customer of the East of England NHS Collaborative Procurement Hub. The hub's own homepage describes a regional footprint across Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Essex, Hertfordshire, Norfolk and Suffolk but names no member trusts, and the trust's own material does not mention it, so membership is not claimed either way; the hub's own membership list would settle it. Not verified: any named procurement post-holder below board level. The annual report refers to 'the Trust's Head of Procurement' in the context of the Modern Slavery statement but does not name the person, no procurement contact page publishes names, and the layer-1 contacts file carries no named buyer for this trust, so no name is given here rather than a guessed one; the published inboxes are the correct first approach. Not verified: any 2026/27 outturn. Only a Month 2 in-year position exists, and the 2024/25 report is the latest set of accounts, so no current-year outturn is asserted. Note also a genuine period conflict a rep should not trip over: the trust's own 2024/25 annual report declares seven Never Events in that financial year, while the layer-1 figure of 6 covers April 2025 to March 2026 and comes from the national return. They are different years, not a contradiction, and the July 2026 board pack records zero Never Events since January 2026.

reportFacts.fact: Patient safety is this trust's weakest oversight domain and it has not moved. The trust scored the worst possible domain outcome for patient safety in every quarter of 2025/26 while its other domains improved or held. For a rep in infection prevention, surgical safety, decontamination or medical devices, this is the single number to open on, because it is the trust's own scoring against the national framework rather than an outside opinion.

reportFacts.where: Public Board of Directors meeting pack, 9 July 2026, part 1, section 4 'NHS Oversight Framework: 2025/26 Quarter 4 - Trust Position' and Appendix E

reportFacts.fact: The trust has named its own next infection prevention priority in writing, and it is antimicrobial stewardship rather than cleaning. Equipment, bed and mattress cleaning was last year's focus. A supplier arriving with a cleaning or surface product is a year late; a supplier with diagnostics, sampling turnaround, isolation or stewardship support is aimed at what the infection prevention and control team says it is working on now.
reportFacts.figure: 10 C. difficile cases in May 2026, seven at Peterborough City Hospital, two at Hinchingbrooke and one community onset healthcare associated, taking the year to date to 25 cases, three over local trajectory; post infection reviews name inappropriate antibiotic prescribing, delayed sample, incomplete stool chart, failure to isolate and diagnostic stewardship among the top five themes

reportFacts.fact: The savings programme is failing early in the year, which changes what a proposal has to prove. At Month 2 the trust had delivered two fifths of its financial improvement target and every clinical division was behind. Anything pitched here has to be argued as recurrent cash released or activity delivered, and a rep who can carry a divisional saving into a business case is more useful to this trust than one selling on features.
reportFacts.figure: Adjusted year-to-date position of £4.9m deficit against a planned deficit of £3.3m at Month 2 2026/27, £1.6m adverse to plan; FIP delivery year to date at 40% of target and £4.7m behind plan, with all divisions except Facilities under-delivering; agency spend has exceeded the year-to-date cap by almost double, 68% of it medical consultant cover

reportFacts.fact: There is a very large capital programme running and two thirds of it is one building. A rep with a capital-funded product should be tracking the New Hospital Programme and the RAAC remediation at Hinchingbrooke, and should note the trust's own warning that the RAAC allocation is less than it asked for and has to be delivered quickly to avoid losing later-year money, which creates real urgency on anything on that critical path.

reportFacts.fact: Clinical consumables spend rose by around £6.8m in a single year, an 18% rise, and the drugs bill rose by around £10.2m. That sets the commercial scale of the account and tells you which conversation carries the bigger number: cost-per-procedure and standardisation on the consumables line, switch and biosimilar programmes on the drugs line.

reportFacts.fact: Read the headline and the accounts together. The trust reports a sixth consecutive year of balance on the regulator's control total basis, but the statutory accounts show a substantial deficit, and unlike several peer trusts its auditor reported nothing by exception on value for money. That combination is worth knowing: the finance function here is credible and the audit position is clean, so a well-evidenced business case will not be dismissed on governance grounds, but the underlying deficit means it still has to pay for itself.

trusts.name: Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: One of the largest acute providers in England: around 20,000 staff, four main hospital sites (Salford Royal, The Royal Oldham, Fairfield General, Rochdale Infirmary) and roughly 2,000 beds, serving over a million people across Salford, Oldham, Bury and Rochdale. Operating income for 2024/25 was £2,013,226k. The elective position is severe and is the headline commercial opening: a waiting list of 133,771, only 57.2% treated within 18 weeks, a median wait of 15.2 weeks, and 3,608 patients waiting over 52 weeks - the highest 52-week breach count in this batch. Quality and infection metrics are also under pressure: 9 Never Events and 132 C. difficile cases. High-risk backlog maintenance stands at £3,369,731. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4 (mandated intensive support), which means external scrutiny of spend and a hard bias towards anything that demonstrably reduces cost or shortens a pathway. Note the trust's own 2024/25 Annual Report, published earlier, states it was then in Segment 3 - the segment 4 position is the later, current one.
trusts.news: On 06/08/2026 the trust announced that Salford Royal had joined a Greater Manchester roll-out of an AI prostate cancer detection tool, a pilot led by Greater Manchester Cancer Alliance also running at Wigan, Bolton and Stockport. The tool analyses prostate MRI scans and flags those most likely to show cancer so radiologists can prioritise the highest-risk men. Mr Sotonye Tolofari, consultant urological surgeon at Salford Royal, is quoted leading the trust's involvement. Commercially this tells a rep two things: NCA is willing to be an early site for diagnostic technology, and the buying decision for that class of product ran through the Greater Manchester Cancer Alliance rather than the trust alone - so a system-level route can matter as much as the trust route. Separately, the 2024/25 Annual Report records that an outline business case was developed during 2024/25 to procure and implement an NCA-wide electronic patient record, with a formal programme team established and a data cleanse and electronic document management workstream under way. Any product that needs to integrate with the EPR should expect that programme to gate it.
trusts.structure:
The trust is organised into five Care Organisations - Salford, Bury, Rochdale, Oldham, and a trust-wide Diagnostics and Pharmacy Care Organisation covering pathology, pharmacy and radiology across all four hospital sites. This is the single most important structural fact for a rep. Each Care Organisation has, as a minimum, its own Chief Officer, Director of Operations, Medical Director, Director of Nursing, Finance Director and Human Resources Director (2024/25 Annual Report, 'Care Organisations', pp.4-7). A trust-wide pitch therefore has at least five internal customers with their own operational leadership, sitting under one corporate board and one set of shared corporate services. Salford Royal carries the specialist weight: the Manchester Centre for Clinical Neurosciences (neurosurgery, neurology, stroke, spinal surgery) and the Greater Manchester Major Trauma Hospital, which opened on 07/05/2024. Royal Oldham has vascular surgery, urology, gynaecology, a trauma unit and a level three maternity unit. Rochdale Infirmary hosts a GIRFT-accredited elective day case surgical hub serving the whole trust - the natural target for elective recovery products. Bury (Fairfield General) covers A&E, elective surgery, ENT and a specialist stroke unit. On the trust's public website the section is now titled 'Our Hospitals', though the URL still reads 'our-care-organisations'.

Pharmacy is run as a trust-wide group service with named, publicly listed contacts (page last updated 03/07/2026): Lindsay Harper as NCA Group Director of Pharmacy, Gavin Leahy as Interim Director of Pharmacy, plus Heads of Pharmacy, Principal Pharmacists and Chief Pharmacy Technicians per site. The Head of Pharmacy post at Royal Oldham is listed as vacant. There are four inpatient dispensaries, one per site. Outpatient dispensing at Royal Oldham and Salford Royal is contracted out to Rowlands Pharmacy; Fairfield General and Rochdale dispense outpatients in-house. Two aseptic services units, at Salford Royal and Royal Oldham, prepare cytotoxic chemotherapy, antibiotics, clinical trial products and parenteral nutrition.

Procurement: the trust runs its own in-house procurement department. The 2024/25 Annual Report ('Procurement and Supply Chain', pp.46-47) states that the majority of the department's senior team are CIPS qualified, many recently upgraded to chartered status, and that the department also uses central framework contract providers and runs a supplier relationship management process with regular contract and supplier meetings. Bidders must evidence Modern Slavery Act compliance under PPN 03/23, and the trust has adopted the Social Value Model from PPN 06/20, applying a minimum 10% weighting in all procurements to net zero and social value - so a bid that ignores social value is losing a tenth of the score before it starts. Procurements from 17/02/2025 fall under the Procurement Act 2023 and the Procurement Regulations 2024.

Not verified: whether NCA buys through a Greater Manchester system-level or shared procurement service, or provides procurement services for other organisations. No public procurement, suppliers or e-tendering page could be found on the trust website, and the Annual Report describes an in-house department without naming a shared service. The trust does act as host for other NHS bodies - notably Advancing Quality Alliance (AQuA), £5,044k of hosted income in 2024/25 - but that is a hosted service, not a buying arrangement. This would be settled by a Freedom of Information request to the trust, or by the trust publishing a supplier/tenders page.

The board page lists only the corporate board; the Annual Report confirms the roles exist but does not name the current post-holders in the section read. A board paper listing Care Organisation leadership, or an FOI request, would settle it.

Also relevant but not among the six named below: Lorna Allan is Chief Digital and Information Officer (joined September 2022) and is the natural first contact for anything touching the EPR programme; Gertie Nic Philib is Chief People and Strategy Officer; Sheena McDonnell is Chair and Professor Chris Harrison is Non-Executive Director and Vice Chair, appointed vice chair in November 2025. trusts.name: Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: One of the largest acute trusts in England — QMC, City Hospital and Ropewalk House — and financially the hardest-pressed trust in this batch. 2025/26 closed £12.2m in deficit against a breakeven plan, having delivered £67.6m of a £97.7m efficiency target. 2026/27 asks for £106m of savings and the Board has already been told the level of ambition must increase. The Board's own view is that the cost base is unsustainable relative to income, so this is not a trust looking for nice-to-haves: bring a cash-releasing number or expect a short meeting. Their estate cannot rescue them either — the Tomorrow's NUH rebuild is postponed to 2037 at the earliest and they carry the fourth largest maintenance backlog in the country.
trusts.news: Month 2 (May 2026) reported to the public Board on 09/07/2026: £23.0m year-to-date deficit, £6.1m adverse to plan, with a £4.5m year-to-date overspend on clinical supplies and services driven by higher-than-planned activity. Efficiency delivery £6.3m against a £7.1m year-to-date plan. A “Plan B” is being worked up for the parts of Tomorrow's NUH that cannot wait until 2037, with backlog maintenance named as a main priority. The National Rehabilitation Centre, a 70-bed purpose-built NHS facility near Loughborough and the first of its kind in the UK, is staffed and run by NUH and due to open.
trusts.structure: NUH operates a strict “no purchase order, no payment” policy — an invoice without an official PO number, and not on the exception list, is rejected outright. The PO is issued before you start supplying and is emailed to the address held in your supplier record, so get your supplier details right before anything ships. Invoices go to NHS Shared Business Services, not to the trust; accountspayable@nuh.nhs.uk handles disputes. They aim to pay within 30 days and frequently do not: in 2024/25 only 59.9% of non-NHS invoices were paid on time by volume and 58.4% by value, so price your working capital accordingly. Contracts over £25k are published on Contracts Finder. The distinctive route in for a device company is CHEATA — the Centre for Healthcare Equipment and Technology Adoption, a contract-based service embedded in the trust's Clinical Engineering department offering value propositions, health economic analysis, evidence gathering, NICE engagement and regulatory advice to manufacturers at any stage. Contacts Dr Sarah Bolton (Business Manager) and Sinead Barker (Programme Co-ordinator), nuhnt.cheata@nhs.net. Not verified whether NUH runs a separate rep booking or accreditation system for ward and theatre access.

trusts.name: Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: A mental health, learning disability and community trust, so it files no consultant-led RTT return and carries no acute oversight segment — the data panel above will be thin, and that is correct rather than missing. It is nonetheless a substantial commercial organisation: turnover rose £66m to £693m in 2024/25, it holds £97.8m of cash, which it describes as one of the strongest positions in its local area, and it increased capital investment to £24.5m. Two things make it unusual. It is lead provider for three NHS provider collaboratives — forensic inpatient mental health, CAMHS Tier 4 and adult eating disorders — holding the budgets and commissioner responsibilities for those specialised services, so it buys as a commissioner as well as a provider. And it runs the Oxford Pharmacy Store, a trading service that grew by £28m in the year.
trusts.news: The Warneford Park programme is the big one: a redevelopment of the Warneford Hospital site in Headington, taken forward through a joint vehicle, Warneford Park LLP, with pre-planning application consultations launched in August 2024. The accounts record a contingent liability capped at £4,175k — if the trust does not proceed once planning permission is achieved and funding identified, it must reimburse in full the jointly incurred planning and preparatory costs. Alongside it, a new Jordan Hill Community Health Hub in North Oxford took £5.2m of estates capital in 2024/25. The trust targets net zero carbon by 2045 and has a revised Green Plan. Not verified: the 2025/26 annual report and accounts had not been published when this profile was written, so no current-year outturn is stated.
trusts.structure: Commercial leadership sits with the Chief Finance Officer, Heather Smith, and her portfolio is unusually wide: the trust states she is responsible for the financial and commercial leadership of the trust and also for the Information Management & Technology and Estates & Facilities teams, and that she is senior responsible officer for the Warneford Park programme. For estates, digital and major capital, that is a single accountable owner. She came from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, where she was also Chief Finance Officer, with earlier senior civil service finance roles at HMRC, BIS and HM Treasury — expect a public-sector business-case discipline rather than an NHS-only frame of reference. Operations are split in two, with separate Chief Operating Officers for Mental Health and Learning Disability (Dr Rob Bale) and for Community Health Services, Dentistry and Primary Care (Emma Leaver, in the role on an interim basis since 01/03/2025) — work out which side of that line your category falls before approaching. A caution on the contacts panel above: some Find a Tender notices associated with this trust carry @ouh.nhs.uk addresses and relate to Oxford University Hospitals sites, such as generator works at the Horton. Check which organisation a notice actually belongs to before using a contact. Not verified: no e-tendering portal or supplier representative booking system is published on the trust's public site, and not publishing one is not proof there isn't one.

trusts.name: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: One of the largest teaching trusts in England, running the John Radcliffe, Churchill, Nuffield Orthopaedic Centre and Horton General. Layer-1 verified position: 90,534 patients on the waiting list, 62.5% treated within 18 weeks, median wait 13.3 weeks and 1,713 waiting over 52 weeks. NHS oversight segment 3. Seven Never Events and 107 cases of C. difficile. High-risk backlog maintenance stands at £54,815,755, which is the single biggest structural story here: the trust's own annual report shows only circa £6.5m spent in 2024/25 on estates compliance and backlog maintenance combined, so the gap between the liability and the annual spend is roughly eight to one. Financially the trust reported a control-total deficit of £6.8m for 2024/25 against a planned position, but the underlying deficit (one-off items stripped out) is estimated at £77m, a deterioration of about 20% on the £61.3m underlying deficit a year earlier. It sits within the Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Berkshire West (BOB) Integrated Care System, which was placed into the national Investigation and Intervention regime during 2024/25 after the system-wide position deteriorated.
trusts.news: The chief executive seat is not settled. Professor Meghana Pandit remains the substantive Chief Executive Officer but has been on secondment to NHS England since 01/04/2025, first as Co-National Medical Director - Secondary Care and, from 01/04/2026, as a Deputy Chief Executive Officer to Sir Jim Mackey, splitting her time 50/50 between OUH and the national role. Simon Crowther took up the post of Acting Chief Executive Officer on 01/04/2025 and was appointed Interim Chief Executive Officer in September 2025 for the remainder of the secondment. Sir Andrew Morris OBE began a fresh term as Chair on 01/08/2026. The board has also refreshed heavily: Lynne Graham joined as a Non-Executive Director on 01/04/2026 and Kenny Kamal on 01/01/2026. Separately, the trust reset its procurement authorisation limits: a board paper taken in public on 11/03/2026 revised contract ratification thresholds upwards, moving the point at which a contract needs Trust Board sign-off from £500,000 to £3,000,000 for goods and services.
trusts.structure: OUH buys for itself. It runs an in-house Procurement and Supply Chain Team under a Director of Procurement and Supply Chain, with a published strategy organised around five areas: Strategic Sourcing - Divisional Procurement / Medical Technology; Strategic Sourcing - Corporate and Non-clinical; Supply Chain Transformation; Commercial and Contract Management; and Innovation and efficiency. There is a single published route in for suppliers: ProcurementandSuppliesQueries@ouh.nhs.uk. The function is not a shared service and the trust's own Standing Financial Instructions place procurement authority internally, with the Director of Procurement and Supply Chain ratifying all contracts up to the published UK regulatory limit. Note the split of a dedicated medical technology sourcing team from corporate/non-clinical sourcing - a device rep should be aiming at the former. The trust does host bodies for others, but the hosting named in the Standing Financial Instructions is the Thames Valley and Surrey Secure Data Environment, a data platform, not a procurement shared service. Not verified: the name of the current Director of Procurement and Supply Chain. The board directors page does not list the role (it is not a board-level post) and the published organisational structure chart does not name it; a direct enquiry to the procurement mailbox, or a recent procurement-related board paper naming the postholder, would settle it. Not verified: whether OUH and Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust operate any joint or shared procurement arrangement. The annual report confirms the two trusts work together at Place level within the Oxfordshire system and share governor-level links, but neither the OUH procurement page nor the Standing Financial Instructions describes any shared buying function, and Find a Tender notices carrying @ouh.nhs.uk addresses for Oxfordshire-wide services were not read in this session. Reading the specific Find a Tender notices, or the OUH Procurement and Supply Chain Strategy document itself, would settle who contracts for what. Not verified: the identity of the Chief Strategy Officer beyond the interim - Jay Mistry is listed as Interim Chief Strategy Officer with no substantive appointment shown.

reportFacts.fact: Clinical supplies and services spend - the line most device and consumables income sits in - grew by £32.3m in a single year, up 18.2%. reportFacts.fact: Drug costs are the trust's largest non-pay line and rose £18.9m year on year. For a pharma rep this is the scale of the medicines budget being managed, and it explains why pharmacy-led switch and biosimilar conversations get board attention here.

Any pitch that does not carry a cash-releasing saving will not clear the room.

Anything that reduces estates dependency - mobile, modular or point-of-care solutions that avoid a fixed-plant upgrade - has a live commercial hook.

Goods and services contracts now only reach the Trust Board above £3m, having previously gone to the board above £500,000; £1m to £3m sits with the Trust Management Executive; and the Director of Procurement and Supply Chain ratifies everything up to the published UK regulatory limit. This tells a rep exactly which door a deal of a given size goes through, and that mid-size deals now clear far faster than they did.

trusts.context: As at June 2026 the trust's RTT waiting list stands at 57,546, with 61.1% treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 13.3 weeks, 2,070 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 97 over 65 weeks and 4 over 78 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier, and recorded 8 Never Events (April 2025 to March 2026) and 73 cases of C. difficile against a threshold-relevant total of 189 (2024/25). High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £812,034 against a total backlog maintenance liability of £8,384,928. The specialty-level waits show Trauma & Orthopaedics (18.6%), Gynaecology (15.2%) and ENT (15.7%) as the longest 18-week performers among those recorded. For a rep, segment 4 combined with heavy T&O and ENT pressure points to elective recovery, theatre productivity and diagnostic capacity as the live conversations, but every proposal will be read against NHS England mandated-support oversight, so cost and activity evidence matters more than preference here.
trusts.news: The most recent published Annual Report and Accounts is for 2023/24 (signed and submitted to NHS England, dated on the ICB's hosted copy August 2024); no 2024/25 or 2025/26 annual report was found publicly available on the trust's own site, the Hampshire and Isle of Wight ICB microsite, or NHS England's publication page as at 28/08/2026. The trust's next Annual General Meeting is scheduled for 23 September 2026, per its own news archive, so the 2025/26 report had evidently not yet been published at the time of this research. All financial figures below are therefore 2023/24 actuals, labelled as such, plus the trust's own published 2024/25 plan. Not verified: the actual 2024/25 outturn, since no 2024/25 accounts have been located.
trusts.structure: The trust's own procurement page (checked live) states its Procurement and Supply Chain Team provides Strategic and Category Sourcing, Data Management, Commissioned Healthcare, Operational Procurement, Supply Chain Management and Advanced Inventory Management 'to Portsmouth Hospitals University NHS Trust (PHU), Isle of Wight NHS Trust (IWT) and Hampshire and Isle of Wight Integrated Care Board (ICB)'. The same page's own metadata brands this function 'NHS South of England Procurement Services (SoEPS)'. This means Portsmouth does not buy only for itself: it is the HOST for a procurement function that also buys for the Isle of Wight NHS Trust and for the Hampshire and Isle of Wight ICB directly, so a supplier win here can reach beyond Portsmouth's own estate. Separately, since 2023 Portsmouth Hospitals and Isle of Wight NHS Trust share a single Chair (Jenni Douglas-Todd, joined April 2025) and a single Chief Executive (Penny Emerit, CEO of PHU since March 2021 and of IWT since June 2023), with a single executive team and, since November 2024, a single corporate service across both trusts, confirmed on the trust's own live board page. Not verified, and not assumed: any link between this arrangement and Hampshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (ODS code RN5). Hampshire Hospitals is a separate organisation with its own board; nothing on Portsmouth's board or procurement pages names Hampshire Hospitals as part of this group or procurement arrangement, and no such link should be inferred from the shared ICB area alone.

trusts.name: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: The Royal Devon carries a waiting list of 74,021 with 63.6% of patients treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard (NHS England referral to treatment, June 2026), a median wait of 12.4 weeks, 1,536 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 175 over 65 weeks and 8 over 78 weeks. The speciality medians in the same June 2026 return spread widely: Trauma and Orthopaedics 18.6 weeks, ENT (ear, nose and throat) 16.9, Cardiology 14.9, General Surgery 14.1, Gynaecology 13.7, Ophthalmology 13.1, Urology 11.3 and Dermatology 9.0. The Care Quality Commission rating is Requires Improvement (as held on 04/08/2026) and the trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. It recorded 8 Never Events across April 2025 to March 2026 and 49 cases of C. difficile in 2024/25. Estates returns for 2024/25 (ERIC) put high-risk backlog maintenance at £13,656,522 within a total backlog of £168,157,279, with no capital equipment backlog recorded. Read commercially, this is an elective-throughput and estate-condition account rather than a crisis account: the long-wait tail is small by national standards but the 18-week percentage is far off standard, and the gap between the orthopaedic and ENT medians and the dermatology median tells a rep exactly which theatres and clinics are the constraint. Segment 3 means NHS England is watching spending decisions closely, so a proposition here has to be argued on activity delivered or cash released rather than on preference, and the near-£170m backlog figure means estate-dependent installations need a site condition conversation before a product conversation.
trusts.news: The trust published its Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26, with the Chair's introduction dated 24 June 2026, so a current-year outturn is available and is not carried forward from the previous edition. It reports a net deficit of £44m for 2025/26 excluding technical accounting adjustments, against a plan to break even, and states plainly that the plan was 'predicated on the delivery of a £68m savings plan' and that 'the key driver of this adverse financial position was significant under-delivery of the savings plan, alongside unfunded cost pressures relating to planned and emergency care demand exceeding expected levels'. The Delivering Best Value savings statement shows £68.8m planned against £39.4m delivered, a variance of £29.4m. In response the trust appointed a turnaround director, redesigned its savings programme architecture and rebuilt its accountability framework. The external auditor had nothing to report by exception on economy, efficiency and effectiveness for 2025/26. Capital expenditure was £101.7m in 2025/26, including community diagnostic centre development, and the chief executive's introduction records £18m secured to expand the Community Diagnostic Centre at the Nightingale Hospital Exeter and the opening of the new Atlantic MRI suite at North Devon District Hospital following a £2.3m NHS England investment. The trust formally exited the National Recovery Support Programme at the end of quarter one 2025/26, having been placed in segment 4 and the programme in November 2022 alongside other acute providers in Devon. The annual report also records that NHS England rated the board's own capability self-assessment as 'red', reflecting significant concerns arising from poor delivery, governance and other issues. The board meeting in public on 29 July 2026 sets the current year: the chief executive's report states the trust now has a plan achieving breakeven in 2026/27 that 'requires a savings programme of £80m', with detailed plans for 91% of it, a net £13.8m unmitigated risk at the end of quarter one, and a voluntary redundancy scheme that approved 114 of 582 applications and removes 81.77 whole time equivalents for a full-year recurrent saving of £4m into 2027/28. At month three the trust reported a £9.6m deficit in line with the revised plan. On capital, the Our Future Hospital report to the same board confirms the main North Devon District Hospital scheme has been placed in New Hospital Programme wave 3 with a build start between 2035 and 2038, while two enabling projects are funded: the staff residences rebuild (BAM on site, superstructure from September 2026) and the Twin MRI Extension Link, whose RIBA stage 2 cost report came back at £27.5m against the £22.6m allocated by the New Hospital Programme.
trusts.structure: The Royal Devon was formed on 1 April 2022 through the merger of The Royal Devon and Exeter NHS Foundation Trust and Northern Devon Healthcare NHS Trust, stated in those words in the trust's own Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26. That matters commercially because it left one organisation running two very different operating models from two main acute sites, the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital (Wonford) in Exeter and North Devon District Hospital in Barnstaple, plus a large community estate inherited from Northern Devon. The trust's own performance reporting still splits into Eastern Services and Northern Services, and the July 2026 board pack discusses northern services infrastructure and service continuity separately from the eastern site. A rep should treat these as two clinical markets with one corporate centre, not one homogeneous account. The single most important structural fact is that this trust no longer runs its own procurement in isolation. University Hospitals Plymouth's page for the Devon Procurement Service states that it 'is the collaborative procurement function for five NHS organisations in Devon, which was established in December 2025', naming Devon Partnership NHS Trust, Livewell South West, Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust and University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust, and that it 'manages all non-pay expenditure on behalf of the partner organisations and is governed by a shared delivery board with representatives from all partners'. The Royal Devon announced the same shared service in its 2024/25 annual report under the heading 'Shared NHS procurement system', naming four partner organisations at that point and stating that they 'spend more than £743m a year on common goods and services used to deliver patient care, yet we usually procure and manage these separately'. The arrangement is live and running: the audit committee report inside the 29 July 2026 board pack discusses feeding waiver themes and learning 'back through Devon Procurement Services and the Trust's usual processes', and the Finance and Operational Committee took a 'Procurement Services Quarterly Update' in July 2026. So a supplier winning here is potentially transacting across five Devon organisations, and the buying conversation sits in a shared function rather than inside the Royal Devon alone. The clinical route into that decision is still local, and the trust remains the customer for its own clinical sign-off. The trust also shares its Epic electronic patient record with Torbay and Plymouth, described in the 2025/26 annual report as paving the way for the first county-wide EPR in the first half of 2026/27, which is the same partner set as the procurement collaborative and is worth knowing for anything that has to integrate. Not verified: which organisation formally hosts the Devon Procurement Service and where accountability sits. The service's page and its plh-tr.devonprocurementservice@nhs.net contact mailbox sit with University Hospitals Plymouth, but no page read here states a host in those words, and the Royal Devon's own audit committee in July 2026 asked for 'clarity on whether the Trust is acting as host, customer or partner' across its shared services. The Devon Procurement Service's shared delivery board terms of reference would settle this. Not verified: whether clinical product choice at the Royal Devon can deviate from a collaborative award. Nothing read here states how far an individual partner trust can differ on clinical products, so do not assume a collaborative win is automatically a Royal Devon win. Not verified: the number of procurement staff and the current combined non-pay spend of the five-organisation service. The £743m figure is the Royal Devon's own 2024/25 statement about four organisations, published before Livewell South West appears on the current partner list, so it is not a current five-organisation figure. Not verified: a named individual to approach in the Devon Procurement Service. No staff are named on its page and the Hub's layer-one contacts file holds no named buyer for this trust, so the published mailbox is the only route evidenced here. Not verified: the trust's current NHS oversight segment. The Hub data layer records segment 3, while the trust's own 2025/26 annual report shows overall trust segmentation of 2 at quarter four 2025/26 and segment 4 for finance and productivity in the assessment published on 11 June 2026, and the chief executive's introduction in the same document gives a different breakdown again. NHS England's own published segmentation for the current quarter would settle it. Not verified: no external procurement or supplier engagement page was found on royaldevon.nhs.uk during this research, so no rep booking or representative access system is asserted here. Note on access: royaldevon.nhs.uk sits behind Akamai bot protection and refuses a plain curl or WebFetch request with HTTP 403. Every trust page and PDF cited here was retrieved with a full browser header set and returned HTTP 200 on 28/08/2026.

reportFacts.fact: The Royal Devon's non-pay buying now runs through a five-organisation Devon-wide collaborative, not through the trust alone. This is the single highest-leverage fact for a rep here: one relationship potentially reaches five Devon organisations, and the first approach should be pitched at that level rather than at a single department.

trusts.name: Sandwell and West Birmingham Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: As at the June 2026 RTT reporting period, Sandwell and West Birmingham Hospitals NHS Trust carries a waiting list of 66,744, with 61.8% of patients treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 14.0 weeks, 291 patients waiting over 52 weeks and a small residual of 2 patients over 65 weeks (0 over 78 weeks). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. It reported 3 Never Events and 61 cases of C. difficile against a trajectory of 149 for 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £3,562,725 against a total estates backlog of £187,290,044, with a capital equipment backlog of £2,705,681. Longest specialty waits are in ENT at 21.3% within 18 weeks and Cardiology at 18.4%, with Ophthalmology the strongest performer at 8.6%. For a rep, this is a mid-tier pressure profile rather than a crisis one: segment 3 gives more local latitude than segment 4, and the small 65/78-week tail suggests the trust has largely cleared its longest-standing backlog, but the sub-62% 18-week performance and the ENT/Cardiology waits are the live conversations.
trusts.news: The Integrated Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25 records a statutory Deficit for the year of £155,821,000 (2023/24: a surplus of £23,083,000), driven substantially by impairments and the year-on-year change in cost base. Measured against the NHS control-total framework, the Directors' Report states the trust delivered an adjusted-basis surplus of £5.951m against a £1.95m deficit plan, a position that included receipt of £41.292m of non-recurrent deficit funding and delivery of almost £42m of cost improvement programme savings; the same section notes the trust exited the year with an underlying deficit position worse than the headline result, because a significant proportion of the in-year improvement was non-recurrent. Gross capital expenditure was £124.208m in 2024/25 (2023/24: £77.133m), with named Estates capital-programme schemes including expenditure on the new Learning Campus on the Midland Metropolitan University Hospital (MMUH) site and £12m on Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (RAAC) remediation schemes on the trust's retained estate. Separately, the trust published a Programme Closure Report in May 2025 formally closing the MMUH capital programme: the hospital opened to patients on 6 October 2024 after a near 17-year programme that survived the 2018 collapse of original contractor Carillion, and the closure report states a Learning Campus was due to open in 2025 in partnership with Sandwell College and two universities, alongside plans for 750 new homes on the former City Hospital site. This directly updates any assumption that MMUH is still mid-build: the hospital is open and its delivery programme is formally closed, so capital and estate-risk framing for this trust should now centre on the retained (older) estate, principally the RAAC remediation programme, rather than the new hospital build itself.
trusts.structure: The trust's own website carries no dedicated procurement or supplier page; a site search returns only Modern Slavery Act references to procurement staff training, not a description of how the trust buys. The shared arrangement is confirmed instead from a Black Country partner trust's own site: The Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust's procurement page states plainly, 'The Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust is a member of the Black Country Alliance (BCA), a collaboration of trust procurement also including Sandwell & West Birmingham NHS Trust.' Wikipedia's account of this trust adds that the Black Country Alliance was formed in July 2015 with Dudley Group and Walsall Healthcare as a jointly-owned company limited by guarantee to enable collaborative contract bidding and shared back-office functions (payroll, IT, estates); this is a secondary source and not independently confirmed on a BCA-branded page of its own, so treat the exact scope of pooled versus separate buying as Not verified beyond what Dudley's page states. Leadership is also shared: the trust's live board page (read 28/08/2026) confirms Sir David Nicholson KCB CBE as Chairman, a role he holds concurrently across all four Black Country acute trusts (this one, Dudley Group, Royal Wolverhampton and Walsall Healthcare) under an arrangement the trust's own news site says runs until 2027. Chief Executive is Diane Wake, who took up the post in 2025 having previously been Chief Executive of The Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust since April 2017; a January 2026 trust news article confirms this and that she remains in post. A predecessor Chief Executive, Richard Beeken, still appears on Wikipedia and in some older search results and should be treated as out of date. Not verified: whether the Black Country Alliance extends to clinical product standardisation and sign-off for this trust or is limited to administrative/back-office pooling and competitive-tender bidding as Dudley's page implies; the BCA's own governance documents, not found live during this pass, would settle it. No CQC rating is asserted here as layer-1 carries no rating field for this trust, only an unrelated reporting-period date.

trusts.name: Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: A £1.76bn teaching trust across the Royal Hallamshire, Northern General, Weston Park, Charles Clifford and Jessop Wing, and one of the few in this batch that is genuinely in surplus — £6.93m, 0.4% of turnover, on turnover up 11.5%. That makes it a different sell from the turnaround trusts: they are not desperate, so a pure price argument carries less weight, and the trust says plainly that 2025/26 brings “an even more constrained financial position”. Their stated approach is driving out unnecessary variation rather than blanket cuts, which favours suppliers who can evidence standardisation and reduced variation over those offering a discount.
trusts.news: Clinical supplies spend rose more than a fifth in a year, to £164.3m. The trust has almost eliminated the longest waits for treatment while its waiting list grew 0.7%. Its stated priorities for the year are “driving out unnecessary variation, refining our ways of working and through partnerships explore how we deliver the best value for the resources we are given”, navigated as a partner in the wider South Yorkshire system rather than alone.
trusts.structure: Two published procurement commitments are directly actionable for a supplier. First, social value is a part of all competitive procurements and environmental considerations are built into procurement processes — so it is scored, not decorative. Second, and more unusually, the procurement teams are explicitly working to increase the use of local businesses and suppliers specifically to reduce the road miles in their supply chain and support the local economy. If you have a Yorkshire or northern distribution point, warehouse or manufacturing site, that is a scoring argument here and not merely a nice story — quantify the road miles saved. Note the trust runs two Chief Medical Officers, split into Development and Operations, so the right clinical sponsor depends on whether you are proposing a new service or improving an existing one. trusts.name: Somerset NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: An unusually integrated trust — acute (Musgrove Park and Yeovil District), community and mental health services under one board — which means a product with a pathway story spanning hospital and community has a single buyer here rather than three. The 2024/25 accounts show a £28.6m deficit, and 2026/27 carries a cost improvement plan of £80m, around 6.6% of operating expenses. They are delivering: May 2026 was breakeven to plan with CIP £0.4m ahead. The Board's stated worry is not the total but the mix — the pace of transformational savings and continued reliance on agency staffing. Something that structurally removes cost, rather than shaving a price, is what they are short of.
trusts.news: Reported to the public Board on 14/07/2026: May 2026 deficit of £3.347m, breakeven to plan; £2.680m of CIP delivered in the month, £0.404m above plan, and £5.081m cumulatively, £0.528m favourable year-to-date. The Board recorded concerns about “the pace of transformational savings, continued reliance on agency staffing” given the scale of savings required during 2026/27. The 2025/26 capital programme was delivered close to plan with a small underspend and the trust ended the year with a strong cash position.

The remainder is transformational, which is where the Board says delivery is slowest and where a supplier with a genuine pathway change has the best hearing. Their integrated structure means acute, community and mental health procurement sit under one executive team. trusts.name: South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: South Tees Hospitals carries a waiting list of 57,120 as at June 2026 (RTT), with 66.5% of patients treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 11.7 weeks, and 707 patients waiting over 52 weeks (12 over 65 weeks, none over 78 weeks). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3 and recorded 5 Never Events. C. difficile cases stood at 106 trust-apportioned against a total of 229 for 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £2,341,000 against a total backlog maintenance figure of £39,349,501. The CQC rating is Good, as recorded in layer-1 (dated 04/08/2026) and consistent with the trust's own 2024/25 annual report, which states it holds an overall rating of Good. For a rep, the combination of a mid-tier oversight segment, a sub-70% 18-week performance and a live, funded estate programme (see structure) points towards elective recovery, diagnostics and capital-equipment conversations rather than a financial-turnaround pitch alone.
trusts.news: The Trust's 2024/25 annual report and accounts (year ending 31 March 2025, published September 2025) records extensive capital investment during the year: a new CT machine installed in the cardiology department at James Cook University Hospital, a full refurbishment of Ward 5, completion of a further phase of the urgent treatment centre waiting and reception areas, and additional CT and MRI diagnostic equipment installed at the new community diagnostic hub at Redcar Primary Care Hospital. The £35.5 million Friarage Surgical Centre was reported as close to handover and on target to open to patients in June 2025. The trust also reported securing £18.95 million of SALIX funding for carbon-saving plant upgrades at James Cook and Friarage, including enhanced glazing at Friarage. Not verified: whether the Friarage Surgical Centre has actually opened as planned, or the current status of the SALIX-funded works, since these are described as in-progress/on-target in the 2024/25 report and no later trust update was checked.
trusts.structure: South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust operates under a joint group model, University Hospitals Tees (UHT), together with North Tees and Hartlepool NHS Foundation Trust. This is CONFIRMED on the trust's own site: the live 'Meet the group board' page at southtees.nhs.uk lists a single set of executive and non-executive directors serving both trusts, and the trust's own news page states the two trusts 'remain as separate organisations, keeping their own existing identities and names' but are 'collectively known as University Hospitals Tees' when working together, with UHT described as the largest health and care employer in the Tees Valley (16,000 staff, budget of around £1.4 billion, serving a population of around 700,000 across the Tees Valley and parts of North Yorkshire and County Durham). The group's joint Chair is Professor Derek Bell OBE and the joint Group Chief Executive Officer is Stacey Hunter, both confirmed live on the group board page (not from a search snippet or a stale annual-report listing). On procurement: the trust's own Procurement page (southtees.nhs.uk/about/procurement/) states in its own words that 'the trust is part of the collaborative procurement network which has been formally established as the procurement organisation for the region', and separately, under its Standing Financial Instructions published on the same page, that the trust uses NHS Logistics/NHS Supply Chain for procurement of goods and services below competitive-tender thresholds unless the chief executive or nominated officers judge it inappropriate, with the decision to use an alternative source required to be documented. Not verified: the trust's procurement page does not name the regional collaborative on that page, so which specific body it is (for example NOE CPC, which serves other North East trusts) could not be confirmed from this source; a supplier would need to raise this directly with South Tees' or UHT's procurement team.

trusts.name: South Tyneside and Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: The waiting list stands at 59,924 with 76.9% treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 8.7 weeks (RTT, June 2026). There are no patients recorded waiting over 52, 65 or 78 weeks in this data. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 2. C. difficile cases stand at 71 against a plan/threshold total of 138 (2024/25). High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £7,673,022 against a total maintenance backlog of £95,596,323. No CQC rating is stated here: layer-1 carries a CQC period date (04/08/2026) but no rating field for this trust, so none is asserted. For a rep, the picture is a mid-tier elective performer with no long-wait cohort to point to, so the opening is more likely to be backlog maintenance/estate risk or infection prevention (C. diff) than elective recovery capacity.
trusts.news: On 11/05/2026 the trust's board and County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust's (CDDFT) board signed a formal strategic alliance agreement. The trust's own news page states both organisations 'will remain as separate legal entities, with their own statutory Boards, responsibilities and accountability', and that over summer 2026 they would work to agree immediate priorities and establish governance arrangements for the alliance, covering a combined population of over 1 million people and around 15,000 NHS staff. Lorraine Nelson (CDDFT's Executive Director of Operations) was seconded to lead alliance development, with Hayley Wardle (this trust's Executive Director of Finance) supporting both organisations. This is a strategic alliance, not a merger or a shared Group-model board of the kind seen at Northumbria or Hull/NLaG: source states each trust keeps its own board. Source: https://www.stsft.nhs.uk/latest-news/our-latest-stories/nhs-trusts-confirm-strategic-alliance-heart-north-east. On finance, the 2024/25 annual report records a Group year-end position of a £15.394m loss (deficit) for the year, driven mainly by a £15.615m downward revaluation charge on land and buildings; after adjusting for that and other technical items, the Group's underlying reported year-end position was a £32,000 surplus, in line with the breakeven plan approved by the Board in May 2024. The trust delivered £33.60m of cost improvement in-year (against a planned £32.7m) and capital expenditure for 2024/25 totalled £27.084m. No 2025/26 annual report has yet been published; all figures above are for 2024/25 and are labelled as such. Source: 2024/25 Annual Report and Accounts, https://www.stsft.nhs.uk/download_file/view/56c88e23-466b-487b-94cd-c6fed4945d60/324 (pages 44-46 of the PDF).
trusts.structure: This trust was itself formed by the 2019 merger of South Tyneside NHS Foundation Trust and City Hospitals Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust (effective 1 April 2019, per the trust's own history and Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyneside_and_Sunderland_NHS_Foundation_Trust); it is not a 2021 merger and there is no separate Group-model board arrangement with another North East trust of the Northumbria type. Instead, the live news page confirms a strategic alliance signed 11/05/2026 with County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust, with both trusts keeping their own separate statutory boards (see news field). Buying: the trust's facilities, procurement and outpatient pharmacy purchasing is run through Choice (CHoICE / City Hospitals Independent Commercial Enterprises Ltd), the trust's wholly owned subsidiary company formed in 2013 and based at Sunderland Royal Hospital. The subsidiary's own page states Choice 'provides a range of services to the Trust, as well as other local organisations', so it buys for this trust and also serves other local bodies; it employs over 1,000 staff across catering, cleaning, portering, facilities, engineering, procurement and outpatient pharmacy. Source: https://www.stsft.nhs.uk/about-us/our-other-companies/choice. This was not inferred: the trust's own subsidiary page states it directly.
