trusts.name: St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: St George's is a large London tertiary centre carrying a big list and a mid-table elective performance. The waiting list stands at 69,326 with 64.8% treated within 18 weeks against the constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 11.9 weeks, 570 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 34 over 65 weeks and 1 over 78 weeks, all for June 2026. Speciality medians for June 2026 show where the pressure actually sits: General Surgery 20.3 weeks, Ophthalmology 17.8, Gynaecology 16.5, ENT 13.5, Cardiology 13.2, Trauma and Orthopaedics 12.1, Urology 11.2 and Dermatology 11.2. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. It reported 6 Never Events for April 2025 to March 2026, the joint highest count in this batch, and 41 trust-apportioned C. difficile cases out of 83 total for 2024/25. ERIC 2024/25 records high-risk backlog maintenance of £24,750,000 within a total backlog of £105,855,000, against capital equipment spend of £9,619,298 in the same year. Commercially that combination points three ways. Six Never Events with a General Surgery median of 20.3 weeks makes theatre safety, checklist and procedural-standardisation propositions unusually easy to open here, because the trust has already commissioned external review of theatre safety. A £24.75m high-risk backlog against under £10m of capital equipment spend means estate risk is being carried rather than bought out, so anything that reduces estate dependency or defers a capital job argues well. And segment 3 means NHS England is watching every spending decision, so a proposal has to be argued on activity delivered or recurrent cash released, never on preference. The layer-1 CQC field carries a snapshot date of 04/08/2026 but no rating value, so the rating is taken from CQC directly and recorded under news rather than asserted here.
trusts.news: CQC rates the trust Requires improvement, from a well-led assessment published on 31/10/2025 and read on the CQC provider page on 28/08/2026. The 2024/25 annual report and accounts, published 12/09/2025, is the most recent set of audited accounts. It reports a deficit of £4.3m in line with plan, but states plainly that this was only possible because of £45.8m of deficit support funding received from NHS England via South West London ICB plus £13.2m of additional non-recurrent monies from the ICB, and that without the deficit support funding the trust would have reported a deficit of £50.1m, which was the planned position. The report names £67.4m of non-recurrent benefits taken in 2024/25 that will not repeat, and says in its own words that the challenge in 2025/26 will be greater than the 2024/25 accounts indicate. The trust delivered its full £68.5m cost improvement programme for 2024/25, 5.5% of operational expenditure, of which £32.3m was non-recurrent, following £60.1m in 2023/24. Capital spend was £47.28m and the report states demand for capital materially exceeded the funds available. The draft 2025/26 plan in that report was a £13.0m deficit and the going concern note records material uncertainties. Fresher than the accounts, the Group Board pack for the meeting in public on 09/07/2026 reports that both trusts delivered their agreed 2025/26 financial plans and Capital Departmental Expenditure Limits, that both remain on plan at Month 2 of 2026/27 but with material pressure on the year-end forecast, and that the Board Assurance Framework finance risk SR1 Financial Sustainability is scored 25 with Limited assurance. The same pack records that NHS Oversight Framework assessments for Quarter 4 of 2025/26 gave both trusts Segment 2 ratings which were then adjusted to Segment 3 by the financial override that caps organisations in deficit. The single biggest service story is the Surgery Strategy 2026 to 2030, which the Group Board was asked to approve on 09/07/2026: Epsom to become a dedicated centre of excellence for short-stay elective and robotic surgery with some operations moving there from St George's, St Helier to become a centre for frailty care and urgent surgery, St George's to concentrate on complex and tertiary surgery, new procedure rooms for local anaesthetic work from 2026, and an increase in the number of surgical robots across the group by 2030. On safety, the 2024/25 annual report records that the trust commissioned reviews from the Royal College of Surgeons to examine theatre safety following a number of Never Events and has developed a set of actions in response.
trusts.structure: Two things matter here and they are different things. First, the group. The trust's own page states that St George's and Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust form the St George's, Epsom and St Helier Hospital Group, styled gesh, formed in late 2021, and that the two trusts 'remain legally separate organisations, each with its own statutory Board' but 'operate with one Group Executive Leadership Team'. The live board members page says St George's 'is governed by a single Group Board' and lists a shared executive with Group titles, and several non-executive directors hold the same chair role at both trusts: Pankaj Dave chairs the joint gesh Audit and Risk Committee, Chiew Yin Jones chairs the People Committee at both trusts, Dr Andrew Murray chairs the Quality Committee at both, and Bidesh Sarkar chairs the Finance and Performance Committee at both. The 2024/25 annual report confirms St George's hosts Group Corporate Affairs, Group Communications, Group Corporate Nursing, Group Corporate Medical and Group Deputy CEO services on behalf of Epsom and St Helier, and the July 2026 Month 2 finance report records a live TUPE of about 100 whole time equivalents from Epsom and St Helier into St George's for group corporate consolidation, so consolidation into St George's is in progress, not theoretical. So one executive team, one board meeting, two statutory boards, and the corporate centre moving to St George's. Second, and separately, procurement. Procurement is NOT held at gesh group level. It is held at a wider South West London level, and St George's is the host. The 2024/25 annual report, Note 1.3 Interests in other entities, states that St George's participates in the 'South West London Procurement Partnership (hosted by St Georges NHS Foundation Trust)'. A live Find a Tender notice published 20/07/2026 for lymphoedema garments and accessories names the buyer as St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust with the South West London Procurement Partnership acting on its behalf, with a named enquiry contact on a stgeorges.nhs.uk address. That is a bigger footprint than the group: the partnership sits alongside South West London Pathology, which the same note confirms St George's also hosts and which covers Croydon, Kingston, Epsom and St Helier and St George's. For a rep, the practical read is that a win routed through the partnership can reach beyond either gesh trust, and that arguing at partnership level rather than departmental level is the higher-leverage move. Do not, however, assume a gesh win is automatically an Epsom and St Helier win. A separate Find a Tender notice for a community audit contract at St George's was published covering St George's only 'with provision to extend to include Epsom and St Helier', which shows contracts are still being let trust by trust with extension options rather than jointly by default. Epsom and St Helier publishes its own buying process page with a procurement helpdesk on 0208 296 4692 and 0208 296 4690 and its own eTendering portal, so the supplier-facing front door is still separate. Not verified: the current full membership and annual spend of the South West London Procurement Partnership. Third-party recruitment and supplier sites describe four partner trusts and a spend figure, but no NHS-published page states it and the trust's own annual report names only the hosting arrangement; the partnership's own governance or hosting agreement, or an FOI to St George's, would settle this. Not verified: the name of the new Chief Procurement Officer. The Group Board pack of 09/07/2026 records the Finance and Performance Committee noting 'the key priority of the new Chief Procurement Officer to make sure the pipeline of contracts is manageable and avoid late extension requests', which tells a rep the post is newly filled and that late extension requests are a live irritation, but the pack does not name the post-holder; the group's declarations of interest register or a direct approach to the procurement team would settle this. Not verified: any published policy for medical representative access, ward visiting or rep booking at either trust. Searches of both trusts' own domains on 28/08/2026 returned no such policy, so no rep access route is asserted here; an FOI request for the trust's commercial representatives policy would settle it. Not verified: any 2025/26 annual report or audited outturn. The 2024/25 accounts published 12/09/2025 are the latest published, so no current-year audited figure is asserted; the 09/07/2026 Group Board pack is used instead for the 2025/26 delivery statement and the Month 2 2026/27 position.

trusts.name: The Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: One of the largest teaching trusts in the UK, running the Royal Victoria Infirmary (including the Great North Children's Hospital and the Great North Trauma and Emergency Centre), the Freeman Hospital (Institute of Transplantation, Northern Centre for Cancer Care, Renal Services Centre), the Newcastle Dental Hospital, Newcastle Fertility Centre and the Northern Genetics Centre. Access performance is the strongest in this batch: a waiting list of 86,740 with 74.6% treated within 18 weeks, a median wait of 9.4 weeks and 702 patients waiting over 52 weeks. NHS oversight segment 3. Safety and infection numbers are less comfortable: 8 Never Events and 157 C. difficile cases. High-risk backlog maintenance stands at £72,648,894. For a rep this is a high-volume tertiary and quaternary account with genuine elective throughput, not a trust in access crisis, so capacity-release arguments land less well here than cost, standardisation and net zero arguments.
trusts.news: The chief executive position is split. Sir James Mackey remains substantively chief executive but is on secondment to NHS England, and Rob Harrison is acting chief executive covering that secondment; the trust's own live board page still showed this arrangement when read on 15/08/2026 (https://www.newcastle-hospitals.nhs.uk/about/board-of-directors-2/board-of-directors/). Sue Hillyard is interim executive director of operations and Jackie Bilcliff took on the interim deputy chief executive role from 01/03/2025 alongside being chief finance officer. The 2024/25 annual report was published in November 2025 and records a break-even position on the NHS England control total basis, with the trust removed from Tier 1 elective support in March 2024 but placed into Tier 2 of NHS England's support framework for cancer and diagnostics performance from February 2025. In September 2024 the trust established a wholly owned subsidiary, Newcastle Hospitals Pharmaservices Ltd, which began trading on 01/12/2024 running an outpatient pharmacy service previously delivered by a third party.
trusts.structure: Procurement is run in-house, not through a shared service and not outsourced. The chief finance officer, Jackie Bilcliff, carries "supplies and procurement" as an explicit named responsibility in her board biography in the 2024/25 annual report, and the trust refers throughout to "our Procurement Team". Its own sustainable procurement page puts annual spend at over £700 million across around 4,000 supply chain companies. The single most important thing for a supplier to know is the gate: it is mandatory for every active tier 1 (direct) supplier to submit carbon data annually by the end of June via a published five-step framework, to register on the SmartCarbon platform using the trust's supplier code NUTHSUPP10, to publish a 2040 net zero commitment, and to publish a carbon reduction plan meeting at least the PPN 006 government template. Social value and net zero are stated as embedded in the procurement strategy, policy and tender processes. Purchased goods and services account for over 85% of the trust's total carbon footprint, so this is a live scoring criterion rather than a formality. Newcastle also sells services outward through a separate commercial arm at commercial.newcastle-hospitals.nhs.uk, with named lines including the North East Innovation Lab, Newcastle Hospitals Biobank, Novopath, Newcastle Hospitals Laboratories, Newcastle Specials (pharmacy production unit), Newcastle Advanced Therapies, the National Centre for Neurotechnology and Neurorestoration, occupational health and data partnerships. That makes the trust a potential partner as well as a customer for diagnostics, cell and gene, and device firms. It also hosts regional infrastructure on behalf of the North East and North Cumbria ICS, specifically the Great North Care Record shared care record and the Connect NENC digital referral platform launched in November 2024, and hosts the North East and Yorkshire Genomic Laboratory Hub contract, which brought in an additional £31 million of income. The 2024/25 report flags clinical supplies as a pressure area, noting medical devices moving onto block funding and more items moving onto the visible cost model - a rep should expect device spend to be scrutinised line by line. Not verified: whether Newcastle procures on behalf of any other trust or hosts a formal collaborative procurement function for the region. The annual report and the trust's public procurement pages say only that the trust "collaborates with other NHS trusts and public sector peers to align approaches", which is not the same as buying for them. A direct enquiry to the procurement team, or a supplier-facing tenders page, would settle it. Not verified: current tender opportunities and the e-tendering portal used, as no public tenders page was located on the trust domain in this session. Not verified: whether the £72,648,894 high-risk backlog maintenance figure appears in the annual report itself - the report confirms capital investment was made to reduce backlog maintenance but does not state a high-risk backlog value, so that figure comes from the ERIC estates return rather than the trust's own narrative.

trusts.name: The Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust
trusts.context: Royal Wolverhampton carries a waiting list of 71,812 with 62.0% treated within 18 weeks against the constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 13.4 weeks and 1,213 patients waiting over 52 weeks, all for June 2026. There are no patients recorded at 65 or 78 weeks, so the tail has been cleared and the problem here is volume and flow rather than extreme breaches. Median waits by speciality for June 2026 are General Surgery 16.5 weeks, Urology 16.4, ENT (Ear, Nose and Throat) 15.9, Gynaecology 15.3, Cardiology 14.9, Ophthalmology 13.6, Trauma and Orthopaedics 10.7 and Dermatology 6.6. The Care Quality Commission rating is Good as at 04/08/2026 and the trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. C. difficile is recorded at 77, against a total of 203, for 2024/25. The 2024/25 Estates Returns Information Collection puts high-risk backlog maintenance at £16,571,675 within a total backlog of £65,422,316, with capital investment in equipment of £3,249,915. Commercially, that pattern points a rep away from crisis-recovery pitches and towards throughput: a Good-rated, segment 3 trust with a long list, no 65-week breaches and surgical and urological medians around sixteen weeks is buying capacity, theatre and outpatient productivity, and day-case conversion, not rescue. The estate numbers say the opposite about buildings: £16,571,675 of the £65,422,316 backlog is classed high-risk, while capital investment in equipment for the same 2024/25 return was £3,249,915, so anything that depends on estate works or a large capital line needs a funded scheme behind it rather than business-as-usual capital.
trusts.news: The trust's own Annual Accounts for 2025/26, published July 2026, state in the Annual Governance Statement that it delivered all of its statutory financial targets, with an end of year surplus of £4.2m, and delivered the capital programme within its Capital Resource Limits. That is a turnaround on 2024/25, where the accounts record a deficit for the year of £12,398,000 and the Foreword shows the breakeven duty missed with a deficit of £12.4m (2023/24: deficit of £18.1m). The 2025/26 auditor's report carries a delay-in-certification paragraph: the auditor cannot issue the audit certificate until work on the trust's consolidation schedules is complete and the National Audit Office confirms the NHS group consolidation audit for the year ended 31 March 2026, while stating this has no material effect on the financial statements. On the previous year, the 2024/25 Annual Governance Statement records that the external auditors 'issued a report stating there were no significant weaknesses with regard to the Trust's processes on Value for Money', with a risk on financial sustainability relating to the uncertainty of the medium-term plans for the Black Country system. The Group Chief Executive's report to the RWT and WHT Group Trust Board in Public on 19/05/2026 sets out the live position: NHS England (Midlands) assessed the two trusts' medium-term plan for 2026 to 2029 as 'Compliant with Conditions', with the non-compliant standards named as ambulance handovers at RWT within 15 and 45 minutes and community waits at both trusts; the plan is balanced only with £16.7m of deficit funding for RWT and £20m for WHT; and the report states 'RWT has moved to NOF 4, largely due to phasing of our financial plan, despite the forecast of a break even position'. The same board pack reports the group has been successful in a bid for additional NHS England capital of £43.71m over four years, allocated to a joint Wolverhampton and Walsall Community Diagnostic Centre at Bilston (£23.15m), a co-located Urgent Treatment Centre with the Emergency Department at Wolverhampton (£8.11m), a Cardiac Cath Lab at Wolverhampton (£6.0m), and community hubs at Wolverhampton (£3.20m) and Walsall (£3.25m). The minutes of the previous meeting record the Group Chief Financial Officer reporting month 11 of 2025/26 with a combined group position of £2.7m, roughly £8m of Integrated Care Board assistance to reach year-end balance, cost improvement delivery of £87m across the group at 93 to 94% of target with a large proportion non-recurring, and a productivity and cost improvement requirement of over 6% for both organisations in the new financial year.
trusts.structure:
The group arrangement is CONFIRMED from the trusts' own board papers, not inferred, and it is bigger than a shared board. The Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust and Walsall Healthcare NHS Trust meet as a single RWT/WHT Group Trust Board and share one executive team: the live board page at royalwolverhampton.nhs.uk carries Group Chairman, Group Chief Executive, Group Deputy Chief Executive and Chief Strategy Officer, Group Chief Financial Officer, Group Chief Medical Officer, Group Chief Safety and Assurance Officer and Group Chief Community and Partnerships Officer. The paper 'Black Country Acute Trusts - Future Group Structure Arrangements' taken to the Group Trust Board in Public on 19/05/2026 states that since 2023 a single shared Chair arrangement has covered the four Black Country acute trusts, that two distinct group models have emerged, the 'Wolverhampton and Walsall Group' and the 'Dudley and Sandwell Group', and asks the four boards to formally recognise and continue that structure, supported by the Black Country Provider Collaborative, and to approve submission of the agreed arrangements to NHS England. The same paper is explicit that this 'does not propose organisational merger or changes to statutory accountability arrangements' and that sovereign boards remain intact. So the group is current, it is formally called the Wolverhampton and Walsall Group, and it sits inside a four-trust Black Country Provider Collaborative under one chair.

Procurement goes further again, and this is the fact that matters most to a rep. Royal Wolverhampton does not run its own procurement function. Its published procurement policy, OP15 (SP01) version 2.0 approved June 2025 and hosted on the trust's own site, is the policy of the North Midlands and Black Country Procurement Group (NMBC). It records that UHNM (University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS Trust) and RWT created NMBC on 01/07/2019 and that NMBC 'is hosted by UHNM'; that Walsall Healthcare and the RWT-hosted Black Country Pathology Service procurement teams joined on 01/12/2021 after a formal management of change; and that Black Country Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust followed on 01/01/2024, when all its supplies and procurement staff TUPE transferred into UHNM. The policy states the integrated model now covers six organisations with approximately 140 staff, an annual trust income of £3.09 billion and approximate annual spend of £1.107 billion, spanning the Staffordshire, Shropshire, Stoke-on-Trent and Black Country ICS footprints. The policy also says 'The NMBC is the Trusts primary source of contact and channel of communication with all suppliers' and that 'Supplier representatives will be seen only by appointment, as unscheduled sales calls are of little or no benefit to either party'. Access is credentialed: the policy names the Medical Industry Accredited (MIA) system as in use across RWT, UHNM and Walsall Healthcare, requires all commercial supplier representatives to register visits via www.miaweb.co.uk with at least 24 to 48 hours' notice, to hold and visibly wear a valid MIA ID card, and to be registered at Gold MIA level for theatres, cardiac catheterisation labs, intensive care or any area where invasive procedures take place. Walsall Healthcare's own live procurement page separately tells suppliers they are 'strongly advised to contact the Procurement department in the first instance, prior to visiting any departments' and says the trust buys through the Black Country (Procurement) Alliance. Practically: a win at Royal Wolverhampton is negotiated through a procurement function that buys for two group trusts and for four further organisations beyond the group, and a rep cannot walk into a Wolverhampton theatre without a Gold MIA credential.

The trust is also unusual in running primary care directly. Its live primary care page states that as of 01/04/2025 eight GP practices are part of the trust, named as Alfred Squire Road Health Centre, Coalway Road Surgery, Lea Road Medical Practice, Oxley Surgery, Penn Manor Medical Centre, Thornley Street Surgery, Warstones Health Centre and West Park Surgery, under a vertical integration model. The 2024/25 annual report confirms the board takes a standing item on GP Vertical Integration and lists 'the continued vertical integration of GP practices' among its strategic matters, and the trust also hosts Black Country Pathology Services, a single pathology service run with Dudley, Sandwell and West Birmingham and Walsall. For a rep that means primary care consumables, diagnostics and pathology reagents at this trust are bought through the same acute procurement route rather than through a GP federation.

Not verified: whether the four sovereign boards subsequently approved the 19/05/2026 future group structure paper and whether it has been submitted to NHS England; the minutes of the four boards' meetings after May 2026 would settle this. Not verified: the trust's current NHS oversight segment. The layer-1 data records segment 3, while the Group Chief Executive's report of 19/05/2026 states RWT has moved to NOF 4 with the expectation that the successful year end would rectify that for quarter 4; the current NHS England oversight segmentation publication would settle which is live now. Not verified: the name of the NMBC Group Director of Procurement. The OP15 policy names the role as author and the Group Chief Finance Officer as executive lead but gives no personal name, and no NMBC contact page was found; a direct approach to UHNM procurement, or the NMBC Procurement Board papers, would settle it. Not verified: whether Gillian Farr, published on Walsall Healthcare's live procurement page as Head of Procurement, remains the right first contact for the Wolverhampton side of the group given that procurement staff TUPE transferred into UHNM; her page does not mention NMBC. reportFacts.fact: Royal Wolverhampton has no procurement function of its own. Buying is done by a shared team hosted by another trust entirely, covering six organisations across two integrated care systems. This is the single most important commercial fact here: a win negotiated at Wolverhampton is negotiated with a team that also buys for Walsall Healthcare, University Hospitals of North Midlands, Black Country Healthcare, North Staffordshire Combined Healthcare and Black Country Pathology Services, so the conversation belongs at NMBC level and not with a Wolverhampton department.

reportFacts.fact: Site access is credentialed and gated, and unscheduled sales calls are refused as a matter of published policy. A rep without a Gold MIA card cannot enter theatres, cath labs or intensive care at Wolverhampton, Walsall or UHNM. Sorting the credential is a prerequisite to selling, not an afterthought, and this is also the practical mechanism by which one credential gets a rep into three acute trusts.

trusts.name: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: Do not sell to this trust as a standalone organisation. ULTH and Lincolnshire Community Health Services NHS Trust operate as the Lincolnshire Community and Hospitals NHS Group, and the Group Board is “the joint board and decision-making body for both statutory organisations” — a single set of group executives covers finance, operations, estates and clinical governance across both. It sits in NHS oversight segment 4 and stayed there at the Quarter 4 2025/26 ratings published in June 2026, with a 70,206 waiting list, 61.9% within 18 weeks and 1,113 people over 52 weeks. The commercial picture is not simply distress, though: the trust over-delivered its savings plan in 2024/25 and fully spent an £88.1m capital programme, and has an unusually visible pipeline of new-build diagnostic and theatre capacity.
trusts.news: The Group Board meeting of 07/07/2026 reported an £8.1m deficit at month two, in line with plan, and confirmed ULTH remained in oversight segment 4 at the Quarter 4 National Oversight Framework ratings while LCHS dropped from segment 2 to 3. The ULTH Electronic Patient Record implementation is “continuing at pace”, with first go-live scheduled for October 2026 and parallel digitisation of existing paper records. The Lincolnshire Community Diagnostic Centre programme now runs CDCs at Grantham, Skegness and Lincoln with a fourth being built at Boston. The Lincolnshire system formally exited Urgent and Emergency Care Tier 2 oversight in May 2026. Implementation of the new Patient Services Hub has been temporarily paused while problems are worked through. The 2025/26 annual report and accounts had been submitted but not yet published when this profile was written.
trusts.structure: Buying decisions sit at group level, not trust level — approach Lincolnshire Community and Hospitals NHS Group, and expect a proposition to be tested against both an acute and a community trust. Group Chief Finance Officer Paul Antunes Goncalves came from 16 years at Nottingham University Hospitals, most recently as Director of Finance, so he will already know the supplier base of a large Midlands teaching trust. Capital is governed through a Capital Delivery Group reporting to the Finance, Performance and Estates Committee, with quarterly reporting, and the capital prioritisation process is informed by the six-facet estate survey — a backlog-maintenance case has a defined route here. Estates is the standout capital relationship: Group Chief Estates and Facilities Officer Mike Parkhill has run the largest capital programme in the trust's history, covering the Lincoln County emergency department, urgent treatment centre and respiratory support unit, new theatres at Grantham, the Grantham CDC, the new Pilgrim emergency department and the Lincoln and Skegness CDCs. Not verified: the trust has a Head of Procurement, named as a contributor to its modern slavery statement, but the post-holder is not publicly named and no procurement team structure is published; nor is any e-tendering portal or supplier representative booking system named on the trust's public site, and not publishing one is not proof there isn't one.

trusts.name: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: The strongest financial position in this batch and the only segment 1 trust in it — a £17m surplus in 2025/26 and £329m of cash at 31 March 2026. It is also the best performer on access here: 65.0% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 11.9 weeks and 884 people over 52 weeks on a 77,531 list. That combination makes it a capital play rather than a cost-cutting one. But read the outlook before assuming an easy year: the trust calls 2026/27 “extremely challenging” and faces a recurrent savings requirement of £92.6m to break even, which it describes as “an unprecedented level of challenge”. Its commissioner also changed on 01/04/2026, when North Central London ICB merged with North West London to form West and North London ICB.
trusts.news: UCLH was chosen by the Department of Health and Social Care as the launch site for its programme to cut reliance on single-use items, with the minister shown reusable and remanufactured theatre products in a mock theatre on site — reusables, remanufacture and Design for Life are live procurement priorities here, not aspirations. The trust is also leading the procurement and commissioning of a PACS shared in common across North Central London hospitals, and a national first-in-type scheme integrating Epic with the national e-prescription service, due to let patients collect UCLH prescriptions from community pharmacies in 2027.
trusts.structure: Procurement sits under Tim Jaggard, deputy chief executive and chief financial officer, who signed the 2025/26 accounts on 25/06/2026. Sustainability is an explicit and published part of buying decisions: the trust commits to “ensure sustainability forms a greater part of our procurement decision-making”, to “meet or exceed NHS England's procurement roadmap”, to increase reuse and remanufacture while reducing single-use, and to engage suppliers to pilot more sustainable items. Supply-chain emissions are the largest part of a 202,818 tCO₂e carbon footprint, with net zero for indirect and supply-chain emissions targeted by 2040. The trust uses NHS Terms and Conditions and weighs modern slavery factors in procurement decisions. It pays well by NHS standards — 91% of invoices by volume and 96% by value paid to terms in 2025/26. Several large buys run at North Central London level rather than trust level, PACS being the current example, so check whether your category is bought by UCLH alone before targeting it. Not verified: whether a rep booking or accreditation system operates — UCLH publishes no supplier representatives policy and no e-tendering portal of its own on its public site, and not publishing one is not proof there isn't one. Also not reconciled: the trust's own annual report declares five never events between April 2025 and March 2026, which differs from the NHS England provisional count in the data panel above; the two are compiled on different bases and neither has been adjusted here.

trusts.name: University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: University Hospital Southampton sits in the middle of the pack for elective pressure among large specialist trusts. The waiting list stands at 63,323 with 65.3% treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 11.7 weeks, 1,397 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 155 over 65 weeks and 8 over 78 weeks, as at June 2026 (RTT period). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3 and reported 7 Never Events (April 2025 to March 2026) and 93 cases of C. difficile against a total of 186 recorded for the trust (2024/25). High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £9,515,170 against a total estate backlog of £164,863,046. CQC rated the trust 'Good' as at 04/08/2026. For a rep, the combination of a mid-table 18-week position with a live major trauma and specialist-services remit means capacity conversations here compete against genuinely complex tertiary caseload, not simple backlog, so any pitch needs to be argued on releasing clinician or theatre time rather than on volume alone.
trusts.news: The 2024/25 Annual Report and Accounts (year ended 31 March 2025) records a deficit of £7.0m against a revenue position of over £1.5bn, after receiving £11.2m of non-recurrent deficit support funding from NHS England; the plan had been for a £3.3m deficit, so the trust missed its own financial plan. In the same year the trust delivered a record cost improvement programme of £85.3m (6% of turnover), described in the report as its highest ever level of CIP delivery, while stating that recurrent savings delivery 'remains a key challenge' and that the underlying deficit persists once one-off support and non-recurrent measures are stripped out. Total capital expenditure for 2024/25 was £96m, including investment in expanded neonatal facilities, decarbonisation schemes, theatres and a new aseptic pharmacy facility, much of it externally funded; the trust also secured a further £19m of Public Sector Decarbonisation Fund money for 2025/26. No 2025/26 annual report has been published yet, so all financial figures above are for 2024/25 and are labelled as such; do not read them as the current-year position.
trusts.structure: UHS buys through a shared subsidiary, not alone and not through a wider Hampshire-wide group model. Wessex NHS Procurement Ltd (WPL), on its own 'About us' page, states it provides 'end-to-end procurement and supply chain services' for two owning trusts, University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust and Hampshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, covering strategic sourcing, tendering, contract support, goods receipting, distribution, inventory and materials management from four sites: Basingstoke, Winchester, Andover and Southampton. Companies House confirms Wessex NHS Procurement Limited (company number 11986173) was incorporated in May 2019, registered at UHS's own Trust Management Offices address, Tremona Road, Southampton. UHS itself remains a standalone foundation trust for governance and clinical decision-making, with its own Trust Board (not a shared board-in-common with HHFT), so procurement is pooled at subsidiary level while clinical and executive leadership stay separate. Not verified: WPL's total influenceable non-pay spend or staff headcount figure (unlike the Humber and North Yorkshire Procurement Collaborative, WPL's own site does not publish these); a direct enquiry to WPL would settle it. Not verified: whether HHFT retains independent clinical sign-off on products sourced through WPL, or whether product standardisation decisions bind both trusts equally; WPL's governance documents, not its public 'About us' page, would settle this. Live tender activity confirms the arrangement is operating in practice: Find a Tender notices for UHS contracts, including a taxi services tender and a Private Patient Unit joint-venture procurement, are run in WPL's name on UHS's behalf.

reportFacts.fact: UHS is a designated major trauma centre and one of only two places in the south of England offering full major trauma care for both adults and children, alongside specialist services (neurosciences, respiratory medicine, cancer, cardiovascular, obstetrics, specialist children's services) reaching nearly four million people across central southern England and the Channel Islands. This is the context for any specialist or high-acuity product conversation here: the buying decision-makers are used to tertiary, not routine, caseload.
reportFacts.figure: Turnover of £1.5 billion in 2024/25; one of the largest acute teaching trusts in England
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, Overview, 'About the Trust: Our services'

reportFacts.fact: The trust missed its own financial plan and only avoided a larger deficit with NHS England support, despite a record savings delivery. A proposal here has to show recurrent cash release, not headline activity, because the trust's own report names recurrent savings delivery as 'a key challenge'.
reportFacts.figure: Deficit for the year of £7.0m against a planned deficit of £3.3m, after £11.2m of non-recurrent deficit support funding and delivery of an £85.3m (6%) cost improvement programme, the highest in the trust's history

reportFacts.fact: Clinical consumables spend fell year on year while drugs spend rose sharply. This is the line a device or consumables rep is competing for, and its direction (down, while general supplies and drugs both rose) suggests the trust is already actively managing this budget rather than letting it drift, so a standardisation or cost-per-use argument will land better than a simple volume pitch.
reportFacts.figure: Supplies and services, clinical (excluding drugs) £105,834,000 in 2024/25, down from £130,598,000 in 2023/24; drug costs £236,916,000 in 2024/25, up from £195,367,000 in 2023/24

reportFacts.fact: Capital spend of £96m in a single year, much of it externally funded, shows real money moving through theatres, neonatal capacity, decarbonisation and pharmacy infrastructure. A rep with a capital-funded product should track the trust's annual capital programme cycle (set each year alongside the CIP) rather than pitching cold.

trusts.name: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: Four hospitals — Queen Elizabeth Birmingham, Heartlands, Good Hope and Solihull — and one of the largest trusts in England. Financially it is under formal NHS England scrutiny: the trust reported an overall deficit of £69.5m in 2024/25 and, on the adjusted measure NHS England judges it on, a £0.9m surplus reached only after a Financial Recovery Plan agreed in September 2024 in response to an £81.4m adjusted deficit at month eight. It is rated 4 — Investigation and Intervention — under the NHSE Rapid Intervention process. The savings that got them there do not repeat: over half were non-recurrent, so the same gap reopens each year. A trust that needs recurrent, provable savings, not one-offs.
trusts.news: The 2024/25 accounts record control weaknesses that delayed the draft accounts and the audit, causing the trust to miss the national timetable. Clinical supplies spend rose to £251.3m. No 2026/27 board papers were publicly locatable on the trust's website as at 14/08/2026 — unlike Leeds and Nottingham, UHB does not publish an accessible board pack archive, so the current-year position here is not verified. Ask your contact directly rather than assuming the 2024/25 picture still holds.
trusts.structure: UHB does not buy only for itself. It hosts the BSol Procurement Collaborative, which provides procurement and supply chain services across the Birmingham and Solihull ICS to five trusts: UHB, Birmingham Women's and Children's, the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital, Birmingham Community Healthcare, and Birmingham and Solihull Mental Health. Win a category here and you have addressed five organisations at once; equally, the other four are not separate ways back in if you lose it. The Collaborative is led by Simon Clarke, Managing Director, whose senior management team reports into a quarterly Partnership Board, chairs the BSol Procurement Collaborative Operational Delivery Group, and approves significant contracts and major projects. UHB describes it as one of the first procurement teams to work across an entire ICS, winner of the HCSA 2023 Procurement and Supply Chain Team of the Year, and holder of a 'Good' CCIAF procurement standards accreditation. Five teams are published, each with its own inbox, so a supplier can approach the right function directly: Strategic Procurement (BSOLCategoryTeams@uhb.nhs.uk), which agrees CIP targets with finance leads and produces strategic sourcing documents and contract award reports; the Clinical Procurement Specialist team (ProcurementCPSTeam@uhb.nhs.uk), clinical experts reporting to a Head of Clinical Procurement who source alternatives during stockouts and national shortages and drive standardisation across the ICS; Data Analytics, Catalogue and Systems (ProcurementData@uhb.nhs.uk), which owns the BSol Master Products Catalogue and is therefore the route to getting a product code listed at all; Transactional Procurement (BSOLProcurementBuyers@uhb.nhs.uk), with set buyers per trust across six different ordering systems; and Pharmacy Procurement (Pharmacy.Procurement@uhb.nhs.uk and BuyingOfficePharmacy@uhb.nhs.uk). UHB's own procurement page was last reviewed 05/09/2024, so confirm the named post-holder is still in place before using it. Unusually, each of the four hospitals has its own Hospital Executive Director sitting outside the main Board — Matt Metcalfe (Queen Elizabeth), Dr Rifat Rashid (Heartlands), Simon Jarvis (Good Hope) and Martin Richardson (Solihull). That matters for targeting: a site-level conversation has a named owner, and a trust-wide pitch has four internal customers, not one. Efficiency is benchmarked through the national Reference Cost Index, GIRFT and Model Hospital data, and the trust says this is shared with the hospital sites for planning — so GIRFT and Model Hospital comparators are the language that lands here. Payment performance is mid-range: 76.9% of non-NHS invoices paid within target by volume, 73.4% by value in 2024/25. Not verified whether UHB runs a rep booking or accreditation system, or which e-tendering portal it uses.

trusts.name: University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust
trusts.context: UHCW carries a waiting list of 72,093 with 57.9% of patients treated within 18 weeks, against a constitutional standard of 92%, a median wait of 14.9 weeks, 2,276 patients waiting over 52 weeks, 31 over 65 weeks and none over 78 weeks (NHS England Referral to Treatment, June 2026). Waits are very unevenly distributed by speciality: ENT sits at a median of 22.6 weeks, Gynaecology 19.4, Urology 17.5 and Ophthalmology 16.4, while Cardiology is 9.5 and Dermatology 7.0 (same June 2026 return). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier. It recorded 2 Never Events (NHS England, April 2025 to March 2026) and 52 trust-apportioned cases of C. difficile out of 132 total cases (UK Health Security Agency, 2024/25). Estate risk is comparatively modest by acute standards: high-risk backlog maintenance of £250,000 within total backlog maintenance of £24,777,000, alongside £1,670,000 of capital investment in medical equipment (NHS England Estates Returns Information Collection, 2024/25). Commercially that combination points a rep at a specific set of doors rather than the whole trust. The elective gap is real and concentrated in ENT, gynaecology, urology and ophthalmology, so capacity, theatre productivity and day-case throughput arguments have a named problem attached to them in those four specialities and much less traction in cardiology or dermatology. The low high-risk backlog figure means the classic estate-failure pitch does not land here. And segment 4 means every spending decision is visible to NHS England, so any proposal has to be argued on activity delivered or cash released, not on clinical preference.
trusts.news: UHCW has published a full Annual Report and Accounts for 2025/26, approved and signed on 18 June 2026, so a current-year outturn is available and no figure here is carried forward from the prior year. The single most significant item in it is in the auditor's report: KPMG record that on 11 June 2026 they made a referral under section 30(1)(b) of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 to the Secretary of State, and notified NHS England, on the basis that the trust's draft financial statements indicated it would be in breach of its breakeven duty for the financial year ending 31 March 2026. The audit opinion on the accounts was nonetheless unqualified and, on value for money, KPMG identified one significant risk relating to financial sustainability but no significant weakness in arrangements. On the numbers, the trust reported a statutory deficit for the year of £16.501 million, an adjusted deficit of £6.020 million against a plan of £11.000 million, and a cumulative breakeven duty position of minus £57.914 million. It delivered total savings of £76.6 million including £38.2 million recurrent, and has set a £74.5 million productivity and efficiency programme for 2026/27 alongside a break-even ambition. The Chief Executive's own foreword confirms placement in segment four, describes it as disappointing, and reports the National Oversight Framework metric score improving from 3.01 in the first quarter to 2.58 in the final quarter while the overall ranking fell to 101st. Service-change items a rep should track: a new Community Diagnostic Centre at the City of Coventry Health Centre, due to open in late 2026, expected to serve around 90,000 patients a year and provide up to 75,000 additional tests annually; continued optimisation of the Electronic Patient Record implemented in June 2024; and work with George Eliot Hospital NHS Trust and South Warwickshire University NHS Foundation Trust towards a single EPR with shared patient records across the local system. Capital in 2025/26 was tightly bounded, with a Capital Resource Limit of £39.5 million spent exactly on target and total gross capital expenditure of £39.9 million.
trusts.structure: UHCW buys for itself. It is not part of a group model, it does not host a shared procurement service for other trusts, and its 2025/26 annual report describes system working with George Eliot Hospital NHS Trust, South Warwickshire University NHS Foundation Trust and Coventry and Warwickshire Partnership NHS Trust as partnership and care collaborative activity, not as joint procurement. The trust's published buyer profile, the Active Procurements page, states that the Procurement and Supplies Department uses the In-tend e-tendering suite at https://in-tendhost.co.uk/uhcw and standardised tender documentation, advertises above-threshold contracts in the official journal and below-threshold contracts on Contracts Finder, and gives a single generic route in: Contracts@uhcw.nhs.uk, Procurement Department, FM Building, Clifford Bridge Road, Coventry CV2 2DX. The same page states the trust spends approximately £110 million a year on medical and non-medical products, surgical products and services, excluding catering, linen, cleaning, buildings, maintenance and utilities. Treat that £110 million with care: the page is undated and demonstrably stale, listing current tenders that closed in October 2017, a procurement strategy covering 2013 to 2018 and thresholds framed under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 rather than the Procurement Act 2023, which the trust's own 2024/25 annual report notes came into effect in February 2025. Use In-tend and Find a Tender for live opportunities, not this page. The single most important structural fact for a device or equipment rep is the PFI. The 2025/26 accounts confirm the trust operates a Private Finance Initiative contract for the construction, operation and maintenance of University Hospital Coventry, including the provision of a significant proportion of the medical and other equipment used in the hospital. The principal contract party is Coventry and Rugby Hospital Company, which in turn contracts hard facilities management to Mitie, soft facilities management to ISS Mediclean, and equipment to GE Medical Systems. The contract terminates on 31 December 2042, and soft facilities management is market tested under the PFI contract every seven years. The practical consequence is that a large slice of equipment replacement at University Hospital runs through the PFI lifecycle fund rather than the trust's own capital programme, so the buying route depends on which asset you are replacing. The Hospital of St Cross at Rugby is also covered by the PFI for those facilities services. For clinical consumables the named gate is the trust's Clinical Procurement Evaluation Group, which the annual report says manages the adoption of new or alternative clinical products in the trust and provides governance for decisions made at the single use items group; assessments explicitly include reusability, recyclability and carbon footprint, and the annual report records a minimum 10% social value weighting on competed tender exercises. Not verified: the name of any current procurement post-holder. The trust publishes no named procurement contact, only the Contracts@uhcw.nhs.uk mailbox, and the layer-1 contacts extract for RKB is empty, so no individual buyer is named here. A direct approach to that mailbox, or the trust's declarations of interest register, would settle this. Not verified: whether Clinical Procurement Evaluation Group papers, membership or meeting cycle are published anywhere; nothing on the public site sets out how a supplier gets an item onto its agenda, and only a direct request to the procurement team would settle this. Not verified: the precise split between what is replaced through the PFI lifecycle fund and what the trust buys directly for any given equipment category; the accounts give only the annual totals, and the PFI equipment schedule held by Coventry and Rugby Hospital Company would settle this. Not verified: the trust's current CQC rating. The layer-1 extract carries a CQC record date of 04/08/2026 but no rating value, so none is asserted here. Note on reading the trust's own website: WebFetch is blocked with HTTP 403 on uhcw.nhs.uk pages, so the live board and procurement pages here were read with a browser user agent via curl on 28/08/2026, and the PDFs were downloaded and extracted locally.

reportFacts.fact: A large part of the equipment at University Hospital Coventry is replaced through the PFI lifecycle fund, with GE Medical Systems as the contracted equipment provider, not through the trust's own capital programme. In 2025/26 the PFI lifecycle fund spent roughly twice what the trust spent on medical and other equipment directly. For an equipment rep this is the difference between a winnable conversation and a wasted year: identify which route your asset sits on before you pitch, because the trust's own capital line is the smaller of the two and the PFI route runs through Coventry and Rugby Hospital Company.
reportFacts.figure: Equipment assets provided through the PFI lifecycle fund £8.5 million, against Medical and other equipment £4.3 million, in 2025/26. The PFI consortium's equipment contractor is GE Medical Systems, with hard facilities management by Mitie and soft facilities management by ISS Mediclean, under principal contract party Coventry & Rugby Hospital Company (CRHC). The PFI contract terminates on 31st December 2042.

reportFacts.fact: The trust's auditors referred it to the Secretary of State over a breach of its breakeven duty. This is a harder external signal than a going-concern comment or a value-for-money weakness, and it sits on top of NHS oversight segment 4. Any proposal that cannot be argued as recurrent cash released or activity delivered will not survive scrutiny at this trust in 2026/27, however good the clinical case.
reportFacts.figure: On the 11 of June 2026 KPMG made a referral under section 30(1)(b) of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 to the Secretary of State, and notified NHS England, on the basis that the trust would be in breach of its breakeven duty for the financial year ending 31 March 2026. Cumulative breakeven duty position at 31 March 2026: minus £57,914,000. Statutory deficit for the year £16.501 million; adjusted deficit £6.020 million against a plan of £11.000 million.

reportFacts.fact: Clinical and general supplies is the line a device or consumables rep is competing for, and it grew faster than the trust's overall cost base. That growth is exactly why cost-per-procedure, standardisation and switch arguments land better here than feature arguments, and it is the number to quote when asking for a conversation with the Clinical Procurement Evaluation Group rather than a single department.
reportFacts.figure: Clinical and general supplies and services (including drugs and other medical/surgical consumables) £218.3 million in 2025/26, up from £205.5 million in 2024/25, an absolute increase of 6.2% and approximately 19% of day-to-day operating expenses, against total operating expenditure growth of 4.3%

reportFacts.fact: The trust has a live, quantified efficiency programme for the year a rep is selling into, and it has a track record of hitting the number. That is a buying signal, not just a warning: a proposition that plugs into a £74.5 million programme with a named recurrent-savings problem has a route to a business case, while one that adds cost does not.
reportFacts.figure: A £74.5 million productivity and efficiency programme for 2026/27, supporting a break-even outcome, following total savings of £76.6 million in 2025/26 of which £38.2 million was recurrent
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26, section 2.5.9 Financial Outlook, and the Chief Finance Officer's statement opening section 2.5

reportFacts.fact: There is a named, dated diagnostic capacity scheme with a stated volume, which is the clearest single opening at this trust for diagnostics, imaging, point-of-care and pathway suppliers. reportFacts.figure: A new Community Diagnostic Centre at the City of Coventry Health Centre, opening in late 2026, to bring tests closer to home for around 90,000 patients each year and provide up to 75,000 additional tests annually once open. Community Diagnostic Centres accounted for £1.4 million of the trust's 2025/26 capital expenditure.

trusts.name: University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: University Hospitals Dorset's RTT waiting list stood at 67,354 patients as at June 2026, with 67.6% treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 12.2 weeks and 671 patients waiting over 52 weeks (no patients recorded over 65 or 78 weeks). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 3. It reported 64 cases of C. difficile against a locally set threshold, out of 209 cases across the wider Dorset system, for 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £389,016 against a total estates backlog of £65,738,637, with a further £1,316,309 attributed to equipment-related backlog risk (ERIC 2024/25). The specialties with the highest proportion of patients waiting over 18 weeks are Gynaecology (17.1%) and Trauma & Orthopaedics (16.5%), with ENT at 14.5% and Ophthalmology at 11.1%. For a rep, this is a trust running a very large, live capital reconfiguration programme (see below) alongside a moderate but real elective backlog, in a system where segment 3 gives more local discretion than segment 4 but still under national oversight.
trusts.news: UHD is partway through the Clinical Services Review, the Dorset-wide reconfiguration that is consolidating planned and emergency care onto separate sites at Poole and Royal Bournemouth Hospital. In 2024/25 the Trust fully opened the One Dorset Pathology Hub, took handover of the BEACH Building for radiology, opened a new main entrance and completed the link road at Royal Bournemouth Hospital, and started work on an Endoscopy Hub at Poole; capital expenditure for the year was £157m against a £157m plan, of which £115m related to the Acute Reconfiguration Programme (source: UHD Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25, page 31, https://www.uhd.nhs.uk/uploads/comms/Publications/uhd_annual_report_and_accounts_24-25.pdf). Separately, the Care Quality Commission rated Poole Hospital's maternity service 'inadequate' (down from 'good') following inspections in autumn 2024, citing insufficient midwifery and medical staffing at times and issues with incident investigation and emergency call-bell systems; it also served the trust a warning notice on the trust's arrangements to summon help in an emergency, which the trust has since acted on. This finding was published on the CQC's press release page, last updated 19 May 2025 (https://www.cqc.org.uk/press-release/cqc-finds-improvement-needed-university-hospitals-dorset-nhs-foundation-trust). This is a service-specific rating for Poole maternity, not a trust-wide rating: layer-1 for this trust carries no overall CQC rating, and the trust's own published overall provider-level rating summary is dated 4 June 2021, over five years old, so no current trust-wide CQC rating is asserted here (https://www.uhd.nhs.uk/about-us/cqc). In January 2026 UHD also published a preliminary market engagement notice for a Private Oncology Service Concession, seeking a long-term partner to occupy an empty linac bunker at Poole (and potentially Dorchester) for private oncology care, with an estimated tender publication date of 25 February 2026 (https://www.find-tender.service.gov.uk/Notice/007807-2026). On governance, Judy Gillow MBE has held the Trust Chair role on an interim basis since 1 May 2025.
trusts.structure: UHD currently procures for itself: the trust is named directly as the contracting authority on its own Find a Tender notices, including one published as recently as 29 January 2026 (https://www.find-tender.service.gov.uk/Notice/007807-2026). However, a Dorset-wide shared-service model is actively in development. UHD's own 2024/25 Annual Report describes a business case, not yet approved at the time of writing, for a single shared service across Dorset covering Estates, Facilities and Procurement (EFMP), intended to be delivered as a subsidiary company while keeping staff on NHS Agenda for Change terms (page 22, https://www.uhd.nhs.uk/uploads/comms/Publications/uhd_annual_report_and_accounts_24-25.pdf). UHD's own 2025/26 Operational Plan (board version) confirms this project is live and being 'worked up', with a preferred option developed and subject to Boards' approval before subsidiary companies (subcos) are set up (https://www.uhd.nhs.uk/uploads/about/docs/our_publications/6.1b_2025-26_uhd_operational_plan_v0.1_draft_master_version_for_updating_by_leads_1.1.pdf). Board papers from partner trust Dorset County Hospital NHS Foundation Trust record that a 'One Dorset Procurement Business Case' and a 'Dorset Shared Services Business Case' were both approved as decisions at its 8 April 2025 board meeting (https://dchft.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/DCH-Board-of-Directors-8-04-2025-part-1.pdf). Not verified: whether that April 2025 partner-trust approval has since been matched by UHD's own board sign-off, or whether the shared procurement service has actually gone live as of August 2026, since UHD's more recent operational plan still describes the project as in development rather than delivered. A rep should treat UHD as buying for itself today, while watching for the shared Dorset procurement service to formalise. UHD sits within the wider Our Dorset Provider Collaborative alongside Dorset County Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Dorset HealthCare University NHS Foundation Trust and South Western Ambulance Service NHS Foundation Trust, chaired throughout 2024/25 by UHD's own Chief Executive, Siobhan Harrington; the Collaborative has no delegated decision-making authority from any partner Trust Board or the ICB (UHD Annual Report and Accounts 2024/25).

trusts.name: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: Seven hospitals and community services across Sussex, close to 20,000 staff. It carries the hardest access position in this batch — 116,122 on the waiting list, only 53.2% within 18 weeks and 4,636 people waiting over 52 weeks — and sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the tier requiring mandated support. 2025/26 closed at a £4.9m surplus on the control-total basis agreed with Sussex ICB, but the trust delivered only £96.8m of a £109m efficiency target. The 2026/27 plan is a £140m efficiency programme the trust says will focus “largely on cost reduction”. Anything that removes cost or releases theatre and outpatient capacity has a stated, funded audience here.
trusts.news: Signed a seven-year contract with Alcidion for the Miya Precision EPR platform, announced 25/06/2026, with phased introduction from spring 2027 across seven hospitals and c. 20,000 staff — the first NHS trust to include Alcidion's Virtual Care module in an EPR programme. A Laboratory Information Management System procurement and a Trust-wide Electronic Records & Document Management System are both named as live programmes in the 2025/26 annual report, as are two new Southlands theatres to increase day-case capacity.
trusts.structure: Tenders run through the LPP eSourcing portal (lppsourcing.org) and Contracts Finder; the trust tells suppliers to register with NHS Commercial Solutions and Contracts Finder as “the locations for all tenders run by the Trust at present”. Unusually for this batch, three supplier-facing policies are published openly: a Supplier Representatives’ Policy (UHSFN011), a Medical Device, Medical Equipment and Product Trials Policy (UHSFN010), and a “No PO, No Pay” letter to suppliers — read all three before a first visit. Category buyers are named on individual notices rather than in a published team list; the trust's own guidance is to “email the buyer stated within the tender document”. A sustainable procurement policy is in force, tied to a Carbon Footprint Plus baseline of 185,667 tCO₂e. Procurement-led savings were £6.5m in 2025/26. Not verified: whether the Supplier Representatives' Policy operates a booking or accreditation system — the policy is published but the document itself has not been read, so the mechanism is unconfirmed. Also not reconciled: the trust's own annual report records nine never events for April 2025 to March 2026, which does not match the NHS England provisional count in the data panel above; the two are compiled on different bases and neither figure has been adjusted to fit the other.

trusts.name: University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: One of the larger acute trusts in the Midlands, with group income of £1,351.887m and an average of 13,890 whole-time-equivalent staff in 2024/25. Operationally it is under pressure: a waiting list of 96,379 with only 61.4% treated within 18 weeks, a median wait of 13.4 weeks and 1,782 patients waiting over 52 weeks. It sits in NHS oversight segment 4 (mandated support), the most intensive tier, which means NHS England is directly involved in its recovery. Quality signals are mixed: 5 Never Events and 131 cases of C. difficile in the period. Estate risk is material, with £14,683,291 of high-risk backlog maintenance outstanding. For a supplier, the commercially important point is that segment 4 status and a 5% efficiency requirement mean every proposition has to be framed around cost release, productivity or waiting-list throughput, not incremental clinical preference.
trusts.news: The trust's own news feed through 2026 has been dominated by productivity and digital stories rather than capital expansion. In May 2026 it reported a national award for a digital system credited with getting patients faster care, over 11,000 patients receiving faster care through staff-led improvement, a further boost to on-site solar power, and recognition for use of the CareScan tool. Also in May 2026 CQC rated Derby and Burton services 'Good'. Earlier in the year the reported innovations were clinical-pathway ones: home phototherapy sleeping bags for babies with jaundice (June 2026) and innovative voice therapy for Parkinson's Disease (April 2026). In the 2024/25 year the trust opened a new centre at Royal Derby Hospital after £10m of construction and a £5.1m facility including an Open MRI scanner described as one of only two of its kind. Source: https://www.uhdb.nhs.uk/latest-news/ and the 2024/25 Annual Report and Accounts.
trusts.structure: The single most valuable structural fact is that UHDB is not only a buyer for itself, it is a host of procurement for others. The trust hosts the East Midlands Pharmacy Collaborative (EMPC), described on its own page as 'a small dynamic procurement team providing a Pharmacy procurement service for its member Trusts', covering twelve member trusts: Chesterfield Royal Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust, Kettering General Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Leicester Partnership NHS Trust, Northampton General Hospital NHS Trust, Northamptonshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust, United Lincolnshire Hospitals NHS Trust, Sherwood Forest Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Derbyshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust and Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust. For a pharma supplier this means a single tendering route at UHDB can reach twelve trusts across the East Midlands, and that losing at UHDB can mean losing far more than one trust's volume. UHDB is also part of Joined Up Care Derbyshire, the system within which its control total and deficit support were agreed. Non-pharmacy procurement (medical and surgical equipment, dressings, laboratory) appears from the annual report to run as the trust's own function, with spend reported by eClass category. Live board titles were taken from the trust's own board page on 15/08/2026 and supersede the annual report, which still lists Andrew Hall as Executive Chief Operating Officer and Debbie Loke as Executive Chief Digital Information Officer; the live page now shows Paran Govender and Andy Carruthers in those roles. Not verified: whether UHDB has a published 'selling to us' or supplier registration page, or which e-tendering portal it uses. Searches restricted to uhdb.nhs.uk returned no procurement or tenders page, and guessed URLs on this site 404 rather than redirect. trusts.name: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust
trusts.context: One of the largest acute trusts in the country and, on the numbers, one of the hardest-pressed in this batch: 115,259 on the waiting list, 60.1% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 14.0 weeks, 2,402 people over 52 weeks, and NHS oversight segment 4. It is also a serious deliverer of savings — £69.4m of cost improvement in 2024/25, after £64.2m, £35m and £17.1m in the three years before — but it has never yet hit the ask, and the 2025/26 target is £92m. Capital is large and consistent, running at £75m to £122m a year. The trust's own stated goal for the year is blunt: “Reduce pay and non-pay costs by £92m.” A proposition that cuts non-pay cost recurrently is aimed directly at a published target here.
trusts.news: For 2025/26 the Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland system plan forecasts an £80m deficit, of which UHL accounts for £65m, on an assumed £92m cost improvement programme — and the trust states plainly that “long term financial sustainability is dependent upon CIP improvements being delivered recurrently”. The New Hospital Programme investment at UHL has been deferred by up to three years, leaving only £1.5m of previously committed NHP funding in the 2025/26 capital allocation. Several executives now hold 'Group' titles — Group Chief Nurse, Group Chief Digital Information Officer — so confirm whether a decision in your category is UHL's alone or made across a wider group before targeting it. Not verified: the 2025/26 annual report and accounts had not been published when this profile was written, so no current-year outturn is stated.
trusts.structure: The most useful thing UHL publishes is its list of senior clinical leaders by service line, which gives a named clinical director for most device-relevant specialities without any need to guess: Chris Allsager for Critical Care, Theatres, Anaesthesia, Pain and Sleep; Monika Kaushik for Musculoskeletal and Specialist Surgery; Kate Hodgson for Cancer, Haematology, Urology, Gastroenterology and General Surgery; Rob Davies for Renal, Respiratory and Cardiovascular; Prashanth Patel for Clinical Screening and Imaging; Jonathan Cusack for Women's and Children's; and Neeta Patel for Emergency and Specialist Medicine. That is the clinical champion, and the trust names them itself. Sustainability is a formal part of buying: the trust has implemented carbon reduction requirements for new procurements, formed a Sustainable Procurement Working Group, and secured representation at LLR system level, with Supply Chain and Procurement run as one of its named sustainability workstreams. It pays suppliers well, at 93% against the Better Payments Practice Code. Not verified: no e-tendering portal or supplier representative booking system is published on the trust's public site. Note also that Find a Tender notices are frequently published against a single central inbox (uhl-tr.uhlprocurementopportunities@nhs.net) rather than a named buyer's own address, so the contacts panel above will often route to a team rather than an individual.

trusts.name: University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS Trust
trusts.context: A £1.29bn-income trust across Royal Stoke University Hospital and County Hospital in Stafford, with around 1,450 inpatient beds, in NHS oversight segment 3. The access position is mid-table for this batch — 72,002 waiting, 63.0% within 18 weeks, a median wait of 13.1 weeks, 1,360 people over 52 weeks. The fact that shapes every commercial conversation here is the Section 30 referral: because of a cumulative deficit, the trust's external auditors referred it to the Secretary of State for Health in June 2021, and that referral was still in place through 2024/25. Expect scrutiny of any spend, and expect recurrent savings to be valued far above one-off ones — the trust says its 2024/25 position “relied heavily on non-recurrent cost improvement scheme delivery and other one-off benefits”.
trusts.news: The trust ended 2024/25 with an £11.8m deficit against a breakeven plan and has appointed a Recovery Director alongside a revised Urgent and Emergency Care improvement programme. Its County Elective Hub has significantly increased procedure numbers, with day case activity running at 107.4% of plan — the elective hub is the growth point. On the supply side, the Procurement Team's Energy Procurement Partnership with Stoke-on-Trent City Council cut a potential £10m cost pressure to around £3m and has been extended for a further two years, and the second and final phase of the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme put £3m into air source heat pumps, LED lighting and solar at Royal Stoke as part of a £5.4m programme. Not verified: the 2025/26 annual report and accounts had not been published when this profile was written, so no current-year outturn is stated.
trusts.structure: The most useful thing to know about this procurement team is that it co-develops products with suppliers rather than only buying them. Its published example is the Eco Box, developed jointly with the trust's anti-embolism stockings supplier: they removed the dye to save energy, water and chemicals, stripped the plastic packaging, trialled it on wards, and then adapted the format again after patients said they preferred individually wrapped take-home packs — projected saving 7.8 tonnes of plastic and 10 tonnes of cardboard a year. A supplier arriving with a sustainability redesign proposal has a proven precedent to point at. Procurement also sits inside the monthly Sustainability Working Group structure, and the team runs supplier awareness work on Modern Slavery Act compliance as part of onboarding new suppliers, so expect that check when trading for the first time. Financial performance, cost improvement schemes and capital schemes are all standing monthly items at the non-executive-led Performance and Finance Committee, which is where a large business case will be seen. Estates, Facilities and PFI are held together by one director, and the trust describes “exemplar relationships” with its PFI partners. Not verified: no e-tendering portal or supplier representative booking system is published on the trust's public site, and not publishing one is not proof there isn't one.

trusts.name: Worcestershire Acute Hospitals NHS Trust
trusts.context: As at the June 2026 RTT reporting period, the trust's waiting list stood at 58,478 patients, with 62.9% treated within 18 weeks against the constitutional standard of 92%. Median wait was 13.2 weeks. 609 patients were waiting over 52 weeks, 3 over 65 weeks and 1 over 78 weeks. The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the most intensively supported tier of the NHS Oversight Framework. It recorded 102 trust-apportioned cases of C. difficile against a total of 241 cases in 2024/25, and 2 Never Events in the period April 2025 to March 2026. High-risk backlog maintenance stood at £14,194,541 against a total backlog maintenance liability of £71,853,140. By specialty, the widest waits recorded were Ear, Nose and Throat (17.9%), Trauma and Orthopaedics (16.9%) and Urology (15.1%) treated within 18 weeks, all well below the national standard.
trusts.news: The trust's 2024/25 annual report and accounts (signed 24 June 2025) show a statutory deficit for the year of £621,000, against £76,649,000 the year before, but the improvement is largely a financing and impairment effect: on the adjusted control-total basis used for the breakeven duty, the deficit was £5,484,000, in line with a planned deficit of £5.7m. The independent auditor, Grant Thornton, reported in its 26 June 2025 report on arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness that a significant weakness in financial sustainability first identified on 25 June 2024 remains in place: although the trust delivered its £45.1m savings plan for 2024/25, 23% of that was achieved non-recurrently, and of the £53.0m savings target set for 2025/26 (6.6% of operating costs), 73% was classified high risk and 15% unidentified at year end. The auditor also confirmed that a separate significant weakness identified in September 2021, over high bank and agency staffing costs and the lack of a sustainable workforce strategy, also remains in place. On 7 June 2024 the auditor referred a matter to the Secretary of State under Section 30 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 over the trust's ongoing breach of its breakeven duty. Separately, the 2024/25 annual report records a fire safety risk at the Alexandra Hospital that resulted in an Enforcement Notice from the Fire Authority; the Board agreed an improvement and oversight plan backed by capital investment, and the trust states it continues to engage closely with the Fire Authority. On leadership, the trust's live board page (checked 28/08/2026) shows Frances Martin took up the Chair role on 1 April 2026, a role she holds jointly across Worcestershire Acute and Wye Valley NHS Trust, replacing the previous chair named in the 2024/25 annual report; that report was itself signed by an Acting Chief Executive, and the live page now shows Sir Glen Burley as the substantive Group Chief Executive with Stephen Collman as Managing Director, so any executive named in the FY2024/25 document should be treated as superseded. Not verified: the identity of the chair named in the 2024/25 annual report and the exact date they stood down; the live board page does not name a predecessor.
trusts.structure: Worcestershire Acute Hospitals NHS Trust is a full member (since August 2023, having been an Associate Member from 2021) of the 'Foundation Group', confirmed on the trust's own live board pages. The Group also comprises South Warwickshire University NHS Foundation Trust and Wye Valley NHS Trust (founding members, 2017) and George Eliot Hospital NHS Trust (joined 2018). All four share one Group Chief Executive, Sir Glen Burley. The Chair role is shared more narrowly: the live board page states Frances Martin 'has taken up the Chair role across both Worcestershire Acute Hospitals NHS Trust and Wye Valley NHS Trust' from 1 April 2026, not across the full four-trust Group. Day-to-day executive leadership at Worcestershire Acute sits with Stephen Collman, Managing Director since November 2023. On buying: the trust's own FOI disclosure page states plainly that it 'use[s] a combination of Frameworks depending on the Service required - Health Trust Europe, NHSSBS and NHS Supply Chain would be the main frameworks', indicating the trust runs its own procurement decisions through national and regional frameworks rather than a single delegated buying body. Its 2024/25 annual report separately discloses that transactional Procurement Services, run on the iProc (Oracle) ordering system, are outsourced to a third-party supplier alongside Finance and Accounting and Payroll, with that supplier's ISAE3402 assurance reports reviewed by the Chief Finance Officer in April 2025; the supplier is not named in the annual report itself. One concrete cross-Group procurement vehicle is confirmed: HealthTrust Europe LLP acts as a central purchasing body on behalf of the 'South Midlands Pathology Network', a group covering University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire, South Warwickshire, George Eliot, Worcestershire Acute and Wye Valley, which in July 2025 awarded a joint Cellular Pathology Managed Service Contract. This is pathology-specific and should not be read as evidence of a single procurement function covering all trust spend. The trust also sits in the Herefordshire and Worcestershire Integrated Care System alongside Herefordshire and Worcestershire Health and Care NHS Trust and Wye Valley NHS Trust; no evidence was found on the trust's own site of a single ICS-wide procurement function beyond this ICS partnership listing. Not verified: the identity of the third-party supplier running the outsourced iProc/Finance/Payroll services (widely reported elsewhere as NHS Shared Business Services, but this was not confirmed on the trust's own site during this session). Not verified: whether Herefordshire and Worcestershire ICS operates a shared procurement service across its three trusts; only the ICS partner list itself was found live.
