trusts.name: York and Scarborough Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
trusts.context: York and Scarborough's waiting list stands at 56,467 with 59.0% treated within 18 weeks against the 92% constitutional standard, a median wait of 14.0 weeks and 1,087 patients waiting over 52 weeks (RTT position, June 2026; no 65 or 78-week breaches recorded). The trust sits in NHS oversight segment 4, the mandated-support tier, and reported 97 cases of C. difficile against a threshold-relevant total of 248 in 2024/25. High-risk backlog maintenance is carried at £20,689,181 against a total backlog maintenance liability of £114,524,322 (ERIC, 2024/25). The CQC rating on file is Requires Improvement, dated 2026-08-04. Worst-performing specialities against the 18-week standard are General Surgery (3.7%), Urology (14.4%) and Cardiology (14.0%), with Gynaecology also under pressure at 17.6%. For a rep, this is a trust under national mandated support with a live elective backlog and an estate-risk profile that includes a major RAAC (Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete) eradication programme, but segment 4 means every spending decision is visible to NHS England and has to be argued on activity delivered or cost released.
trusts.news: The Trust's Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26 (year ended 31 March 2026) records a change of Chief Executive: Simon Morritt retired in September 2025 after joining in August 2019, and Clare Smith took up the post at the end of November 2025. Martin Barkley has chaired the Trust since November 2023 and remains in post. The Trust's financial outturn for 2025/26 was a reported income and expenditure deficit of £33.1m (Group: £33.135m), reducing to £32.3m (Group: £32.293m) after NHS England's technical adjustments. The external auditor's report on arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness for the year ended 31 March 2026 found a significant weakness in financial sustainability remains, first identified for 2024/25 and unresolved: the Trust reported a £32m deficit, its three-year plan forecasts further deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, and the 2026/27 planned deficit depends on delivering £54m of savings through the Waste Reduction and Productivity programme. Against a 2025/26 Cost Improvement Programme target of £55.29m (a £25.35m core efficiency requirement plus a £29.939m central efficiency programme), the Trust over-delivered the core target by £9.156m but fell short on the central programme by £23.947m, giving total delivered efficiencies of £40.498m, described in the report as the highest level the Trust has ever delivered. The 2025/26 capital programme totalled £88.2m planned against £87.2m outturn expenditure, including circa £48m of Public Dividend Capital secured for RAAC eradication at Scarborough Hospital.
trusts.structure: York and Scarborough buys through a shared function, not entirely alone, but it is structurally distinct from Hull and Northern Lincolnshire and Goole (NLaG), which operate as a merged Group with one shared executive team (NHS Humber Health Partnership). York and Scarborough retains its own trust board, its own Chair (Martin Barkley) and its own Chief Executive (Clare Smith) and has not joined that Group model. What it does share is procurement: the Trust's own 2025/26 Annual Report states the Group 'continued to participate in collaborative procurement arrangements through the Hull and North Yorkshire procurement collaborative' and that 'Partner Trusts remain committed to developing a more integrated procurement model' (emphasis on ongoing development, not a completed merger), and separately describes itself as 'part of the Hull & North Yorkshire (HNY) procurement collaborative, which has been set up to provide procurement and supply chain services to 8 hospitals across the ICS (Integrated Care System)'. The collaborative's own page (hosted on the Northern Lincolnshire and Goole site) names York and Scarborough as one of three Partner Trusts, states it is 'managed through a Procurement Board which has representation from each Partner Trust and is accountable to each of the three Trust Boards', and gives the same headline figures used in the Hull profile: 119 staff and £538m of annual influenceable non-pay spend. On the hint under test: whether York and Scarborough defers fully to the collaborative for buying, and whether it retains its own clinical sign-off, is still Not verified either way. The collaborative's own page does not state how far individual trusts can deviate on clinical product choice, and York's Annual Report does not resolve it either, though it does note the collaborative engages 'care groups through Procurement Business Partners and Clinical Procurement Specialists', which reads as clinical input feeding into a shared process rather than proof that local clinical sign-off is bypassed. What is now settled, that was not settled in the Hull entry, is that York and Scarborough is not part of the Hull/NLaG Group governance structure, only the procurement collaborative; its Board, Council of Governors, Chair and Chief Executive are its own. A direct approach to the collaborative's Procurement Board terms of reference, or to York and Scarborough's own Resources Committee papers, would settle the clinical sign-off question definitively.

reportFacts.fact: York and Scarborough is one of three Partner Trusts in a shared procurement function covering an annual influenceable non-pay spend of £538m, but unlike Hull and NLaG it has not merged its board or executive team into the collaborative's host organisation, so the buying relationship and the governance relationship are not the same thing here.
reportFacts.figure: 119 procurement staff managing £538m of annual influenceable non-pay spend across Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, Northern Lincolnshire and Goole NHS Foundation Trust and York and Scarborough Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
reportFacts.where: Humber and North Yorkshire Procurement Collaborative page, sections describing the function, partner trusts and governance

reportFacts.fact: Clinical consumables spend rose by £4.316m year on year, a 4.6% rise, while the drugs bill also grew. Both lines sit in a trust reporting a significant financial sustainability weakness, so any proposal in this space needs to be argued on recurrent savings or activity released, not feature preference.
reportFacts.figure: Supplies and services - clinical (excluding drugs costs) £97,353,000 in 2025/26, up from £93,037,000 in 2024/25; drug costs £78,060,000 in 2025/26, up from £77,231,000 in 2024/25
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26, Notes to the Accounts, Note 6 Operating Expenses (Group)

reportFacts.fact: The external auditor has now confirmed, for a second consecutive year, an unresolved significant weakness in the Trust's financial sustainability arrangements, with further deficits planned through 2027/28. This is the context a rep needs before pitching any non-essential spend: cost improvement delivery is under direct external scrutiny.
reportFacts.figure: Reported income and expenditure deficit of £33.1m (Group £33.135m; £32.3m/£32.293m after technical adjustments) for the year ended 31 March 2026; three-year plan forecasts further deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28 with the 2026/27 plan reliant on £54m of savings
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26, Independent Auditor's Report, 'Matter on which we are required to report by exception', and Statement of Comprehensive Income

reportFacts.fact: The Trust over-delivered its core, locally-led efficiency target but fell substantially short on the central, cross-organisational programme (bed occupancy, workforce deployment, non-recurrent spend). That split is useful for a rep: locally-led, care-group-level savings are landing; centrally-driven structural savings are not.
reportFacts.figure: 2025/26 Cost Improvement Programme of £55.29m (core £25.35m plus central £29.939m): core over-delivered by £9.156m, central fell short by £23.947m, total delivered £40.498m, described as the highest level of efficiencies the Trust has delivered to date
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26, Performance Report, Cost Improvement Programme (CIP) section

reportFacts.fact: A large share of the year's capital spend was defensive estate risk (RAAC eradication), not new clinical capacity, which matters for any capital-funded proposition: the Capital Programme Executive Group's near-term priority has been securing an at-risk building, and headroom for discretionary capital spend should be checked before pitching.
reportFacts.figure: 2025/26 Capital Plan of £88.2m, year-end outturn expenditure of £87.2m, including circa £48m of Public Dividend Capital secured for Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (RAAC) eradication at Scarborough Hospital
reportFacts.where: Annual Report and Accounts 2025/26, Capital Projects Department overview
